div.p: You have often asked me, dearest Innocentius, not to keep silent about the marvel of that event which fell within our own age. When I refused, both modestly and truthfully — as I now find by experience — and despaired of being able to do it, whether because all human speech is inferior to praise that is heavenly, or because idleness, like a kind of rust upon the mind, had blunted even the small talent I once had for eloquence, you on the contrary argued that in the things of God one ought not to look at the possibility but at the spirit, and that he who had believed in the Word could never run short of words.

The page ought not to divide those whom mutual love has joined together, nor should the courtesies of my speech be parcelled out to each of you one by one, since you so love one another that love unites three of you no less than nature has bound two. Indeed, if the nature of the case allowed it, I would shut you all under one stroke of the pen, an undivided name, since your letters too summon me in such a way that I count three in one and one in three. For after the holy Evagrius forwarded them and they were brought to me in that part of the desert which draws its vast frontier between the Syrians and the Saracens, I so rejoiced that I outdid that day of Roman happiness on which, in the battle of Marcellus at Nola, the first since the field of Cannae, the proud columns of Hannibal were cut down. And although the brother named above often visits me and cherishes me as his own heart in Christ, yet, parted from me by a long stretch of road, in going away he has left me no less longing than in coming he had brought me joy.

With what zeal and love I strove that we might dwell together in the desert, the heart that shares our mutual love well knows. With what laments, with what grief, with what groaning I followed you when you were gone, these very pages are witnesses, which you see smudged here and there with my tears. But you, like a spoilt little child, fed your contempt of the one who begged you with flatteries, and I, taken off guard, did not know what to do then. Should I be silent? But I could not, with any restraint, conceal what I so ardently wanted. Should I plead more urgently? But you were unwilling to listen, because you did not love in return as I did. The one thing that was possible, scorned love has done. It could not keep you when you were present, so it seeks you when you are gone. Since, then, you yourself at your departure had asked that, once I had moved to the wilderness, I should send you an invitation written by my hand, and I had promised to do so — here is my invitation: now make haste. I do not want you to recall the obligations of the past — the desert loves the naked. I do not want the difficulty of your former journey to frighten you. You who believe in Christ, believe also his words: "Seek first the kingdom of God, and all these things shall be added to you." You need take no wallet, no staff; he is rich in abundance who is poor with Christ.

\"Hearken, O daughter, and see, and incline your ear; and forget your own people and your father's house; and the king shall desire your beauty.\" In the forty-fourth psalm God speaks to the human soul, that after the example of Abraham it should go out from its own land and from its kindred and leave the Chaldeans — who are interpreted as \"like demons\" — and dwell in the land of the living, for which the prophet sighs elsewhere, saying: \"I believe I shall see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living.\" But it is not enough for you to go out from your homeland unless you also forget your own people and your father's house and, despising the flesh, are joined to the embraces of the Bridegroom. \"Do not look back,\" he says, \"and do not stay anywhere in the surrounding country; make for the mountain, lest you be caught.\" It is not fitting, when one has set hand to the plough, to look back over the shoulder, nor to return home from the field, nor, having put on Christ's tunic, to come down from the housetops to take another garment. A great marvel: a father exhorts his daughter, \"Do not remember your father.\"

\"You are of your father the devil, and you wish to do the desires of your father,\" is said to the Jews; and elsewhere: \"Whoever commits sin is of the devil.\" Begotten first of such a parent, we are black; and after repentance, before we have yet climbed to the summit of virtue, we say: \"I am black and beautiful, O daughters of Jerusalem.\" I have gone out from the house of my infancy, I have forgotten my father, I am born again in Christ. What reward do I receive for this? It follows: \"And the king shall desire your beauty.\" This, then, is that great mystery: \"For this cause a man shall leave father and mother and shall cleave to his wife, and the two shall be\" — in one flesh? No longer, as there, in one flesh, but in spirit. Your Bridegroom is not arrogant, not proud: \"He took an Ethiopian woman to wife.\" As soon as you wish to hear the wisdom of the true Solomon and come to him, he will confess to you all that he knows, and the king will lead you into his chamber, and, your colour wondrously changed, that saying will fit you: \"Who is this that comes up made white?\"

Abraham is tested in his son and is found the more faithful for it; Joseph is sold in Egypt so that he may feed his father and his brothers; Hezekiah is carried to the brink of death so that, dissolved in tears, he may have his life extended by fifteen years; the apostle Peter is shaken by the Lord's passion so that, weeping bitterly, he may hear the words, "Feed my sheep"; Paul, a ravening wolf and the youngest son of Benjamin, is blinded in a trance so that he may see, and, hemmed in by a sudden horror of darkness, he calls upon the Lord whom a moment before he had been persecuting as a mere man.

Surgeons, as they call them, are thought cruel, and they are wretched men. For is it not misery to grieve over wounds that are not one's own, and to cut away dead flesh with a merciful blade? Is it not misery that the healer does not shrink from what the sufferer himself shrinks at, and is reckoned an enemy for it? Such is the way of nature: truth is bitter, while vices are accounted sweet. Isaiah, as an example of the captivity to come, does not blush to go about naked; Jeremiah is sent from the midst of Jerusalem to the Euphrates, the river of Mesopotamia, that among hostile nations, where the Assyrian is and the camps of the Chaldeans stand, he may lay down a girdle to be spoiled; Ezekiel is commanded to eat bread sprinkled with every kind of seed, baked first over human dung and then over cow dung, and he watches the death of his wife with dry eyes; Amos is driven out of Samaria—and why, I ask? Surely for this reason, that these spiritual surgeons, by cutting away the vices of sinners, were urging them on to repentance. The apostle Paul says: "Have I become your enemy by telling you the truth?" And because the words of the Savior seemed harsh, many of his disciples drew back.

Ambrosius—by whose supplying of paper, expenses, and copyists Adamantius, truly our own "Man of Brazen Bowels," set forth so countless a number of books—relates in a certain letter, which he had written to that same man from Athens, that he never took a meal in Origen's presence without a reading, that sleep never came upon him unless one of the brethren was sounding out the sacred Scriptures, and that this was his practice by day and by night, so that the reading took up the prayer and the prayer the reading.

If I should think that thanks could be returned to you by me, I would have no sense. God is able, over and above my own poor person, to repay your holy soul what it deserves. For I, unworthy as I am, could never have reckoned on or even hoped for so great a love as you would lavish on me in Christ. And although certain people think me a criminal, overwhelmed with every disgrace—and even these are too little for my sins—yet you do well in that out of your own goodness you think even the wicked good. For it is dangerous to pass judgment on another man's servant, and there is no easy pardon for having spoken ill of the upright. That day will come, it will come, when you will grieve with me that not a few are burning.

You ask me, dearest Nepotian — you ask in letters from across the sea, and ask repeatedly — to set out for you in a short book the precepts of living, and to show by what method a man who has left the world's military service and begun to be either a monk or a cleric may hold to the straight path of Christ and not be swept aside into the various byways of the vices. When I was a young man — indeed, almost a boy — and was reining in the first onsets of a wanton age by the hardship of the desert, I wrote to your uncle, the holy Heliodorus, a letter of exhortation, full of tears and complaints, such as might show the feeling of a deserted companion. But in that work I played the part of my years, and, while still warm with the studies and teachings of the rhetoricians, I painted certain things with the flower of the schools. Now my head is white and my brow lined, and the dewlaps hang from my chin like an ox's: The chill blood stiffens around my heart;
and so the same poet sings elsewhere: Time bears away all things, the mind as well; and shortly after: Now so many songs are gone from my memory, and even my voice fails Moeris.

You implore me in a letter, and entreat me as a suppliant, to write to you — or rather to write back — how you ought to live and to preserve the crown of widowhood with the name of chastity unimpaired. My mind rejoices, my heart leaps, my affection exults that you desire to be, after your husband, what your mother Titiana of holy memory was for a long time while her husband lived. Her prayers and supplications have been heard. She has obtained in her only daughter what she possessed while alive. You have, besides, the great distinction of your family: that from Camillus onward it is written that none — or hardly any — of your house has known a second marriage, so that you are not so much to be praised if you persevere as a widow, as to be cursed if, as a Christian, you do not keep what for so many ages heathen women have preserved.

Great themes are not borne by small talents, and in the very attempt, having dared beyond their strength, they sink down; and the greater the thing to be said, the more is he overwhelmed who cannot unfold the magnitude of the matter in words. My Nepotian, yours, ours — nay, Christ's, and because he is Christ's, therefore the more ours — has left behind old men, and, wounded by the dart of longing for him, has worn them out with intolerable grief. Him whom we thought our heir, we hold as a corpse. For whom now shall my talent sweat? Whom shall my little writings be eager to please? Where is that taskmaster of ours, and the voice sweeter than the swan's song? My mind is stunned, my hand trembles, my eyes grow dim, my tongue stammers. Whatever I say, since he will not hear it, seems mute. The very pen, as if feeling it, and the wax, somewhat sadder, are overspread with rust or mould. As often as I strive to burst forth into words and to scatter the flowers of this epitaph over his tomb, so often my eyes fill, and with renewed grief I am wholly at his funeral. It was once the custom that over the bodies of the dead the children should speak their praises in the assembly from the rostra, and, like mournful songs, should rouse the breasts of the hearers to weeping and groaning: behold, the order of things is changed for us, and to our calamity Nature has lost her rights: what a young man should have rendered to old men, this we old men render to a young man.

It is now several years since, while the wound was yet fresh, I consoled Paula, that venerable woman, upon the falling asleep of Blesilla. The circuit of the fourth summer is rolling round since, in writing to Heliodorus the bishop the epitaph of Nepotian, I spent in that grief whatever strength I could have. About two years ago I gave my Pammachius a short letter on the sudden departure of Paulina, blushing to say much to so eloquent a man and to thrust his own back upon him, lest I should seem not so much to console a friend as, by foolish vainglory, to instruct a perfect man. Now, my son Oceanus, you lay a debt upon one willing and even seeking it of his own accord, that, on account of the novelty of her virtues, I should make old matter new. For in those former cases the affection of a parent, or the mourning of an uncle, or the longing of a husband had to be tempered, and, according to the diversity of the persons, a different medicine from the Scriptures had to be applied.

The blessed apostle Paul, writing to the Corinthians and instructing the untrained Church of Christ in sacred discipline, among his other commands set down this one too, saying: If any woman has an unbelieving husband, and he consents to dwell with her, let her not put away her husband. For the unbelieving husband is sanctified in the believing wife, and the unbelieving wife is sanctified in the brother. Otherwise your children would be unclean, but now they are holy. If to anyone the bonds of discipline have hitherto seemed too loosely relaxed and the indulgence of the teacher headlong, let him consider the house of your father — a most distinguished and learned man indeed, but still walking in darkness — and he will understand that the Apostle's counsel has so far prevailed that the sweetness of the fruits has compensated for the bitterness of the root, and the shoots of the vine have sweated precious balsams. You are born of an unequal marriage; from you and my Toxotius Paula was begotten. Who would have believed that the granddaughter of the pontiff Albinus should be born from the promise of her mother, that, with the grandfather present and rejoicing, the little one, her tongue still stammering, should sing alleluia, and that the old man should cherish in his bosom a virgin of Christ? We have waited well and happily. A holy and faithful house sanctifies the one unbeliever. He is a candidate of the faith whom the throng of his believing children and grandchildren surrounds. I think that even Jove himself, had he had such a family, might have been able to believe in Christ. Let him spit upon and laugh at my letter, and cry out that I am either a fool or a madman; this her son-in-law too used to do before he believed. Christians are made, not born. The gilded Capitol grows filthy; soot and spiders' webs have covered all the temples of Rome; the city is moved from its foundations, and the overflowing people, before the half-ruined shrines, run to the tombs of the martyrs. If prudence does not wring out faith, let shame at least wring it out.

A certain brother from Gaul told me that he had a sister, a virgin, and a mother, a widow, who, dwelling in the same city in separate cells, had taken to themselves certain clerics as patrons, either because of the loneliness of lodging alone or to guard their little fortunes, so that they were joined to strangers with greater disgrace than they had been separated from each other. And when I groaned, and signified by silence far more than by speaking, he said: "I beg you, rebuke them by a letter of yours, and call them back to concord, that the mother may acknowledge the daughter, the daughter the mother." To whom I said: "You enjoin upon me an excellent province, that I, a stranger, should reconcile those whom a son and a brother could not — as though I held an episcopal chair and were not shut up in a cell and removed far from the crowds, either lamenting my past faults or striving to avoid the present ones. But it is also unfitting to lie hidden in body and to wander through the world by the tongue." And he: "You are too fearful," he said; "where is that former firmness in which, rubbing the city down with much salt, you reported something Lucilian?" "This is the very thing," I say, "that drives me off and does not allow me to part my lips. For after, by reproving crimes, I became a criminal myself, and, according to the well-worn proverb of the common people, with all swearing and denying — 'You love me, and I neither believe it nor touch it' — and the very walls echoed back curses against me, And they who drank wine sang against me, compelled by this evil I learned to keep silence, thinking it better to set a guard upon my mouth and a fortified door upon my lips than to incline my heart to words of malice and, while I carp at vices, to fall into the vice of detraction." When I had said this, he replied: "It is not detraction to speak the truth, nor does private rebuke make general doctrine, since either rare or none is he who falls under the guilt of this fault. I beg you, then, not to suffer me, worn out by so long a journey, to have come in vain. For the Lord knows that, after seeing the holy places, I had this for my chief cause: that by your letters you should restore me to my sister and my mother." And I said: "Now, now I will do what you wish; for the letter is for those across the sea, and a discourse specially dictated can find few whom it may sting. But I warn you to keep this discourse secret. And when you have carried it as provision for the road, if it be heard, let us rejoice together; but if it be despised — which I rather think — I shall have lost my words, you the length of your journey."

Nothing is happier than the Christian, to whom the kingdoms of heaven are promised; nothing more toilsome, who daily is in peril of his life. Nothing is stronger than he who conquers the devil; nothing weaker than he who is overcome by the flesh. Of both these things there are very many examples. The thief believed on the cross, and at once deserved to hear: Amen, amen I say to you: today you shall be with me in paradise. Judas slips from the height of the apostolate into the hell of betrayal, and is broken neither by the intimacy of the meal nor by the dipping of the morsel nor by the grace of the kiss, so as not to betray as a man one whom he had known to be the Son of God. What is cheaper than the Samaritan woman? Not only did she herself believe, and after six husbands find one Lord, and recognize the Messiah at the well whom the people of the Jews in their temple knew not, but she becomes the author of the salvation of many, and, while the apostles were buying food, she refreshes the hungry one and sustains the weary one. What is wiser than Solomon? And yet he is befooled by the loves of women. Salt is good, and no sacrifice is received without its sprinkling — whence the Apostle too commands: Let your speech be seasoned with salt — but if it lose its savour, it is cast out, and so loses the dignity of its name that it is not useful even on the dunghill, with which the fields of believers are wont to be enriched and the barren soil of souls to be fattened. We say these things, that at the very first we may teach you, my son Rusticus, that you have begun great things, are pursuing lofty ones, and, trampling on the incentives of youth — nay, of puberty — are climbing a step indeed of the perfect age; but the road by which you enter is slippery, and the glory after victory is not so great as the disgrace after a fall.

Often and much do you demand, Principia, virgin of Christ, that I should recall in writing the memory of the holy woman Marcella, and describe, for others too to know and imitate, the good which we long enjoyed. And I grieve enough that you exhort one running of his own accord, and think that I, who would not yield even to you in love for her, and who receive far more benefit than I bestow in the remembrance of such great virtues, have need of entreaty. For that I have hitherto kept silence and passed over two years in silence was not, as you ill suppose, the part of indifference, but of an incredible sorrow, which so oppressed my mind that I judged it better at present to be silent than to say nothing worthy of her praises. Nor will I praise your Marcella — nay, mine, and, to speak more truly, ours, and the renowned glory of all the saints, and especially of the city of Rome — by the rules of the rhetoricians, so as to set forth her illustrious family, the glory of high blood, and the pedigrees running down through consuls and praetorian prefects. I will praise nothing in her except what is her own, and the nobler in this, that, having despised wealth and nobility, she became nobler by poverty and humility.

It is a difficult business to write to a little girl who does not understand what you say, whose soul you do not know, of whose will you make promises at peril — so that, according to the opening of a distinguished orator, the hope in her is more to be praised than the reality. For why should you exhort to continence one who longs for cakes, who babbles with prattling voice in her mother's lap, to whom honey is sweeter than words? Should she hear the deep things of the Apostle, who is delighted rather by old wives' tales? Should she perceive the riddles of the prophets, whom the sadder face of her bearer frightens off? Should she understand the majesty of the Gospel, at whose lightnings every sense of mortals was dulled? Should I exhort her to be subject to her parent, who with tender hand strikes her laughing mother? Therefore let our Pacatula receive this little letter to read afterward; for the present let her only learn the elements of the little letters, join syllables, learn nouns, link words together; and, that she may rehearse these with ringing voice, let a little cake of honey be set before her as a reward, and let her hasten to take whatever is sweet to the taste, whatever blooms in flowers, whatever glows in gems, whatever charms in dolls; meanwhile let her also try with her tender thumb to draw out the threads, let her often break the strands, that one day she may not break them; after labour let her exult in play, let her hang from her mother's neck, let her snatch the kisses of her kinsfolk, let her sing psalms for a reward, let her love what she is compelled to say, that it may be not a task but a delight, not a necessity but a wish.

What, then, am I to do? What I cannot accomplish I do not dare to refuse. As an untaught passenger I am set aboard a freighting ship, and a man who has never yet handled an oar even on a lake is entrusted to the roaring of the Black Sea. Now, with the land slipping out of sight, there is sky on every side and on every side the deep; now the waves bristle in darkness, and through the blind night of the storm-clouds the foaming billows turn white. You urge me to spread the swelling sails to the mast, to pay out the ropes, to steer the helm. I now obey your command, and because love can do all things, I will trust — with the Holy Spirit speeding my course — and find comfort either way: if the tide drives me to the harbour I long for, I shall be reckoned a pilot; but if my rough speech runs aground amid the harsh windings of my discourse, you may perhaps look for skill, yet you will certainly not be able to demand goodwill.

Now I converse with your letters, I embrace them, they speak with me, they alone here know Latin. For here one must either learn a barbarous tongue in one's old age, or keep silent. And as often as the familiar hand brings back to me your faces, so dear to me, the impressed footprints of the script, so often either I am not here or you are here. Believe love when it tells the truth: even as I was writing this, I saw you. With this complaint I begin: why, with so many stretches of sea and land lying between, did you send so short a letter — unless it is that I deserved it, who, as you write, did not write to you first? I do not suppose paper was lacking, since Egypt furnishes the trade. And if some Ptolemy had closed the seas, still King Attalus sent parchments from Pergamum, so that the want of paper was made up with skins; from which the name 'parchment' has been kept to this very day, posterity handing it down to one another. What then? Am I to think the messenger was in a hurry? Even for a long letter a single night is enough. Or that you were held back by some occupation? No necessity is greater than love. Two possibilities remain: that either you were too lazy or I did not deserve it. Of these I prefer to charge you with slowness than to condemn myself with not deserving it. For negligence can be more easily corrected than love can be born.

But what am I doing? Am I again pleading without forethought? Away with prayers, let flatteries depart; love ought now to be angry. You who had scorned the one who begged you, will perhaps listen to the one who rebukes you. What are you doing in your father's house, you pampered soldier? Where is your rampart, where your ditch, where the winter spent under hides? Look, from heaven the trumpet sounds; look, the armed Commander goes forth to make war upon the world with the clouds; look, the two-edged sword that proceeds from the King's mouth mows down whatever it meets — and do you go for me from your bedroom to the battle-line, from the shade out into the sun? A body used to a tunic cannot bear a breastplate; a head that has been covered with linen refuses the helmet; the hard sword-hilt galls a hand softened by idleness. Hear the edict of your King: "He who is not with me is against me; and he who does not gather with me scatters." Remember the day of your enlistment, on which, buried together with Christ in baptism, you swore the words of the sacrament: that for his name you would spare neither mother nor father. Look, the adversary is trying to kill Christ within your breast; look, the enemy camp longs for the bounty you received when you were to go to war. Though your little nephew hangs from your neck, though your mother, with hair undone and clothes torn, shows you the breasts that nursed you, though your father lies across the threshold — trample over your father and go on, fly with dry eyes to the standard of the cross! In this matter it is a kind of devotion to be cruel.

I have said all this for this reason, my lady Eustochium — for I ought to call the bride of my Lord \"lady\" — that from the very beginning of my discourse you may recognize that I do not now intend to speak the praises of virginity, which you have approved most excellently in following it, nor to enumerate the troubles of marriage — how the womb swells, the infant wails, a rival torments, the cares of a household keep one anxious, and how the final death cuts off all that is thought good (for married women too have their own order, with honourable marriage and an undefiled bed) — but that you may understand that, going out from Sodom, you must fear the example of Lot's wife. There is no flattery in this little book — for the flatterer is a smooth enemy — there will be no pomp of rhetorical speech to set you already among the angels and, with the blessedness of virginity laid out, to put the world beneath your feet.

So now too, my dear Marcella, we have seen our own Blesilla burn for nearly thirty days together in the heat of fever, so that she might learn to cast off the indulgences of a body soon to be furrowed by worms. The Lord Jesus came to her also and touched her hand, and she rose and ministered to him. There was about her a certain air of negligence; bound in the wrappings of riches, she lay in the tomb of the world. But Jesus groaned, and, troubled in spirit, he cried aloud, saying: "Blesilla, come forth." At the call she rose, and coming out she now feasts with the Lord. Let the Jews threaten and swell with rage, let them seek to kill the one who has been raised; the apostles alone rejoice. She knows that she owes her life to him in whom she has believed; she knows that she now embraces the feet of him whose judgment she dreaded a little while ago. Her body lay all but lifeless, and approaching death shook her gasping limbs. Where then were the helps of kinsmen, where the words emptier than any smoke? You are owed nothing, ungrateful family, by one who has died to the world and come alive again to Christ. Whoever is a Christian, let him rejoice; whoever is angry shows that he is not a Christian.

So it is no wonder if we too, by inveighing against vices, give offense to many. I have determined to cut off a stinking nose: let the man with a scrofulous swelling be afraid. I want to pull at a chattering little crow: then let the crow understand that it is rancid. Is there but one man in the Roman world whose nostrils have been hacked off by a shameful wound? Is Onasus of Segesta the only one who weighs out hollow words, swollen like bladders, with puffed-out cheeks? I say that certain men have risen to some dignity or other by crime, perjury, and falsehood: what is that to you, if you know yourself to be innocent? I laugh at an advocate who needs an advocate himself; I turn up my nose at eloquence that is worth a farthing: what is that to you, who are eloquent? I want to attack venal priests: why are you angry, you who are rich? I want lame Vulcan to burn in his own fires: are you his guest or his neighbor, that you should strive to keep the blaze away from the idol's shrines? It pleases me to laugh at ghosts, at the screech-owl, at the horned owl, at the monsters of the Nile: whatever is said, you think it is said against you. Against whatever vice the point of my pen is turned, you cry out that you are the one meant, you come to grips with me and summon me to court, and you foolishly arraign a satirical writer for writing in prose. Or do you think yourself a fine fellow because your name is one of good omen? As though a grove were not called a *lucus* for the very reason that it has the least light, and the Snakes named for not sparing, and the Furies called the Kindly Ones, and Ethiopians commonly called Silvermen. But if you will always be angry when foul things are described, then I will sing of you, with Persius, as a handsome man: "May king and queen long for you as a son-in-law, may the girls carry you off; whatever you tread upon, let it turn to a rose."

And what have we, creatures of the belly, ever done of the kind? If anyone finds us reading at the second hour, we yawn; we rub our faces with our hands and hold back a yawn, and as though after much labor we busy ourselves once again with worldly affairs. I pass over the dinners with which the overloaded mind is weighed down. I am ashamed to speak of the round of calls, in which either we ourselves go each day to others or wait for the rest who come to us. Then it comes to talk; conversation is worn threadbare; the absent are torn to pieces; the lives of others are described; and biting one another, we are devoured by one another. Such is the food that both occupies us and dismisses us. But when our friends have departed, we cast up our accounts. Now anger puts upon us the mask of a lion; now needless care plans ahead for many years to come, and we do not remember the Gospel saying: "You fool, this night they require your soul of you; and the things you have prepared, whose shall they be?" Clothes are sought out not merely for use but for indulgence. Wherever there is a profit to be had, the foot is quicker, the speech swifter, the ear more attentive; if a loss is reported—and this often happens in household affairs—the face is cast down with grief. We rejoice over a penny, we are saddened over a halfpenny. And so, since in one and the same man there is so varied a face of moods, the prophet entreats the Lord, saying: "Lord, in your city you shall bring their image to nothing." For though we were created in the image and likeness of God, by our own fault we put upon ourselves besides a multitude of masks; and just as on the theater's stage one and the same actor now displays a brawny Hercules, now in soft guise breaks into Venus, now quivers as Cybele, so we too—who, were we not of the world, would be hated by the world—have as many likenesses of masks as we have sins.

I, the backslider, the turncoat, the slippery one; I, the liar, deceiving by Satan's art! Which is the more cunning: to have believed or invented such things about the innocent, or to have refused to believe them even of the guilty? Some men kissed my hands and with viperous mouth disparaged me; they grieved with their lips, while in their heart they rejoiced. The Lord saw it and mocked them, and was reserving his wretched servant to be judged together with them at the last. Another slandered my gait and my laughter; one found fault with my expression; a woman suspected something other than what simplicity intended. For nearly three full years I lived among them; many a time a throng of virgins surrounded me; I often expounded the divine books to some of them as best I could. Reading produced constant attendance, attendance produced intimacy, intimacy produced trust. Let them say what they ever thought of me that was otherwise than befitted a Christian. Whose money did I take? Did I scorn gifts, whether small or great? Did anyone's coin chink in my hand? Was my speech crooked, my eye wanton? Nothing else is laid to my charge but my sex, and even this is never laid to my charge except when Paula sets out for Jerusalem. So be it: they believed me when I lied; why do they not believe me when I deny? It is the same man he ever was: the one who a little while ago called me guilty now confesses me innocent; and surely torments draw out the truth more than smiles do—except that what is either gladly heard, if it is invented, or not wept over, so that it may be invented, is the more readily believed.

But that I may not seem to draw this only from heathen literature, learn also the mysteries of the sacred volumes. David, at seventy years of age, once a warlike man, could not be warmed in the chill of his old age. So a girl is sought from all the borders of Israel, Abishag the Shunammite, that she might sleep with the king and warm his aged body. Does it not seem to you, if you follow the surface of the letter, either a fiction out of a mime or the buffoonery of the Atellan farces? A chilled old man is wrapped in clothing, and grows warm only in the embrace of youth. Bathsheba was still living, Abigail still survived, and the rest of his wives and concubines whom Scripture records: all of them are passed over as though they too were cold, and the old man warms in the embraces of one alone. Abraham was far older than David, and yet, while Sarah lived, he sought no other wife; Isaac was twice David's years, and never grew cold with Rebecca, though she was now old; I say nothing of the men before the flood, who, after nine hundred years, with limbs not merely aged but almost decayed, by no means sought the embraces of girls; Moses, certainly, the leader of the people of Israel, was a hundred and twenty years old, and did not exchange Zipporah for another.

I say nothing of Paula and Eustochium, the flowers of your stock, lest I seem, on the occasion of exhorting you, to be praising them; and I pass over Blesilla, who, following her husband, your kinsman, in a brief span of life fulfilled many seasons of virtue. And would that men imitated the renown of women, and that wrinkled old age rendered what youth offers of its own accord! Knowingly and seeing it, I put my hand into the flame: eyebrows will be drawn up, an arm will be stretched out, and an angry Chremes will rage with swollen mouth. The nobles rise up, and against my letter the patrician throng will thunder, crying out that I am a magician, a seducer, to be carried off to the ends of the earth. Let them add, if they wish, "Samaritan" too, that I may recognize the title of my Lord. Certainly I do not divide a daughter from a parent, nor do I quote that saying of the Gospel: "Let the dead bury their dead." For he lives who believes in Christ, and he who believes in him ought himself to walk as he walked.

What, then, shall I do? Shall I join with you in tears? But the Apostle forbids it, calling the dead among Christians "those who sleep," and the Lord in the Gospel says: The girl is not dead, but sleeps. Lazarus too, because he had slept, was raised. Shall I be glad and rejoice that he was taken away, lest wickedness should change his mind, because his soul pleased God? But against my will and resistance the tears flow down my cheeks, and amid the precepts of virtue and the hope of the resurrection the feeling of longing breaks my believing mind. O Death, who dividest brothers and, cruel and hard, severest those joined in love! The Lord brought a burning wind, rising from the desert, which dried up your veins and made desolate your fountain. You devoured Jonah indeed, but even in your belly he was alive. You bore him as though dead, that the tempest of the world might be stilled and our Nineveh be saved by his proclaiming. He, he conquered you, he slew you — that fugitive prophet who left his house and gave his beloved soul into the hands of those who sought it. He who once threatened you sternly through Hosea: I will be your death, O Death; I will be your sting, O hell — by his death you have died, by his death we live. You devoured, and you were devoured; and while you are caught by the allurement of the assumed body and think it a prey for your greedy jaws, your inward parts were pierced through with a hooked tooth.

At present you hand over to me Fabiola, the praise of Christians, the marvel of the heathen, the mourning of the poor, the consolation of the monks. Whatever I first take up, it grows cheap by comparison with what follows. Shall I proclaim her fasting? Her almsgiving outstrips it. Shall I praise her humility? Greater is the ardour of her faith. Shall I tell of her sought-out squalor, and, to the condemnation of silken garments, the plebeian dress and servile clothing she chose? It is more to have laid aside pride than dress. We part with arrogance more hardly than with gold and gems. For when these are cast away, we sometimes swell with a vainglorious squalor and offer our marketable poverty to the breath of the crowd. Virtue concealed, and cherished in the secret of conscience, looks to God alone as judge. Hence she is to be extolled by me with new proclamations, and, the order of the rhetoricians passed over, the whole must be taken up from the cradles of her conversion and penitence. Another, perhaps, mindful of the schools, would bring forward Quintus Maximus, The one man who by delaying restored our state to us, and the whole house of the Fabii; he would tell of battles, describe combats, and boast that Fabiola came through so many degrees of nobility, so as to display in the roots what he could not in the branch. I, the lover of the lodging at Bethlehem and of the Lord's manger, in which the virgin mother brought forth God as an infant, will produce the handmaid of Christ not from the nobility of ancient history but from the humility of the Church.

Let this be said, Laeta, most religious daughter in Christ, that you may not despair of your father's salvation, and may, with the same faith by which you deserved a daughter, receive your father too, and enjoy the blessedness of your whole house, knowing that promised by the Lord: The things that are impossible with men are possible with God. Conversion is never too late. The thief passed over from the cross to paradise; Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, after the wildness of both heart and body, and after living among the beasts in the desert, recovered the mind of a man. And, to pass over old things, lest among unbelievers they seem too fabulous, a few years ago, did not your kinsman Gracchus, whose name sounds of patrician nobility, while he governed the prefecture of the city, overturn, break, and shatter the cave of Mithras and all the monstrous images by which the raven, the bridegroom, the soldier, the lion, the Persian, the runner of the sun, and the father are initiated, and, having sent these forward as it were as hostages, obtain the baptism of Christ? Heathenism suffers solitude even in the city. The gods of the nations of old remain with the owls and the night-birds on the lonely roofs; the standards of the soldiers bear the emblems of the cross; the kings' purples and the burning gems of the diadems the painting of the saving gibbet adorns. Now even the Egyptian Serapis has become a Christian; Marnas of Gaza mourns shut up, and continually trembles at the overthrow of his temple. From India, Persia, and Ethiopia we daily receive throngs of monks; the Armenian has laid down his quiver, the Huns learn the psalter, the Scythians glow with the heat of faith; the ruddy and fair army of the Getae carries about the tents of churches, and perhaps for that reason fights against us on an equal line of battle, because they trust in a like religion.

First I wish you to know, sister and daughter, that I do not write for this reason, because I suspect anything about you, but, that others may not suspect, I pray for your concord. Otherwise — which God forbid! — if I judged that you had clung together by the glue of sin, I would never write, and I would know that I was telling a tale to the deaf. Next, I beseech this, that, if I write anything rather sharp, you should think it the part not so much of my austerity as of the disease. Rotten flesh is cured with the knife and the cautery, poisons are driven out with the serpent's antidote; what pains enough is expelled by a greater pain. Lastly I say this, that, even if the conscience has no wound, yet the reputation has disgrace. Mother and daughter, names of piety, words of duty, bonds of nature, and the second confederation after God — it is no praise if you love one another; it is a crime that you hate. The Lord Jesus was subject to his parents: he reverenced the mother whose father he himself was, he honoured the foster-father whom he had nourished, and he remembered that he had been carried in the womb of the one, in the arms of the other. Hence too, hanging on the cross, he commends his parent to a disciple, the parent whom he had never dismissed before the cross.

You are not now to be led by me through the meadows of the virtues, nor must I labour to show you the beauty of the various flowers, what the lilies have of purity in them, what the modesty of roses possesses, what the purple of the violet promises in the kingdom, what the painting of glowing gems pledges. For already, the Lord being favourable, you hold the plough-handle; already you have climbed to the roof and the upper room with the apostle Peter, who, hungering among the Jews, is filled with the faith of Cornelius, and quenches the hunger of their unbelief by the conversion of the Gentiles, and in the four-cornered vessel of the gospels, which came down from heaven to the earth, is taught and learns that all men can be saved. And again, what he had seen, in the likeness of a most white sheet, is carried up to the heights, and snatches the crowds of believers from the earth to heaven, that the promise of the Lord may be fulfilled: Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God. The whole of what, having taken your hand, I desire to instil into you — what, like a skilled sailor after many shipwrecks, I try to teach an untrained passenger — is this: that you may know on what shore the pirate of chastity lies, where is Charybdis and the root of all evils, avarice, where are the Scyllan dogs of detractors, of whom the Apostle speaks: Lest, biting one another, you be consumed one of another; how, in the midst of calm, we may, secure, be sometimes overwhelmed by the Libyan Syrtes of the vices, and what venomous living creatures the desert of this world nourishes.

Bereaved by the death of her father, she was also deprived of her husband in the seventh month after her marriage. And when Cerealis, whose name is famous among the consuls, sought her hand somewhat too ambitiously, on account of her age and the antiquity of her family and her remarkable beauty of body — which is wont especially to please men — and her remarkable temperance, and, being aged, promised her his wealth and wished to transfer the gift to her not as to a wife but as to a daughter, and when her mother Albina of her own accord desired so distinguished a protection for the widowhood of the house, she answered: "If I wished to marry, and did not desire to dedicate myself to perpetual chastity, I should seek a husband, not an inheritance." And when he urged that old men too can live long and young men quickly die, she gracefully jested: "A young man indeed can quickly die, but an old man cannot live long." Rejected by this saying, he was an example to the rest, that they should despair of her marriage. We read in the Gospel according to Luke: And there was Anna a prophetess, daughter of Phanuel, of the tribe of Asher; and she was of advanced age in many days. And she had lived with her husband seven years from her virginity, and was a widow of eighty-four years, and did not depart from the temple, serving with fastings and prayers night and day. Nor is it any wonder if she deserved to see the Saviour whom she sought with so great labour. Let us compare seven years with seven months, to hope for Christ and to hold him, to confess him born and to believe in him crucified, not to deny him as a little one and to rejoice in him as a man reigning: I make no difference between holy women, as some have foolishly been wont to do among holy men and the chiefs of the churches; but my assertion tends to this, that of those whose labour is one, the reward also is one.

Some, when they have promised a future virgin, are wont to clothe her in a dark tunic and cover her with a black little cloak, to take away the linens, to allow no gold on the neck, none on the head — with good counsel indeed, lest she learn to have in her tender years what afterward she may be compelled to lay aside. To others the opposite seems best. "For what," they say, "if she herself has not had it, will she not see others who have?" The female sex is fond of adornment, and we know that many even of distinguished chastity, though for no man, yet for themselves, gladly deck themselves out. Nay rather, let her be sated by having, and see others praised who do not have these things. And it is better that, being sated, she should despise them, than that, not having them, she should desire to have them. The Lord did something of the kind too for the people of Israel, when, to those longing for the flesh of Egypt, he furnished swarms of quails even to nausea and vomiting; and many men of the world have by experience more easily done without the pleasure of the body than those who from boyhood know nothing of lust; for things known are trampled by the one, things unknown sought by the other; the former by repenting avoid the snares of sweetness which they fled, the latter are caught by the allurements of the flesh and the sweet titillation of the body's flattery, while they think to find honey and discover noxious poisons; for honey distils from the lips of a harlot woman, which for a time fattens the throats of those who eat it, and afterward is found bitterer than gall. Hence too honey is not offered in the Lord's sacrifices, and the wax, which is the lodging of honey, being despised, oil is kindled in the temple of God, which is pressed out from the bitterness of olives; the Passover too is eaten with bitter herbs, in the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth, and whoever has these will endure persecution in the world. Hence too the prophet mystically sings: I sat alone, because I was filled with bitterness.

Vercellae, then, is a city of Liguria, set not far from the roots of the Alps, once powerful, now half in ruins and thinly inhabited. When the consular governor was visiting it, as is the custom, a certain poor woman was brought before him together with the man charged as her adulterer — for that was the accusation her husband had laid — and he had her shut up in the dreadful horror of prison. Not long after, when the bloody iron claw was tearing at her bruised flesh and pain was searching for the truth in her furrowed sides, the most wretched young man, wishing to escape long torments by a quick death, lied against his own blood and so accused another; and he alone of all seemed to deserve, miserably, the blow that fell on him, because he left the innocent woman no ground on which to deny the charge. But the woman, braver than her sex, when the rack stretched her body and bonds bound behind her back the hands fouled with the filth of the prison, looked up to heaven with the eyes that the torturer alone could not bind, and with tears rolling down her face she said: "You are my witness, Lord Jesus, from whom nothing is hidden, who search the reins and the heart, that it is not in order to escape death that I refuse to deny. But you, most wretched man, if you are in haste to die, why do you destroy two innocent people? I too desire to die, I too desire to put off this hated body — but not as an adulteress. I offer my throat, I receive without flinching the flashing blade, I will carry away with me only my innocence. No one truly dies who is killed only to live."

Bonosus, as you write, like a son of the Fish seeks the watery places, while we, still soiled with the old infection, like serpents and scorpions make for whatever is dry and parched. He already treads upon the head of the snake; we are still food for the serpent who by the divine sentence eats the earth. He can climb to the topmost of the gradual psalms; for us, still on the first step of our ascent, I do not know whether it will ever fall to us to say: "I have lifted up my eyes to the mountains, from where my help shall come." He, amid the threatening floods of the world, sits in the safe bosom of the island — that is, of the Church — and perhaps already, after the example of John, devours the book; while I, lying in the tomb of my crimes and bound with the chains of my sins, await the Lord's cry from the Gospel: "Jerome, come forth." Bonosus, I say — since, according to the prophet, all the strength of the devil is in the loins — carried his girdle across the Euphrates, hid it there in the cleft of the rock, and afterwards, finding it rent, sang: "Lord, you have possessed my reins; you have broken my bonds; to you I will sacrifice a victim of praise." As for me, the true Nebuchadnezzar led me away in chains to Babylon — that is, to the confusion of my mind; there he laid the yoke of captivity upon me, there, binding on the iron ring, he commanded me to sing from the songs of Sion. To him I said: "The Lord looses the prisoners, the Lord gives light to the blind." And, to make a brief end of the contrast I have begun: I am begging for pardon, he is awaiting his crown.

Afterward a day will come when you return a victor to your homeland, when, a brave man crowned, you march into the heavenly Jerusalem. Then you will take up your citizenship with Paul; then you will claim for your parents too the right of the same city; then you will pray even for me, who urged you on that you might conquer. Nor indeed am I unaware of the fetter by which you now say you are held back. We have not a heart of iron nor hard breasts; we were not born of flint, nor did Hyrcanian tigers nurse us. We too have passed through these things. Now a widowed sister clings to you with caressing arms; now the home-born servants with whom you grew up say: "To whom do you leave us, to serve?" Now the woman who once carried you, now an old woman, and your foster-father, second in devotion only to your natural one, cry out: "Wait a little while and bury us when we die." Perhaps even your nurse, with the loose skin of her breasts and her brow ploughed with wrinkles, will repeat the old lullaby. Let the grammarians say too, if they wish: "Upon you the whole house leans and rests." The love of Christ and the fear of hell easily break these chains. But Scripture, you say, bids us obey our parents. Yes — but whoever loves them above Christ loses his own soul. The enemy holds the sword to slay me, and shall I think of my mother's tears? Shall I desert my service for the sake of a father to whom, for Christ's sake, I do not owe even burial — when, for his sake, I owe burial to all? Peter, timidly advising the Lord who was to suffer, became a stumbling-block. Paul, to the brethren who held him back from going to Jerusalem, answered: "What are you doing, weeping and troubling my heart? For I am ready not only to be bound, but to die at Jerusalem for the name of our Lord Jesus Christ." This battering-ram of family affection, with which faith is shaken, must be beaten back by the wall of the Gospel: "My mother and my brethren are these, whoever do the will of my Father who is in heaven." If they believe in Christ, let them wish me well as I go to fight for his name; if they do not believe, let the dead bury their dead.

I do not want pride to come to you from your resolve, but fear. You walk laden with gold; the robber must be avoided. This life is a racecourse for mortals: here we contend, that we may be crowned elsewhere. No one walks secure among serpents and scorpions. \"My sword is made drunk in heaven,\" says the Lord — and do you suppose there is peace on earth, which brings forth briars and thorns, which the serpent feeds upon? \"Our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against the principalities and powers of this world and of this darkness, against the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places.\" We are surrounded by great armies of enemies; all things are full of foes. The flesh, fragile and soon to be ashes, fights alone against many. But when it has been dissolved, and the prince of this world comes and finds nothing in it, then you will hear without fear, through the prophet: \"You shall not fear the terror of the night, nor the arrow flying by day, nor the trouble that walks in darkness, nor the assault of the noonday demon. A thousand shall fall at your side and ten thousand at your right hand, but it shall not come near you.\" And if their multitude troubles you, and you begin to seethe at each incitement of the vices, and your own thought says to you, \"What shall we do?\" — Elisha answers: \"Do not fear, for there are more with us than with them,\" and he prays and says: \"Lord, open the eyes of your handmaid, that she may see.\" And with your eyes opened you will see the chariot of fire that lifts you to the stars after the example of Elijah, and then you will sing in gladness: \"Our soul has been snatched like a sparrow from the snare of the fowlers; the snare is broken, and we are set free.\"

A widow who has been loosed from the marriage bond has nothing she needs to do but persevere. But her dark dress offends someone: then let John offend, than whom no one greater has been born among the children of women, who was called an angel and who baptized the Lord himself, who was clothed in a covering of camel's hair and girded with a leather belt. Cheaper food is found unpleasing: nothing is cheaper than locusts. Far more should Christian eyes be offended by those women who paint their faces and eyes with rouge and various dyes, whose plastered faces, disfigured by excessive whiteness, are the counterfeits of idols, on which, if by some mischance an unforeseen teardrop breaks out, it runs down in a furrow; whom not even the number of their years can teach that they are old; who build up the crown of their head with hair that is not their own, and burnish a vanished youth out of the wrinkles of age; who, in short, prink themselves up as trembling little girls before a flock of grandchildren. Let a Christian woman blush if she forces the comeliness of nature, if she takes care of the flesh to gratify desire—for those who are in the flesh, according to the apostle, cannot please Christ.

Yet I will give you advice by which, with certain things concealed, you may appear more beautiful: let your nose not be seen on your face, and let your speech make no sound when you talk—and so you may seem both handsome and eloquent.

Therefore, since we have already passed a great span of life in tossing to and fro, and our ship has now been battered by the whirlwind of storms, now holed by collision with the rocks, let us, as soon as we may, enter the seclusion of the countryside as into some harbor. There let common bread, and herbs watered by our own hands, and milk, the dainties of country life, provide us with food that is cheap, indeed, but innocent. Living thus, sleep will not call us away from prayer, nor a full stomach from reading. If it is summer, the shade of a tree will offer seclusion; if autumn, the very mildness of the air and the leaves strewn underfoot point out a place of rest. In spring the field is painted with flowers, and among the plaintive birds the psalms will be sung the more sweetly. If there is cold and the snows of winter, I will not buy wood: I will keep vigil, or sleep, the warmer for it, and at least, so far as I know, I will not shiver at less cost. Let Rome keep her tumults to herself, let the arena rage, the circus run mad, the theaters riot in luxury, and—since something must be said of our own people—let the senate of matrons be visited daily: for us it is good to cleave to God, to put our hope in the Lord, so that, when the kingdom of heaven shall have exchanged this poverty for itself, we may burst into the cry: "For what is there for me in heaven, and what have I desired from you upon earth?" To this end, namely, that when we have found such great things in heaven, we may grieve to have sought small and perishable things on earth.

Before I came to know the household of holy Paula, the whole city was in agreement in its zeal for me. In the judgment of almost everyone I was deemed worthy of the highest priesthood. My speech was on the lips of Damasus of blessed memory. I was called holy, I was called humble and eloquent. Did I ever enter the house of any too wanton woman? Did silken garments, gleaming gems, a painted face, the ambition for gold ever lay hold of me? There was no other matron at Rome who could subdue my mind but one who mourned and fasted, squalid with dirt, almost blinded with weeping, whom, as she prayed through whole nights for the Lord's mercy, the sun often surprised at her prayers; whose song is the psalms, whose speech the Gospel, whose delight is continence, whose life is fasting. No other could give me pleasure but the one whom I never saw eating; and after I had begun to venerate, to cherish, to look up to her, for the merit of her holiness, all my virtues forthwith deserted me.

Who, then, is this Shunammite, a wife and a virgin so fervent that she warmed the cold, so holy that she did not provoke the warmed man to lust? Let the wisest Solomon set forth his father's delight, and let the man of peace tell of the warrior's embraces: Get wisdom, get understanding. Forget it not, neither decline from the words of my mouth, neither forsake her, and she will lay hold of you; love her, and she will keep you. The beginning of wisdom: get wisdom, and in all your getting get understanding; embrace her, and she will exalt you; honour her, and she will encompass you, that she may give to your head a crown of graces, and may protect you with a crown of delights. Almost all the powers of the body are altered in the old, and while wisdom alone increases, the rest decrease: fastings, sleeping on the ground, running here and there, the receiving of strangers, the defence of the poor, perseverance in standing at prayer, the visiting of the sick, the labour of the hands by which alms are supplied, and — that I may not draw out my discourse too far — everything that is performed through the body grows less as the body breaks down. Nor do I say this as though wisdom grew cold in the young and those still of firmer age — at least in those who have pursued knowledge through labour and the most ardent zeal, through holiness of life too and frequency of prayer to God — wisdom that withers with age in most of the old; but rather that youth endures many wars of the body, and amid the incentives of the vices and the ticklings of the flesh is choked, like fire in greener wood, and cannot unfold its full radiance. But old age — again I remind you — in those who have furnished their youth with honourable arts and have meditated in the law of the Lord day and night, grows more learned with age, more practised by use, wiser with the passage of time, and reaps the sweetest fruits of its old studies. And so that wise man of Greece, when, having completed a hundred and seven years, he saw that he was about to die, is said to have grieved that he was then leaving life just when he had begun to be wise; Plato died in his eighty-first year, pen in hand; Isocrates filled out ninety-nine years in the labour of teaching and writing; I say nothing of the other philosophers — Pythagoras, Democritus, Xenocrates, Zeno, Cleanthes — who flourished in the studies of wisdom when already of great age: I come to the poets, Homer, Hesiod, Simonides, Stesichorus, who, far advanced in years, with death near, sang some swan-song sweeter than their wont. Sophocles, when on account of his extreme old age and the neglect of his household affairs he was accused of madness by his sons, recited to the judges the tragedy of Oedipus which he had lately written, and gave so great a proof of wisdom in his now-broken age that he turned the severity of the tribunal into the applause of the theatre. Nor is this any wonder, since even Cato, the most eloquent of the Roman race, when already a censor and an old man, neither blushed at nor despaired of learning Greek letters. Homer, certainly, relates that from the tongue of Nestor, now aged and almost decrepit, speech flowed sweeter than honey. But the mystery of the very name Abishag indicates the fuller wisdom of the old. For it is interpreted "my father is superabundant," or "the roaring of my father." The word "superabundant" is ambiguous, and in the present passage signifies virtue, in that wisdom in the old is fuller and overflowing and lavish; but in another passage "superabundant" is put for "superfluous," as not necessary. "Sag," that is, "roaring," is properly so named when the waves of the sea resound, and, so to speak, the roar coming from the deep is heard. By this it is shown that the most abundant thunder of the divine word, beyond the human voice, abides in the old. Furthermore, "Shunammite" in our tongue is rendered "scarlet," to signify that wisdom is warm and glows with divine reading; which, though it points to the mystery of the Lord's blood, nevertheless also shows the fervour of wisdom. And so that midwife in Genesis binds the scarlet thread upon the hand of Pharez, who, from the fact that he had divided the wall that separated two peoples before him, received the name of the "divider," that is, Pharez. And Rahab the harlot, as a type of the Church, let down the little cord that contained the mysteries of the blood, that she might be saved at the destruction of Jericho. And in another passage Scripture records concerning holy men: These are the Kenites who came from the warmth of the house of Rechab. And our Lord in the Gospel: I have come, he says, to send fire upon the earth, and how I wish that it were already kindled! It was this fire, kindled in the hearts of the disciples, that compelled them to say: Did not our heart burn within us while he spoke on the way and opened to us the Scriptures?

Let envy depart — that envy which the inborn malice of slanderers ever fastens upon the Christian name, so that, while men fear reproaches, they may not be roused to the virtues. Apart from letters we do not know one another, and there is no cause but that of piety where there is no acquaintance of the flesh. Honour your father, but only so long as he does not separate you from your true Father. Know the bond of blood only so long as he himself acknowledges his Creator; otherwise David will straightway sing to you: Hear, O daughter, and see, and incline your ear, and forget your own people and your father's house; and the King shall desire your beauty, for he is the Lord your God. Great is the reward of the parent forgotten: The King shall desire your beauty. Because you have heard, because you have seen, because you have inclined your ear and forgotten your people and your father's house, therefore the King shall desire your beauty and shall say to you: You are all fair, my nearest, and there is no spot in you. What is more beautiful than the soul which is called the daughter of God and seeks no outward ornaments? She believes in Christ and, enriched by this ambition, goes forth to her Bridegroom, having the same one as Lord whom she has as husband.

We give you thanks, Christ our Saviour — we, your creature — that, while you were slain, you slew so powerful an adversary of ours. Who before was more wretched than man, who, prostrate with the eternal terror of death, had received the sense of living only for this, that he might perish? For death reigned from Adam to Moses, even over those who had not sinned after the likeness of Adam's transgression. If Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob were in hell, who was in the kingdom of heaven? If your friends, under the penalty of Adam's offence, and even those who had not sinned, were held liable for the sins of others, what is to be believed of those who said in their hearts, "There is no God," who became corrupt and abominable in their desires, who turned aside, and together became unprofitable; there is none that does good, no, not one? But if Lazarus is seen in Abraham's bosom and in a place of refreshment, what likeness is there between hell and the kingdom of heaven? Before Christ, Abraham among the dead; after Christ, the thief in paradise. And therefore at his resurrection many bodies of those who slept arose, and were seen in the heavenly Jerusalem. And then was fulfilled that saying: Arise, you who sleep, and lift yourself up, and Christ shall enlighten you. John the Baptist cries aloud in the desert: Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is at hand. For from the days of John the Baptist the kingdom of heaven has suffered violence, and the violent take it by force. That flaming sword, the guardian of paradise, and the cherubim presiding at the gates, have been quenched and unbarred by the blood of Christ. Nor is it any wonder that this is promised to us at the resurrection, since all of us who live in the flesh but not according to the flesh have our citizenship in heaven, and to us, still placed on earth, it is said: The kingdom of God is within you.

And because at the very outset a kind of rock and storm of her detractors is set against me — that, having drawn a second marriage by lot, she first left the prior one — I will not praise her conversion until I have absolved her of the charge. So great are the vices her first husband is said to have had that not even a harlot or a cheap slave could endure them. If I should choose to tell them, I should destroy the virtue of the woman, who preferred to undergo the blame of divorce rather than defame a certain part of her own body and uncover its stains. This only will I bring forward, which is enough for a modest and Christian matron. The Lord commanded that a wife ought not to be put away except for the cause of fornication, and that, if she be put away, she should remain unmarried. Whatever is enjoined upon men consequently redounds upon women too. For an adulterous wife is not to be put away while an adulterous husband is to be kept. If anyone is joined to a harlot, he makes one body; therefore she also who is joined to a fornicator and an impure man becomes one body with him. The laws of the Caesars are one thing, the laws of Christ another; Papinian commands one thing, our Paul another. Among them the reins of chastity are loosened for men, and, condemning only defilement and adultery, lust is permitted everywhere, through brothels and serving-maids, as though it were rank that made the fault, not pleasure. Among us, what is not lawful for women is equally not lawful for men, and the same servitude is reckoned on an equal footing. She put away, then, as they say, a vicious man; she put away one guilty of this and that crime; she put away — I almost said what the neighbourhood proclaimed and the wife alone did not betray. But if it is objected, why, the husband being divorced, she did not remain unmarried, I will readily confess the fault, provided that I report the necessity. It is better, says the Apostle, to marry than to burn. She was young; she could not keep her widowhood. She saw another law in her members warring against the law of her mind, and herself bound and captive being dragged to union. She thought it better openly to confess her weakness and to undergo a kind of shadow of a wretched marriage than, under the glory of having had one husband, to practise harlotry. The same Apostle wishes young widows to marry, to bear children, to give no occasion for the sake of reviling. And straightway he sets forth why he wishes this: For some are already turned aside after Satan. Therefore Fabiola too, because she had persuaded herself and thought her husband lawfully put away by her, and did not know the rigour of the Gospel, in which all pretext of marrying, the husbands living, is cut off from Christian women, while she shunned many wounds of the devil, incautiously received one.

I have almost slipped to another subject, and, while, the wheel running, I think to make a jug, my hand has fashioned an amphora. For my purpose was, invited by the prayers of the holy Marcella and your own, to direct my discourse to the mother — that is, to you — and to teach how you ought to instruct our little Paula, who was consecrated to Christ before she was born, whom you received by vows before you conceived her in the womb. We have seen something in our own times out of the prophetic books: Anna exchanged the barrenness of her womb for fruitfulness; you have exchanged a sorrowful fruitfulness for living children. I speak confidently that you will receive sons, you who have rendered your first offspring to the Lord. These are the firstborn that are offered under the law. So was Samuel born, so Samson came forth, so John the prophet leapt and played at the entrance of Mary. For he heard through the mouth of the virgin the words of the Lord thundering, and from his mother's womb was eager to burst forth to meet him. Therefore, let her who was born from the promise have an upbringing from her parents worthy of her birth. Samuel is nourished in the temple, John is prepared in the wilderness. The one is venerable for his sacred hair, drinks no wine or strong drink, while still a little one converses with God; the other flees the cities, is girded with a leathern belt, is fed on locusts and wild honey, and, as a type of penitence, preaches clothed in the spoils of the most winding of animals.

But you, daughter — for now I cease to speak to the mother, whom perhaps age and weakness and loneliness make excusable — you, I say, daughter, do you judge her house narrow whose womb was not narrow for you? You lived ten months shut in her womb, and do you not endure one day in one chamber with your mother? Or can you not bear her eyes, and, because she who bore you, who nourished you and brought you to this age, understands all your motions as by torches, do you flee a witness of your own household? If you are a virgin, why do you fear diligent guardianship? If corrupted, why do you not marry openly? The second plank after shipwreck is, where you have begun ill, at least to temper it by this remedy. Nor indeed do I say this to take away penitence after sin, so that what began ill should persist ill, but because in a union of this kind I despair of a separation. Otherwise, if you should migrate to your mother after your fall, you could more easily mourn with her what you lost by her absence. But if you are still whole and have not lost, keep it, lest you lose. What need is there for you to dwell in that house in which you have it necessary daily either to perish or to conquer? Does any mortal take his sleep secure next to a viper? Even if it does not strike, certainly it disturbs. It is safer not to be able to perish than, next to peril, not to have perished; in the one is tranquillity, in the other steering; there we rejoice, here we escape.

Those sailing the Red Sea — in which it is to be wished for us that the true Pharaoh be drowned with his army — come with many difficulties and dangers to the city of Auxuma. On either shore dwell wandering nations — nay, most ferocious beasts. Always anxious, always armed, they carry the provisions of a whole year. All things are full of hidden rocks and most dangerous shoals, so that a lookout and pilot sits at the very top of the mast and from there proclaims his orders for steering and turning the ship. The voyage is happy if after six months they reach the harbour of the aforesaid city, from which the ocean begins to open out, through which scarcely in a whole year one comes to India and to the river Ganges — which Holy Scripture calls Phison — which encircles all the land of Havilah and is said to carry forth many kinds of spices from the fountain of paradise. There is born the carbuncle and the emerald and the gleaming pearls and the unions, with which the ambition of noble women burns, and the golden mountains, which it is impossible for men to approach because of the dragons and griffins and the monsters of immense bodies, that it may be shown us what guardians avarice has.

It is difficult, in a slanderous city, and in a town in which there was once the people of the whole world and the palm of the vices — if they disparaged the honourable and stained the pure and clean — not to draw upon oneself some tale of sinister rumour. Hence the prophet wishes for, rather than presumes, as for a most difficult and almost impossible thing, saying: Blessed are the undefiled in the way, who walk in the law of the Lord, calling undefiled in the way of this world those whom no obscene breath of rumour has stained, who have not received reproach against their neighbours. Of whom the Saviour too in the Gospel: Be, he says, well-disposed — or well-thinking — toward your adversary while you are with him in the way. Who ever heard of this woman anything that would displease, so as to believe it? Who believed it, so as not rather to condemn himself of malignity and infamy? By her first the heathen were confounded, when it became plain to all what Christian widowhood was, which she promised both by her conscience and by her dress. For they are wont to paint their faces with rouge and white lead, to gleam in silken garments, to glitter with gems, to carry gold on their necks, and from their pierced ears to hang the most precious grains of the Red Sea, to reek of musk, and at last to rejoice that they have been freed from the dominion of husbands, and to seek others, not whom, according to God's sentence, they may serve, but whom they may command. Hence too they choose poor men, that they may seem to have only the name of husbands, who may patiently endure rivals, and, if they have muttered, are to be thrown out at once. Our widow used such garments as kept off the cold, not bared the limbs, refusing gold even to the signet of a ring, and laying it up rather in the bellies of the needy than in purses. Nowhere without her mother; she saw none of the clerics and monks — as the need of a great house sometimes required — without witnesses. She always had in her company virgins and widows, and these grave women, knowing that from the wantonness of the maids the manners of the mistresses are often judged, and that each is delighted by the company of such as she herself is.

What then? Must one revel in youth, that afterward luxury may be more strongly despised? "God forbid," they say; For let each one, in the calling in which he was called, in that abide. Is anyone called circumcised — that is, a virgin? Let him not draw on the foreskin — that is, let him not seek the skin-tunics of marriage, with which Adam, cast out of the paradise of virginity, was clothed. Is anyone called in the foreskin — that is, having a wife and girded about with the skin of matrimony? Let him not seek the nakedness of virginity and eternal chastity, which he has once ceased to have, but let him use his own vessel in sanctification and chastity, and drink from his own fountains, and not seek the shattered cisterns of the brothels, which cannot contain the purest waters of chastity. Hence too the same Paul, in the same chapter, disputing of virginity and marriage, calls those constituted in matrimony servants of the flesh, and free those who, without any yoke of marriage, serve the Lord with all liberty. What we say, we say not of all in general, but treat in part, nor speak of all, but of certain ones. Our discourse is directed to both sexes, not to the weaker vessel only. You are a virgin: why does the society of a woman delight you? Why do you commit a frail and patched raft to the great waves, and, secure, embark on the great peril of an uncertain voyage? You know not what you desire, and yet you so join yourself to her as though you had either desired before or — to speak most lightly — would desire afterward. "But that sex is more fit for service." Choose, then, an old woman; choose a deformed one; choose one of proved continence in the Lord. Why does a young one delight you, why a beautiful one, why a luxurious one? You use the baths, with shining skin, you walk about ruddy, you feed on flesh, you abound in riches, surrounded with precious garments, and do you believe that you sleep secure next to a deadly serpent? Or do you not dwell in the same lodging — at night at least? But spending whole days in conversation of this kind, why do you, alone with a woman alone, sit and not with witnesses? Even though you yourself do not sin, you may seem to others to sin, so that you are an example to the wretched, who by the authority of your name may transgress. You too, virgin or widow, why do you detain a man with so long a discourse? Why, left alone with one alone, do you not fear? At least let the necessity of the bowels and the bladder compel you to go out, that you may leave him, with whom in this matter, more freely than with a brother, far more modestly you have acted than with a husband. "But you ask something of the Holy Scriptures": ask in public; let your maids hear, let your companions hear. Everything that is made manifest is light. Good speech does not seek secret places; nay rather, it delights in its own praises and the testimony of very many. The excellent master despises men, scorns brothers, and sweats over the secret instruction of one little woman.

So the consular governor, his eyes glutted with blood, like a wild beast that, having once tasted blood, forever thirsts for it, ordered the torments to be doubled, and, gnashing his teeth in fury, threatened a punishment like the executioner's own unless the weaker sex confessed what manly strength had not been able to keep silent.

My sister is the fruit in Christ of holy Julian: he planted, you are to water, the Lord will give the increase. Jesus has granted her to me in place of that wound which the devil had inflicted, giving her back alive in place of the dead. For her, as the pagan poet says, I fear all things, even the safe ones.
