You yourselves know the slippery road of youth, on which I too have fallen, and which you do not pass without fear. And as she, above all, now sets out upon it, she must be propped up with everyone's counsels, must be sustained with everyone's comfort — that is, must be strengthened by the frequent letters of your holiness; and because love bears all things, I beg you to obtain even from Pope Valerianus a letter to comfort her. You know that girls' minds are for the most part steadied by such things, if they perceive that they are a care to their elders.

But this, you say, applies to martyrdom. You are wrong, brother, you are wrong, if you think a Christian ever suffers no persecution; and you are most of all under attack now, when you do not know that you are under attack. "Our adversary, like a roaring lion, goes about seeking someone to devour" — and you think there is peace? "He sits in ambush with the rich in secret places, to slay the innocent; his eyes are fixed upon the poor man; he lies in wait in secret like a lion in his den; he lies in wait to seize the poor" — and you, hidden under the shade of a leafy tree, snatch soft slumbers, the prey of what is to come? On this side luxury hounds me, on that avarice tries to break in, on that my belly wants to be my god in Christ's place; lust drives me to put to flight the Holy Spirit who dwells in me, to defile his temple; the enemy hounds me, I say — he who has a thousand names and a thousand arts of harming — and shall I, wretched, count myself the victor while I am being taken captive?

As long as we are held in this fragile little body, as long as we have this treasure in earthen vessels, and the spirit lusts against the flesh and the flesh against the spirit, there is no sure victory. Our adversary the devil, like a roaring lion, goes about seeking something to devour. \"You appointed darkness,\" says David, \"and it became night. In it all the beasts of the forest will go about, the roaring young lions, to seize and to seek their food from God.\" The devil does not seek faithless men, nor those who are outside and whose flesh the Assyrian king burns in the pot: he hastens to seize from the Church of Christ. His foods, according to Habakkuk, are choice: he longs to overthrow Job, and, having devoured Judas, he seeks power to sift the apostles. The Saviour did not come to send peace upon the earth, but a sword. Lucifer fell, who used to rise in the morning, and he who was nurtured in the paradise of delights deserved to hear: \"Though you raise yourself up like an eagle, from there I will bring you down, says the Lord.\" For he had said in his heart: \"I will set my throne above the stars of heaven, and I will be like the Most High.\" Therefore God speaks daily to those who descend by the ladder that Jacob saw in his dream: \"I said, you are gods, and all of you sons of the Most High; but you shall die like men, and shall fall like one of the princes.\" For the devil fell first; and although God stands in the assembly of the gods, and in the midst distinguishes between the gods, the apostle writes to those who cease to be gods: \"For where there are dissensions and rivalries among you, are you not men, and walking according to man?\"

Our widow once adorned herself with necklaces and spent whole days at the mirror searching out what she lacked; now she says with confidence: "But we all, with unveiled face beholding the glory of the Lord, are transformed into the same image from glory to glory, as by the Spirit of the Lord." Then maidservants arranged her hair, and her harmless head was cramped under crimping kerchiefs; now her neglected head knows that it is enough for it merely to be veiled. In those days even the hard softness of feathers seemed too much for her, and she could scarcely lie upon her piled-up couches; now she rises in haste to pray, and in a tuneful voice, leading the rest in their alleluia, she is the first to begin praising her Lord. Her knees are bent upon the bare ground, and the face that her white lead once soiled is washed clean with frequent tears. After prayer the psalms ring out, and her weary neck, her tottering knees, her eyes sinking toward sleep are scarcely granted rest by the great ardor of her mind. Her tunic is dark: it is the less stained when she lies upon the ground. Her shoe is cheaper: the price of a lover's footwear she will lavish on the needy. Her belt is not picked out with gold and gems, but is of wool, of the purest simplicity throughout, and made rather to bind her clothes together than to tear them. If the scorpion envies this resolve of hers and with smooth talk persuades her once again to eat of the forbidden tree, let him be crushed, and let an anathema serve her for a sandal against him, and over him as he dies in his own dust let it be said: "Get behind me, Satan," which is to be interpreted "the adversary"; for the antichrist is indeed the adversary of Christ, and to him the precepts of Christ are displeasing.

O envy, first to gnaw at your own self! O cunning of Satan, ever persecuting what is holy! No other women furnished a tale for the city of Rome but Paula and Melania, who, having despised their fortunes and abandoned their children, raised the cross of the Lord as a kind of banner of piety. Had they made for Baiae, chosen perfumes, kept their riches and their widowhood—the materials of luxury and license—they would have been called great ladies and saints; but now, in sackcloth and ashes, they wish to be seen as beautiful, and to go down with their fastings and their squalor into the fire of hell. No doubt it is not permitted them, with the people's applause, to perish along with the crowds. If the heathen carped at this life of theirs, or the Jews, I would have the comfort of not pleasing those whom Christ displeases; but as it is—oh, the shame!—those who bear the name of Christian neglect the care of their own houses, and, overlooking the beam in their own eye, look for the mote in another's. They tear a holy resolve to pieces, and reckon it a remedy for their own punishment if no one is holy, if everyone is disparaged, if there is a great crowd of the perishing, a multitude of sinners.

To what end has all this been recalled in so long a preface? That you may not seek from me boyish declamations, little flowers of maxims, the allurements of words, and at the close of each chapter certain pointed and briefly concluded turns of phrase, such as rouse the applause and shouts of the hearers. Let wisdom alone embrace me, and let our Abishag, who never grows old, rest in my bosom. She is unpolluted and of perpetual virginity, and, after the likeness of Mary, since she daily brings forth and is ever in travail, she is uncorrupted. From this, I think, the Apostle too said that he was "fervent in spirit," and the Lord proclaimed in the Gospel that at the end of the world, when, according to the prophet Zechariah, a foolish shepherd shall arise, wisdom shall decrease and the love of many shall grow cold. Hear me, then — as blessed Cyprian says — words not eloquent but strong. Hear a brother by fellowship, a father by age, who would lead you from the cradle of faith to the perfect age, and who, in laying down precepts for living through each of its degrees, may through you instruct others as well. I know indeed that from your uncle, the blessed Heliodorus, who is now a bishop of Christ, you have both learned the things that are holy and learn them daily, and have the example of his virtues as your rule of life; but receive also my own contributions, such as they are, and join this little book to his, so that, while he has trained you as a monk, this may teach you to be a perfect cleric.

What straits marriage holds you learned in your very marriage, and you were sated to the point of nausea, as if with the flesh of quails. Your throat has tasted the bitterest gall; you have vomited up the sour and sickening food and relieved your seething stomach: why do you wish to take in again what was harmful to you? A dog returning to its vomit, and a sow to its wallowing in the mire. Even the brute beasts and the wandering birds do not fall twice into the same snares and nets. Or do you fear that the offspring of the Furian line should fail, and that your father should have from you no little child to crawl on his breast and smear his neck with filth? Why not? All who have had marriages have children, and all to whom children are born answer to the worth of their kind! Did Cicero's son show his father's image in eloquence? Did your Cornelia, that pattern of chastity and fruitfulness alike, rejoice that she had borne her Gracchi? It is ridiculous to hope as a certainty for what you see that many do not have, and, when they have had it, have lost it. To whom do you bequeath such great riches? To Christ, who cannot die. Whom will you have as heir? Him whom you have also as Lord. Your father will be saddened, but Christ will rejoice; your household will mourn, but the angels will give thanks. Let your father do as he wishes with his own: you belong not to him to whom you were born, but to him to whom you were reborn, and who redeemed you at a great price, with his own blood.

Add that before the resurrection of Christ God was known only in Judaea, in Israel his name was great, and even those who knew him were nevertheless dragged down to hell. Where then were the men of the whole world, from India to Britain, from the rigid region of the north to the heats of the Atlantic ocean — so innumerable peoples and the multitudes of so many nations, as various in tongue as in dress and arms? Like fishes and locusts, like flies and gnats, they were ground down; for without the knowledge of his Creator, every man is a beast. But now the passion of Christ and his resurrection are sounded by the voices and the writings of all nations. I say nothing of the Hebrews, Greeks, and Latins, which nations the Lord consecrated to his faith in the title of the cross. The soul immortal and subsisting after the dissolution of the body — which Pythagoras dreamed of, which Democritus did not believe, which Socrates discoursed of in prison for the consolation of his condemnation — the Indian, the Persian, the Goth, the Egyptian now philosophize about. The fierceness of the Bessi and the throng of skin-clad peoples, who once sacrificed men at the funeral rites of the dead, have broken their harsh cry into the sweet melody of the cross, and the one voice of the whole world is Christ.

But why do I linger over things abolished and old, seeking to excuse a fault whose penitence she herself has confessed? Who would believe this — that after the death of her second husband, having returned to herself, at the time when negligent widows, the yoke of servitude shaken off, are wont to conduct themselves more freely, to frequent the baths, to flit through the streets, to carry about a harlot's countenance, she should put on sackcloth, publicly confess her error, and, with all Rome looking on, before the day of Passover, in the basilica that was once Lateranus's — who was beheaded by the sword of Caesar — should stand in the rank of the penitents, while the bishop and the presbyters and all the people wept together, and submit her scattered hair, her pallid face, her squalid hands, her dirty neck? What sins does that weeping not purge? What inveterate stains do these laments not wash away? Peter blotted out his threefold denial by a threefold confession. The fraternal prayers corrected Aaron's sacrilege and the head of the calf cast out of gold. The seven days' fast amended the homicide and adultery alike of David, a holy and most gentle man. He lay on the ground, he rolled in the ashes, and, forgetful of his royal power, sought light in the darkness, and, looking to him alone whom he had offended, said with weeping voice: Against you only have I sinned, and done evil before you; and: Restore to me the joy of your salvation, and strengthen me with a princely spirit. And so it came to pass that he who had first taught me by his virtues how, standing, I might not fall, taught me by his penitence how, falling, I might rise again. What so impious do we read among the kings as Ahab, of whom Scripture says: There was no other like Ahab, who was sold to do evil in the sight of the Lord. When this man had been rebuked by Elijah for the blood of Naboth, and had heard the wrath of the Lord through the prophet: You have killed, and moreover you have taken possession; and: Behold, I will bring evils upon you, and I will reap away your posterity, and the rest — he rent his garments, and covered his flesh with sackcloth, and fasted in sackcloth, and walked with his head bowed. Then came the word of the Lord to Elijah the Tishbite, saying: Have you not seen the humility of Ahab before me? Because, then, he has humbled himself in the fear of me, I will not bring the evil in his days. O happy penitence, which drew to herself the eyes of God, which by confession of her error changed the raging sentence of the Lord! This same thing we read that Manasseh did in the Chronicles, and Nineveh in the prophet, and the publican too in the Gospel — of whom the first deserved to receive not only pardon but a kingdom, the second broke the impending wrath of God, the third, beating his breast with his fists, would not lift his eyes to heaven, and departed far more justified by the humble confession of his vices than the Pharisee by the proud boasting of his virtues. This is not the place to preach penitence, and, as if writing against Montanus and Novatus, to say that it is the propitiable victim of the Lord, and that the sacrifice to God is a troubled spirit, and: I prefer the penitence of the sinner to his death; and: Arise, arise, Jerusalem; and many other things which the trumpets of the prophets sound.

So must the soul be trained which is to be the temple of the Lord. Let it learn to hear nothing else, to speak nothing else, except what pertains to the fear of God. Let her not understand foul words, let her be ignorant of the songs of the world, let her tongue, while still tender, be steeped in sweet psalms. Far off be the wanton company of boys; let the very girls and attendants be kept from the society of worldlings, lest, what they have learned of evil, they teach worse. Let her be given letters of boxwood or ivory, and let them be called by their names. Let her play with them, so that her play too may be instruction; and let her not only keep the order of the letters, so that the memory of their names may pass into a song, but let the order itself be frequently disarranged among them, and the last be mixed with the middle, the middle with the first, that she may know them not only by their sound but by their sight. But when she begins to draw the pen over the wax with trembling hand, let either another's hand be placed over hers and the little fingers guided, or let the letters be carved into the tablet, so that her tracings, enclosed within the margins, may be drawn along the same furrows and may not be able to wander outside. Let her join syllables for a reward, and let her be enticed by such little gifts as that age can delight in. Let her have companions too in learning, whom she may envy, by whose praises she may be stung. She is not to be chided if she is rather slow, but her talent is to be excited by praises; let her rejoice when she has won, and grieve when she is beaten. Above all it must be guarded against that she should hate her studies, lest the bitterness of them, perceived in infancy, pass beyond the untaught years. The very names through which she will grow accustomed to weave words together should not be casual, but fixed and heaped up of set purpose — those of the prophets, namely, and the apostles, and let the whole series of the patriarchs from Adam descend from Matthew and Luke, so that, while she does another thing, she may be prepared for a future memory. A teacher of approved age and life and learning is to be chosen, nor, I think, does a learned man blush to do, for a kinswoman or a noble virgin, what Aristotle did for the son of Philip, that he himself, with the lowliness of the booksellers, should impart to her the beginnings of letters. Things are not to be despised as small, without which great things cannot stand. The very sound of the elements and the first instruction of the teacher come forth differently from a learned mouth than from a rustic one. Hence you too must take care that you do not, by the foolish blandishments of women, accustom your daughter to say words by halves, and to play in gold and purple, of which the one is harmful to the tongue, the other to the manners, lest she learn in her tender years what she must afterward unlearn. The eloquence of the Gracchi is written to have owed much to the speech of their mother from infancy; the oratory of Hortensius grew strong in his father's bosom. With difficulty is that uprooted which untrained minds have drunk in. Who could call back the purple of wools to its first whiteness? A new jar long retains both the taste and the odour with which it was first steeped. Greek history relates that Alexander, a most powerful king and the conqueror of the world, could not, in his manners and in his gait, be free of the vices with which, while still a little one, he had been infected by Leonides his tutor. For the imitation of evil is downhill, and you quickly imitate the vices of those whose virtue you cannot attain. Let the nurse herself be neither drunken, nor wanton, nor talkative; let her have a modest bearer, a grave foster-father. When the child sees her grandfather, let her leap onto his breast, hang from his neck, sing alleluia to him whether he will or no. Let her grandmother snatch her up, let her recognize her father with smiles, let her be lovable to all, and let the whole kindred rejoice in the rose born from itself. Let her learn at once what other grandmother, what aunt she has, for what Commander, for what army the little recruit is being reared. Let her long for them, let her threaten you that she will go off to them.

But perhaps you will answer: "My mother is not of good character; she desires the things of the world, she loves riches, she is ignorant of fasting, she smears her eyes with antimony, she wishes to go out adorned, and she harms my resolve, nor can I live with one of this kind." First indeed, even if she is such as you allege, you will have a greater reward if you do not forsake one such. She carried you long, she nourished you long, and bore with the more difficult ways of your infancy with coaxing affection. She washed the filth of your swaddling-clothes and was often defiled with unclean dung. She sat by you when sick, and what loathings she had borne for your sake she suffered for you also. She brought you to this age; she taught you to love Christ. Let her way of life not displease you, who consecrated you a virgin to your Bridegroom. But if she cannot be borne, and you flee her delicacies and, as you are wont commonly to say, your mother is worldly, you have other virgins, you have the holy choir of chastity. Why, forsaking your mother, do you choose him who perhaps left his own sister and mother? She is difficult, but he is easy; she is quarrelsome, he is placable. I ask whether you followed him or found him afterward. If you followed him, it is manifest why you left your mother; if you found him afterward, you show what you could not find in your mother's lodging. A harsh teacher, and wounding me with my own sword: He who walks simply, he says, walks confidently. I would be silent if my conscience bit me back, and I would not reprove my own crime in others, nor see another's mote through the beam of my own eye. But now, since, dwelling far off among brethren and enjoying their fellowship, I both rarely see and am seen honourably under witnesses, it is most shameless that you do not follow the modesty of him whose example you testify that you follow. But if you say: "My conscience is enough for me too; I have God as judge, who is the witness of my life; I do not care what men say" — hear the Apostle writing: Providing things good not only before God but also before men. If anyone carps at you because you are a Christian, because you are a virgin, because you have therefore left your mother to live in a monastery among virgins, do not care; such detraction is your praise. Where it is not luxury that is carped at in a virgin of God, but hardness, that cruelty is piety. For you prefer to your mother him whom you are bidden to prefer even to your own soul. And if she too prefer him, she will feel you to be both a daughter and a sister.

To what end these things? It is clear. If the merchants of the world endure so much to come to uncertain and perishable riches, and keep at the risk of their life what they have sought with many dangers, what is not to be done by the merchant of Christ, who, having sold all things, seeks the most precious pearl, who with all the resources of his substance buys the field in which he may find the treasure that neither thief can dig up nor robber carry off?

Her ardour for the divine Scriptures was incredible, and she ever sang: In my heart have I hidden your words, that I may not sin against you, and that saying about the perfect man: And his will is in the law of the Lord, and in his law will he meditate day and night, understanding the meditation of the law not as repeating what is written, as the Pharisees of the Jews suppose, but as in works, according to that apostolic saying: Whether you eat or drink or whatever you do, do all things to the glory of the Lord, and the prophet's words, saying: From your commandments I understood, so that, after she had fulfilled the commandments, she should then know herself to merit the understanding of the Scriptures. Which we read elsewhere too: That Jesus began to do and to teach. For however distinguished a doctrine, it blushes when its own conscience reproves it, and in vain does the tongue preach poverty and teach almsgiving when one swells with the riches of Croesus and, covered with a cheap little cloak, fights against the moths of silken garments. Moderate fastings, abstinence from flesh, the smell rather than the taste of wine on account of her stomach and frequent infirmities. Rarely did she go out into public, and especially she avoided the houses of noble matrons, lest she should be compelled to see what she had despised, celebrating the basilicas of the apostles and martyrs with secret prayers, and shunning the throng of the peoples. To her mother she was so obedient that sometimes she did what she did not wish. For when her mother loved her own blood, and wished, having no children or grandchildren, that all should be conferred upon her brother's children, while Marcella chose the poor, yet she could not go against her mother, and yielded her necklaces and whatever furniture there was to wealthy relations destined to perish, wishing rather to lose money than to sadden her parent's mind.

I have turned a little from the way on the occasion of others, and, while I instruct the infant Pacatula — nay, nourish her — I have suddenly taken up wars with many women ill at peace with me. I will return to my purpose. Let the female sex be joined to its own sex; let her not know — nay, let her fear — to play with boys. Let her know no unchaste word, and, if perchance in the tumult of the bustling household she hear anything foul, let her not understand it. Let her have her mother's nod for words and her warning for a command. Let her love her as a parent, be subject to her as a mistress, fear her as a teacher. But when the seventh year of her age has received the little maiden, still untaught and toothless, and she has begun to blush, to know what to keep silent, to be in doubt what to say, let her learn the psalter by heart, and until the years of puberty let her make the books of Solomon, the gospels, the apostles, and the prophets the treasure of her heart. Let her not go out too freely into public, nor always seek the gatherings of the churches. Let her have all her delights in her own chamber. Let her never see young men, never curled fellows wounding the soul through the ears with sweetness of voice. The wantonness of girls too is to be repelled, who, the more freely they approach, the more difficultly they are avoided, and who teach in secret what they have learned, and violate a shut-in Danaë by the talk of the crowd. Let her teacher be a companion, her tutor a guardian, not much given to wine, not, according to the Apostle, idle and wordy, but sober, grave, a worker of wool, and speaking only those things which instruct the minds of girls to virtue. But as water in a little channel follows the finger going before it, so the soft and tender age is flexible to either side, and is drawn wherever you lead it. Wanton and trim young men are wont to seek for themselves, through the nurses, an approach to the foster-children by blandishments, affability, and little gifts, and, when they have gently entered, to rouse fires from sparks and gradually to advance to shamelessness, and to be by no means able to be prevented, that little verse being proved upon them: You can hardly find fault with what you allow to become a habit. It is shameful to say, and yet it must be said: noble women, destined to have nobler suitors, are coupled with men of the cheapest condition and with servants, and, under the name of religion and the shadow of continence, sometimes desert their husbands. They are Helens following Alexanders, and do not fear the Menelauses. These things are seen, are lamented, and are not avenged, because the multitude of those who sin supplies the license of sinning.

Come to her help, Lord Jesus! How many forms of torture were devised against this one creature of yours! Her hair is bound to a stake, and when her whole body has been tied yet more tightly to the rack, fire is set close to her feet; the executioner gores both her sides, and no respite is granted even to her breasts — yet the woman remains unmoved, and, her spirit cut off from the body's pain, while she enjoys the good of a clear conscience, she forbids the torments to rage about her. The cruel judge rises up as though defeated; she begs help of the Lord. Her limbs are wrenched from their joints; she lifts her eyes to heaven. Another man confesses to the common crime; she, on his behalf, denies it, and at her own peril she defends the other who stands in peril.

For in my native land, where rusticity is the homegrown speech, the belly is god, and people live for the day: the holier man is the richer one. To this dish, according to the people's worn proverb, a fitting lid has been added — the priest Lupicinus — in line too with that saying about which Lucilius says Crassus laughed but once in his life: "Like lips have like lettuce, when an ass eats a thistle." That is to say, a crippled helmsman steers a leaking ship, and the blind lead the blind into the pit, and the ruler is such as those whom he rules.

I do not want you, brother dearest, after weighing the burden of sins, to think that the offences I have spoken of are lesser than idolatry; rather, learn the verdict of the apostle, who says: "Know this, and understand, that no fornicator, or unclean person, or covetous man, which is idolatry, has any inheritance in the kingdom of God and of Christ." And although whatever belongs to the devil savours generally of opposition to God, and what is the devil's is idolatry — to which all idols are made over — yet in another place too he specifies it by particular name, saying: "Mortify your members which are upon the earth: fornication, uncleanness, evil concupiscence, and covetousness, which is the service of idols, on account of which the wrath of God comes." The service of an idol does not consist only in this, that a man cast incense pinched between two fingers onto the altar's brazier, or pour out wine drawn in a cup. Let avarice deny that it is idolatry — if it can call it righteousness that the Lord was sold for thirty pieces of silver. Let lust deny that it is sacrilege — but only that lust which has defiled the members of Christ and a living sacrifice pleasing to God with the victims of public debauchery in a foul commingling. Let it not admit that such men are idolaters, but only like those who, in the Acts of the Apostles, kept back part of the price out of their own patrimony and perished by immediate vengeance. Take note, brother: it is not lawful for you to keep anything of your own goods. "Everyone," says the Lord, "who does not renounce all that he possesses cannot be my disciple."

If Paul the apostle, a chosen vessel and prepared for the Gospel of Christ, on account of the stings of the flesh and the goads of vice, chastens his body and brings it into subjection, lest, while preaching to others, he himself be found a castaway, and yet sees another law in his members fighting against the law of his mind and taking him captive in the law of sin — if, after nakedness, fasting, hunger, prison, scourgings, and tortures, turning upon himself he cries out: \"Wretched man that I am, who shall deliver me from the body of this death?\" — do you think you ought to be secure? Take care, I beg you, lest God ever say of you: \"The virgin of Israel has fallen; there is none to raise her up.\" I speak boldly: although God can do all things, he cannot raise up a virgin after her ruin. He has power indeed to deliver from punishment, but he has no power to crown the corrupted. Let us fear lest that prophecy be fulfilled in us also: \"and the good virgins shall faint.\" Mark what he says: \"and the good virgins shall faint\" — because there are also bad virgins. \"Whoever looks on a woman to lust after her,\" he says, \"has already committed adultery with her in his heart.\" Therefore virginity perishes even in the mind. These are the bad virgins, virgins in the flesh and not in the spirit, foolish virgins, who, not having oil, are shut out by the Bridegroom.

I ask you, what have we ever done such as the apostles did, that men should rightly be offended at us? They leave their aged father with his boat and net; the publican rises from his tax-booth and follows the Savior; a disciple who wishes to return home and first take leave of his own is forbidden by the master's word; a man is not allowed to bury his father, and it is a kind of piety to be unfilial for the Lord's sake. We, because we do not wear silk garments, are judged to be monks; because we are not drunk and do not loosen our faces in guffaws, we are called continent and gloomy. If a tunic is not gleaming white, at once comes that gibe from the crossroads: "An impostor and a Greek!" Let them jeer with sharper wit if they like, and parade men stuffed out with fat little paunches: our Blesilla will laugh, and will not deign to listen to the abuse of croaking frogs, since her Lord himself was called Beelzebub.

It pleases you to bathe every day; another thinks such refinements filthy. You belch up moorfowl and boast of the sturgeon you have eaten; I fill my belly with beans. Troops of cacklers delight you, but Paula and Melania those who weep. You long for others' goods; they despise their own. Wines flavored with honey delight you; they drink cold water that they find sweeter. You think you have lost whatever you do not in the present moment swallow down, eat up, devour; and they long for things to come and believe that the things which are written are true. So be it: foolishly and like old wives, you say, are those persuaded of the resurrection of bodies; what is that to you? To us, on the contrary, your way of life is displeasing. Be fat, much good may it do you; leanness and pallor delight me. You think such men wretched; we think you the more wretched. Each in turn seems mad to the other.

Therefore let the cleric who serves the Church of Christ first interpret his own title, and, having set the definition of the name before him, strive to be what he is called. For if kleros in Greek is called sors ("lot") in Latin, clerics are so named either because they are of the Lord's lot, or because the Lord himself is the lot — that is, the portion — of the clerics. Now he who is either himself a portion of the Lord, or has the Lord as his portion, ought so to conduct himself that he both possesses the Lord and is himself possessed by the Lord. He who possesses the Lord and says with the prophet, "The Lord is my portion," can have nothing apart from the Lord; for if he have anything else besides the Lord, the Lord will not be his portion. For example, if he have gold, if silver, if possessions, if various furnishings — with such portions the Lord does not deign to become his portion. But if I am a portion of the Lord and the cord of his inheritance, and receive no portion among the rest of the tribes, but, like a Levite and a priest, live by the tithes and, serving the altar, am sustained by the offering of the altar — having food and clothing, with these I shall be content, and naked I shall follow the naked cross. I beseech you, then, and, repeating it again and again, I shall warn you, not to think the office of the clergy a kind of the old military service — that is, not to seek the world's gains in the warfare of Christ, not to have more than when you began to be a cleric, lest it be said to you: Their portions shall not profit them. Let the poor and strangers, and with them Christ, know your little table as their guest; flee like a kind of plague a cleric turned trader, made rich from poor, made glorious from low-born. Evil conversations corrupt good manners. You despise gold, another loves it; you trample on riches, he pursues them; silence, gentleness, seclusion are dear to your heart, but to him wordiness, a brazen brow, the marketplaces, the public squares, and the doctors' shops are pleasing: amid so great a discord of manners, what concord can there be?

Let women's feet rarely or never enter your little lodging. Either be equally ignorant of all maidens and virgins of Christ, or love them equally. Do not stay under the same roof; do not trust in your past chastity. You cannot be holier than David nor wiser than Solomon; remember always that a woman cast the dweller of paradise out of his possession. When you are sick, let some holy brother attend you, or a sister, or a mother, or any woman of approved faith in the eyes of all. But if there be no persons of such kinship and chastity, the Church maintains many old women who may both render service and receive a benefit by ministering, so that even your sickness may have the fruit of almsgiving. I know of some who have recovered in body and begun to sicken in soul. She ministers to you at peril whose face you frequently regard. If, on account of the clerical office, you visit a widow or a virgin, never enter the house alone, and keep such companions as will not bring you into disrepute by their company. If a reader, an acolyte, or a singer follows you, let them be adorned not with clothing but with character, nor let them curl their hair with a curling-iron, but let them promise chastity by their dress. Do not sit alone and without a witness with a woman alone. If something more private must be said, she has a nurse, the elder virgin of the house, a widow, a married woman; she is not so unsociable as to have no one but you to whom she would dare to confide. Beware of all suspicions, and whatever can plausibly be invented, avoid beforehand, that it may not be invented. Holy love has no place for frequent little gifts, napkins and garters and garments laid to the mouth, tasted morsels, and coaxing, sweet little notes. "My honey, my light, my desire," and the other follies of lovers, all the dalliances and charms and laughable refinements — these we blush at in comedies, we detest in men of the world: how much more in clerics, and in clerics who are monks, whose priesthood is adorned by their profession and whose profession by their priesthood! Nor do I say this because I fear such things in you or in holy men, but because in every profession, in every rank and sex, both good men and bad are found, and the condemnation of the worse is the praise of the good.

Beware of nurses and bearers and wine-loving creatures of that kind, who long to fill their bellies from your skin. They counsel not what profits you but what profits themselves, and often they whine out that verse: "Will you alone, mourning, waste your perpetual youth, and never know sweet children nor the rewards of love?" Where there is chastity and holiness, there is frugality; where frugality, there is loss to the servants. Whatever they have not received, they think taken from themselves, nor do they consider how much someone has, but how much they themselves receive; wherever they see a Christian, at once comes that street-cry: "The Greek, the impostor!" These men sow the foulest rumours and pretend to have heard from others what has gone out from themselves, being at once the authors and the magnifiers of it. Thence comes a report born of a lie, which, when it has reached the matrons and has been fanned by their tongues, penetrates the provinces. You may see very many raging with rabid mouth and painted face, with viperish eyes and pumice-smoothed teeth, carping at Christians. Here is some woman, who has a hyacinth-coloured cloak about her shoulders, mumbling something rancid through her stammering nostrils, and tripping up her words with her dainty palate. The whole chorus chimes in, and all the benches bark. Men of our own order are joined to them, who are both gnawed at and gnaw — talkative against us, mute on their own behalf — as though they themselves were something other than monks, and as though whatever is said against monks did not redound upon clerics too, who are the fathers of monks. The loss of the flock is the shepherd's disgrace, just as, on the other hand, that monk's life is praised who holds the priests of Christ in veneration and does not disparage the rank by which he was made a Christian.

What are we doing, O my soul? Whither do we turn? What do we take up first? What do we pass over in silence? The precepts of the rhetoricians have slipped from you, and, taken up with mourning, oppressed with tears, hindered by sobs, you do not keep the order of speaking! Where is that study of letters from infancy, and the ever-praised maxim of Anaxagoras and Telamon: "I knew that I had begotten a mortal"? We have read Crantor, whose volume Cicero followed to console his own grief; we have run through the little works of Plato, Diogenes, Clitomachus, Carneades, Posidonius, written to assuage mourning — men who in various ages, in books or letters, strove to lessen the laments of various people, so that, even if our own talent were dry, it might be watered from their fountains. They set forth innumerable men, and especially Pericles and Xenophon the Socratic, of whom the one, having lost two sons, discoursed crowned in the assembly, the other, when while sacrificing he had heard that his son was killed in war, is said to have laid down his crown and to have set it again on his head, after he found that the youth had fallen fighting bravely in the line of battle. Why should I mention the Roman generals, by whose virtues, like so many stars, the Latin histories shine? Pulvillus, while dedicating the Capitol, on hearing — so it was reported — of the sudden death of his son, ordered him to be buried in his absence; Lucius Paulus, within seven days, between the funerals of two sons, entered the city in triumph. I pass over the Maximi, the Catos, the Galli, the Pisos, the Bruti, the Scaevolae, the Metelli, the Scauri, the Marii, the Crassi, the Marcelli, and the Aufidii, whose virtue in mourning was no less than in war, and whose bereavements Tullius set forth in his book On Consolation — lest I seem to have sought what belongs to others rather than what is our own; although these things too have been briefly said to our reproach, if faith does not furnish what unbelief has shown.

This one thing I will say, which is both useful to readers and suited to the present case. She was not ashamed before the Lord on earth, and he will not be ashamed of her in heaven. She laid bare her wound to all, and weeping Rome beheld the scar on her discoloured body. She had her sides unstitched, her head bare, her mouth closed. She did not enter the church of the Lord, but, like Miriam the sister of Moses, sat apart outside the camp, that she whom the priest had cast out he might himself recall. She came down from the throne of her delights, took the millstone, ground meal, and with unshod feet passed over the floods of tears. She sat upon the fire of coals; these were her helpers. She struck the face by which she had pleased her second husband; she hated gems; she could not bear to look upon linen; she fled ornaments. So she grieved as though she had committed adultery, and with many expenditures of remedies desired to heal one wound.

Let her very dress and clothing teach her to whom she has been promised. Take care that you do not pierce her ears, that you do not paint with white lead and rouge the face consecrated to Christ, that you do not weigh down her neck with pearls and gold, that you do not load her head with gems, that you do not redden her hair and foretell for her something of the fires of Gehenna. Let her have other pearls, by selling which afterward she may buy the most precious pearl. Praetextata, once a most noble woman, at the bidding of her husband Hymetius, who was the paternal uncle of the virgin Eustochium, changed her dress and adornment, and arranged her neglected hair into a waving headdress, desiring to overcome both the virgin's resolve and the mother's longing. And behold, that very night she sees in her sleep that an angel came to her, with terrible face threatening punishments and breaking forth into these words: "Have you dared to prefer your husband's command to Christ? To handle the head of God's virgin with sacrilegious hands? Those hands shall now this instant wither, that you may feel, tormented, what you have done, and at the end of the fifth month you shall be led to hell. But if you persist in your wickedness, you shall be bereaved at once of your husband and your children." All was fulfilled in order, and a swift death sealed the late penitence of the wretched woman. Thus does Christ avenge those who violate his temple, thus does he defend his gems and most precious ornaments. And I have related this not because I wish to insult the calamities of the unfortunate, but to warn you with how great fear and caution you ought to keep what you have promised to the Lord.

What then? Is it a crime to have the companionship of a holy man? You drag me into court by the throat, that I should either prove what I do not wish, or undergo the ill-will of many. A holy man never separates a daughter from a mother; he respects both, he venerates both. However holy the daughter may be, a widowed mother is a sign of chastity. If that certain someone is your contemporary, let him honour your mother as his own; if older, let him love you as a daughter and subject you to a parent's discipline. It is not expedient for the reputation of both that you love him more than your mother, lest he seem to choose in you not affection but age. And I would say this even if you had not a brother who is a monk, if you lacked the protections of your household; but now — alas! — between a mother and a brother, and a widowed mother and a brother who is a monk, why does a stranger thrust himself in? It is good indeed that you should know yourself both a daughter and a sister; but if you cannot do both, and the mother is rejected as harsh, let at least the brother please. If the brother is rather rough, let her be gentler who bore you. Why do you turn pale? Why do you seethe? Why do you suffuse your face with a blush, and, with quivering lips, testify to the impatience of your breast? Nothing surpasses the love of a mother and a brother except the affection of a wife alone.

I know that I shall offend very many, who refer a general discussion of the vices to their own reproach, and, while they are angry with me, reveal their own conscience, and judge much worse of themselves than of me. For I will name no one, nor, with the license of the old comedy, will I choose out and brand definite persons. It is the part of a prudent man and of prudent women to dissemble — nay, to amend — what they understand in themselves, and to be indignant with themselves rather than with me, and not to heap curses on the admonisher, who, even if he be held by the same crimes, is certainly better in this, that his own evils do not please him.

No noble woman at Rome at that time had known the profession of the monks, nor dared, on account of the novelty of the thing, to assume a name then accounted disgraceful and cheap among the peoples. She learned, from the priests of Alexandria, and from Pope Athanasius and afterward Peter — who, fleeing the persecution of the Arian heresy, had taken refuge at Rome as in the safest harbour of their communion — the life of the blessed Antony, then still living, and the monasteries of Pachomius in the Thebaid, and the discipline of virgins and widows; nor did she blush to profess what she had learned to be pleasing to Christ. Many years after, Sophronia imitated her, and others, to whom that saying of Ennius can most rightly be applied: Would that not in the Pelian grove. Of her friendship the venerable Paula enjoyed; in her chamber Eustochium, the glory of virginity, was nurtured, so that it is easy to reckon what the teacher was, where the pupils were such. The unbelieving reader will perhaps laugh at me for lingering in the praises of weak women; but if he recall the holy women, the companions of the Lord and Saviour, who ministered to him of their substance, and the three Marys standing before the cross, and Mary Magdalene in particular, who, for her diligence and the ardour of her faith, received the name "towered," and first, before the apostles, deserved to see Christ rising again, he will condemn himself of pride rather than us of folly, who judge of virtues not by sex but by mind. Hence too Jesus loved John the evangelist most, who, on account of the nobility of his birth, was known to the high priest and did not fear the snares of the Jews, so much so that he brought Peter into the hall, and alone of the apostles stood before the cross, and received the Saviour's mother into his own keeping, that a virgin son might receive, as the inheritance of the virgin Lord, the virgin mother.

Oh, the wickedness! The world is falling to ruin, and in us our sins do not fall. The renowned city, the head of the Roman Empire, has been swallowed up by one conflagration. There is no region that does not have its exiles. Churches once sacred have fallen into ashes and embers, and yet we are zealous for avarice. We live as though about to die the next day, and we build as though always about to live in this world. The walls gleam with gold, the panelled ceilings with gold, the capitals of the columns shine with gold, and naked and hungry before our doors Christ dies in the person of the poor. We read that Aaron the high priest went to meet the raging flames, and, the censer kindled, checked the wrath of God; the great priest stood between death and life, and the fire dared not advance beyond his footsteps. God says to Moses: Let me alone, and I will destroy this people. When he says "Let me alone," he shows that he is held back from doing what he had threatened; for the servant's prayers were hindering the power of God. Who, do you think, is there under heaven who could now meet the wrath of God, who could go to meet the flames and, with the Apostle, say: I myself wished to be anathema for my brethren? The flocks perish with the shepherds, because, as the people, so the priest. Moses spoke with the affection of compassion: If you forgive this people, forgive; but if not, blot me out of your book. He wishes to perish with those who perish, nor is he content with his own salvation. For the glory of a king is the multitude of his people. In these times Pacatula was born; amid these rattles she snatches her first age, destined to know tears before laughter, to feel weeping before joy. Scarcely has she entered, and already is the exit; she thinks the world has always been such. She knows not the past, she flees the present, she desires the future. That I should dictate these things in hasty speech, and that I, an old man, should write to an infant, after the deaths of friends and perpetual mourning, by a long return from exile, your love, brother Gaudentius, impelled me; and to give my hand to one asking less than nothing at all — because in the one case the will is oppressed by grief, in the other there is a dissembling of friendship.

Meanwhile her one voice: "Strike, burn, tear me apart; I did not do it. If my words win no belief, a day will come that will weigh this charge with care; I shall have my own Judge." By now the weary torturer was sighing in his groans, and there was no room left for a fresh wound; by now his cruelty was beaten, and he shuddered at the body he had mangled. At once the consular, roused to anger, said: "Why do you wonder, you who stand around, that the woman would rather be tortured than die? Adultery surely cannot be committed without two parties, and I hold it more credible that a guilty defendant should deny a crime than that an innocent young man should confess to one."

Our common mother — who, though joined to you in holiness, surpasses you in this, that she gave birth to such children, and whose womb may truly be called golden — we greet with that honour you know of; and likewise her sisters, to be looked up to by all, who have conquered their sex along with the world, who, with oil abundantly prepared for their lamps, await the coming of the Bridegroom. O blessed house, in which dwell Anna the widow, virgin prophetesses, a twofold Samuel reared in the temple! O happy dwellings, in which we behold a martyr mother girt with the crowns of the Maccabean martyrs! For although you confess Christ daily, while you keep his commandments, yet to this private glory there has come to you a public and open confession — that through you the poison of the Arian doctrine was once driven out from your city. And perhaps you wonder that, at the very end of my letter, I have begun again. What am I to do? I have no power to deny my heart its voice. The brevity of a letter compels me to be silent, longing for you forces me to speak. My speech runs ahead of itself; my discourse is thrown into confusion; love knows no order.

Why are you a Christian with a timid spirit? Look at the net abandoned, along with the father; look at the publican rising from the toll-booth, at once an apostle. "The Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head" — and you measure out broad porticoes and the vast spaces of roofs? You await an inheritance of this world, you who are a co-heir of Christ? Interpret the word 'monk,' which is your name: what are you doing in a crowd, you who are alone? And this I urge as forewarning, not like a skilled sailor whose vessel and cargo are still whole giving notice to men ignorant of the waves, but, like one but lately cast up on the shore from a shipwreck, I warn those about to sail with a fearful voice. In that surge the Charybdis of luxury swallows up salvation; there, with a maiden's face, lust, smiling like Scylla, allures men to work the shipwreck of their chastity; here is the barbarous shore, here the devil the pirate with his companions carries chains for those he means to take. Do not believe, do not be without care. Though the spread-out sea smile like a still pool, though the surface of the lying element scarcely ruffle its back under the breeze, this great plain has its mountains; the danger is shut up within, within is the enemy. Make ready the ropes, hoist the sails. Let the cross of the yard-arm be fixed upon your brow: this calm is a storm.

What then? Are not those who are in the city Christians? Your case is not the same as the others'. Listen to the Lord saying: "If you would be perfect, go, sell all you have and give to the poor, and come, follow me." But you have promised to be perfect. For when, having left the army, you made yourself a eunuch for the sake of the kingdom of heaven, what else did you pursue but the perfect life? And the perfect servant of Christ has nothing besides Christ; if he has anything besides Christ, he is not perfect. And if he is not perfect, then, since he promised God that he would be perfect, he lied beforehand. But "the mouth that lies kills the soul." Therefore, to conclude: if you are perfect, why do you desire your father's goods? If you are not perfect, you have deceived the Lord. The Gospel thunders with divine voices: "You cannot serve two masters" — and does anyone dare make Christ a liar by serving both Mammon and the Lord? He cries out again and again: "If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me." And shall I, laden with gold, think that I am following Christ? "He who says that he abides in Christ ought himself also to walk as he walked."

But if even those virgins are virgins, yet on account of other faults are not saved by the virginity of their bodies, what shall become of those who have prostituted the members of Christ and changed the temples of the Holy Spirit into a brothel? At once they will hear: \"Come down, sit in the dust, virgin daughter of Babylon; sit on the ground; there is no throne for the daughter of the Chaldeans. You shall no more be called soft and delicate. Take the millstone, grind the meal, uncover your veil, bare your legs, cross the rivers, and your shame shall be revealed and your disgrace shall appear\" — and this after the bridal chambers of the Son of God, after the kisses of the kinsman and Bridegroom, the woman of whom the prophetic word once sang in harmony: \"The queen stood at your right hand in gilded clothing, surrounded with variety.\" She shall be stripped, and her hinder parts shall be set before her own face; she shall sit by the waters of the wilderness, and, with her vessel set down, shall spread her legs to every passer-by, and shall be polluted to the very crown of her head. It would have been better for a person to have undergone marriage, to have walked on the level ground, than, while striving for higher things, to fall into the depth of hell.

Let not faithful Sion become a harlot city, I beg, lest after the lodging of the Trinity demons dance there and sirens and hedgehogs make their nests. Let not the breast-band be loosed; but as soon as lust tickles the senses, as soon as the soft fire of pleasure has flooded us with its sweet warmth, let us break out into the cry: \"The Lord is my helper; I will not fear what the flesh may do to me.\" When the inner man begins to waver even a little between vices and virtues, say: \"Why are you sad, my soul, and why do you trouble me? Hope in the Lord, for I will confess to him, the salvation of my countenance and my God.\" I do not want you to let the thought grow; let nothing of Babylon, nothing of confusion, grow up in you. While the enemy is small, kill him; let wickedness be crushed in the seed. Hear the psalmist speaking: \"O wretched daughter of Babylon, blessed is he who shall repay you your recompense; blessed is he who shall take and dash your little ones against the rock.\" Since, then, it is impossible that the inborn heat of the marrow should not rush into the senses of man, that man is praised, that man is proclaimed blessed, who, as soon as he begins to think, kills the thoughts and dashes them against the rock: and the rock is Christ.

These things, my lady Asella, I wrote in haste, weeping and grieving, just as I was about to go aboard ship; and I give thanks to my God that I am counted worthy to be one whom the world hates. But pray that I may return from Babylon to Jerusalem, and that Nebuchadnezzar may not rule over me, but Jesus, the son of Josedech; that Ezra, whose name is interpreted "helper," may come and bring me back to my own homeland. Foolish was I, who wished to sing the Lord's song in a foreign land, and, having deserted Mount Zion, begged the help of Egypt. I did not remember the Gospel: that the man who goes down from Jerusalem at once falls among robbers, is stripped, wounded, and left for dead. But although priest and Levite pass him by, that Samaritan is merciful—to whom, when it was said, "You are a Samaritan and have a demon," he denied the demon but did not deny that he was a Samaritan, for whom we call the Keeper the Hebrews call the Samaritan. Some chatter that I am a worker of magic; I, a servant, acknowledge the title of faith; the Jews too called my Lord a magician, and the apostle was called a seducer. No temptation has laid hold of me but such as is common to man. How small a portion of hardships have I endured, I who serve the cross? They have brought against me the infamy of a false charge, but I know that it is through good report and ill report that one comes to the kingdom of heaven.

I am ashamed to say it: the priests of idols, mime-actors and charioteers and harlots receive inheritances; to clerics and monks alone this is forbidden by law — and forbidden not by persecutors but by Christian emperors. Nor do I complain of the law, but I grieve that we have deserved this law. A cautery is a good thing, but what is the wound that I should need a cautery? The provision of the law is foresighted and stern, and yet not even thus is avarice restrained. By trusts we mock the laws, and, as though the decrees of emperors were greater than those of Christ, we fear the laws and despise the Gospels. Let there be an heir, but the mother of her sons — that is, the Church, the mother of his flock — who bore them, nourished them, and fed them. Why do we thrust ourselves between mother and children? It is the glory of a bishop to provide for the needs of the poor; it is the shame of all priests to study their own riches. Born in a poor house and in a country hut, I who could scarcely fill my roaring belly with millet and coarse bread now turn up my nose at fine flour and honey; I know the kinds and the names of fishes, on what shore a shellfish was gathered; by their flavour I distinguish the provinces of birds, and at last the very rarity of foods and their cost delight me. I hear, moreover, of the shameful servility of some men toward childless old men and women. They themselves set out the chamber-pot, they besiege the bed, and with their own hands they take up the corrupt matter of the stomach and the phlegm of the lungs. They tremble at the entrance of the physician, and with quivering lips ask whether the patient is better; and if the old man grows a little stronger, they are in peril, and with feigned gladness the mind within is tortured with avarice. For they fear lest they lose their service, and they compare the long-lived old man to the years of Methuselah. Oh, how great would be the reward with the Lord, if he hoped for no present price! With what great sweats is a vain inheritance sought! With less labour Christ's pearl might have been bought.

I have said these things, my daughter in Christ, not doubting of your purpose — for you would never have asked for a letter of exhortation if you wavered about the good of a single marriage — but that you might understand the wickedness of the servants who carry you about for sale, the snares of your kinsfolk, and the well-meaning error of your father, to whom, though I grant love toward you, I do not grant knowledge of love, saying with the Apostle: I confess, they have a zeal for God, but not according to knowledge. Imitate rather — for I shall repeat it again and again — your holy mother, of whom, as often as I recall her, there comes to my mind her ardour for Christ, her pallor from fasting, her almsgiving to the poor, her service to the servants of God, her humility both of heart and of dress, and in all things her moderate speech. Let your father — whom I name for honour's sake, not because he is of consular and patrician rank, but because he is a Christian — fulfil his name and rejoice that he has begotten a daughter for Christ, not for the world; nay rather, let him grieve that you have both lost your virginity in vain and lost the fruit of your marriage. Where is the husband whom he gave you? Even had he been lovable, even had he been good, death would have ended everything, and destruction would have dissolved the bond of the flesh. Seize the occasion, I beg, and make a virtue of necessity. In Christians it is not the beginning that is sought, but the end: Paul began ill, but ended well; Judas's beginnings are praised, but his end is condemned for treachery. Read Ezekiel: The righteousness of the righteous shall not deliver him, in whatever day he shall sin, and the wickedness of the wicked shall not harm him, in whatever day he shall turn from his wickedness. This is the ladder of Jacob, by which the angels ascend and descend, on which the Lord leans, stretching out his hand to the fallen and sustaining the weary steps of those who climb by the contemplation of himself. But as he does not will the death of the sinner, but only that he should turn and live, so he hates the lukewarm and they quickly make him sick. To whom more is forgiven, he loves the more.

Let us come, then, to our own. I will not lament with Jacob and David their sons who die under the Law, but with Christ in the Gospel I will receive those who rise again. The mourning of the Jews is the joy of Christians. In the evening weeping shall linger, and in the morning gladness. The night has gone before, but the day has drawn near. Hence too Moses, dying, is mourned, while Joshua is buried on the mountain without funeral and tears. Whatever can be said from the Scriptures about lamentation, we set forth briefly in that book in which we consoled Paula at Rome. Now we must come to the same place by another path, lest we seem to tread footsteps once past and worn.

We have lingered long on her penitence, in which we have settled as in shallow places, that a greater field of her praises, without any hindrance, might open before us. Received under the eyes of the whole Church into communion, what did she do? Did she, forsooth, in the good day forget her ills, and after shipwreck wish again to try the perils of sailing? Nay rather, the whole fortune she could have — and it was very ample, answering to her birth — she broke up and sold, and, gathered into money, prepared it for the uses of the poor. And first of all she established a hospital, in which she might gather the sick from the streets and refresh the limbs of the wretched, worn out by sickness and want. Shall I now describe the various calamities of men — the mutilated noses, the gouged eyes, the half-burned feet, the livid hands, the swollen bellies, the wasted thighs, the bloated legs, and the little worms swarming in the eaten and putrid flesh? How often did she carry on her own shoulders those consumed by jaundice and filth! How often did she wash the festering matter of wounds which another could not bear to look at! She furnished food with her own hand, and watered the breathing corpse with little sips. I know that many rich and religious people, on account of the weakness of their stomach, exercise mercy of this kind through the services of others, and are merciful with money, not with the hand. These indeed I do not blame, and I by no means interpret tenderness of mind as unbelief; but as I grant pardon to the weakness of the stomach, so I bear to heaven with my praises the ardour of a perfect mind. This great faith despises such things; it knows what the rich man in purple once failed to do for Lazarus, and to what retribution that proud mind was condemned. He whom we despise, whom we cannot bear to see, at whose sight a vomiting bursts from us, is like ourselves, formed of the same clay with us, compacted of the same elements. Whatever he suffers, we too can suffer. Let us reckon his wounds our own, and all hardness of mind toward another will be broken by a merciful thought toward ourselves. Not if I had a hundred tongues and a hundred mouths, a voice of iron, could I run through all the names of the diseases which Fabiola turned into such great refreshments for the wretched, that many of the poor in health envied the sick. And yet she was of like generosity toward clerics and monks and virgins — what monastery was not sustained by her wealth? Whom, naked and bedridden, did the garments of Fabiola not cover? Upon whom of the needy did her headlong and hasty bounty not pour itself out? Rome was too narrow for her mercy; she traversed the islands, therefore. She went round the Tuscan sea and the province of the Volsci, and the hidden bays of the curving shores, in which the choirs of monks are settled, either in her own person or by a bounty sent through faithful and holy men.

The priest Eli offended the Lord on account of the vices of his children; he cannot become a bishop who has had children luxurious and not subject. But on the contrary it is written of a woman that she shall be saved by the bearing of children, if she continue in faith and love and sanctification with modesty. If the perfect age, and one of legal responsibility, is imputed to the parents, how much more the suckling and frail child, who, according to the Lord's saying, does not know her right hand from her left — that is, knows not the difference between good and evil! You provide anxiously that your daughter may not be struck by a viper; why do you not provide with the same care that she may not be smitten by the hammer of the whole earth, that she may not drink from the golden cup of Babylon, that she may not go out with Dinah and wish to see the daughters of a strange land, that she may not play with her feet, that she may not drag her tunics? Poisons are not given except smeared round with honey, and vices do not deceive except under the appearance and shadow of virtues. And how, you will say, are the sins of the fathers not rendered to the children, nor those of the children to the parents, but the soul that sins shall itself die? This is said of those who can have understanding, of whom it is written in the Gospel: He is of age, let him speak for himself. But he who is a little one and has understanding as a little one, until he comes to the years of understanding and the letter of Pythagoras brings him to the fork in the road, his evils as well as his goods are imputed to his parents — unless perhaps you reckon that the children of Christians, if they have not received baptism, are themselves alone guilty of sin, and that the crime is not referred to those who refused to give it, especially at the time when those who were to receive it could not contradict; just as, on the other side, the salvation of children is the gain of their elders. Whether or not to offer your daughter was in your power — although your condition is different, who vowed her before you conceived her — but to neglect her, once offered, pertains to your peril. He who offers a lame and mutilated victim, or one stained with any defilement, is guilty of sacrilege; how much more shall he be punished who, having prepared a part of his own body and the purity of an undefiled soul for the royal embraces, has been negligent!

I hear, besides, that you go about the suburbs, the pleasant places of country houses, with relations and kinsfolk and men of that kind. Nor do I doubt that it is either a cousin or a sister to whose solace you are led as an attendant of a new kind — for far be it that, however near and kindred they be, I should suspect you of seeking the company of men — I beg you, then, virgin, to answer me: do you go alone in the company of your kinsfolk, or with your lover? However shameless you may be, you will not dare to thrust him upon the eyes of worldlings. For if you do this, the whole household will sing of you and him, all men's fingers will mark you out, and even the sister or relation or cousin who, in flattery of you, call him in your presence "holy" and "father," if he turns himself a little aside, will laugh at the monstrous husband. But if you go alone — which I rather think — surely among young servants, among married women and women about to marry, among wanton girls and long-haired and linen-clad young men, you, a girl in dark clothing, will walk. Some little bearded fellow will give you his hand, will support you when weary, and, with pressed fingers, will either be tempted or will tempt. There will be a banquet for you among men and matrons: you will await another's kisses, foretasted foods, and, without scandal to yourself, will admire silken and gilded garments on others. At the very banquet too, that you may eat meat, you are as if compelled against your will; that you may drink wine, the creature of God is praised; that you may wash in the baths, squalor is disparaged; and all will cry out that you, when you have done anything of what they urge, drawing back from it, are pure, simple, a mistress, and truly noble. Meanwhile some singer will sound at the table, and, among the psalms running with sweet modulation, since he will not dare to look at other men's wives, he will more often glance back at you, who have no guardian. He will speak by nods, and whatever he fears to say he will signify by his feelings. Amid these and so great allurements of pleasures, lust tames even iron minds, which suffers a greater hunger in virgins, since it thinks everything sweeter that it does not know. The fables of the heathen tell that by the songs of the Sirens sailors were dashed headlong onto the rocks, and that to the cithara of Orpheus the trees and beasts and the hardness of flint were softened. With difficulty is chastity preserved amid feasts. A gleaming skin displays a filthy mind.

I hear that you have a religious mother, a widow of many years, who nourished you, who instructed you as an infant, and after the studies of the Gauls, which are of the most flourishing, sent you to Rome, not sparing expense, and bearing the absence of her son in the hope of the future, that Roman gravity might season the richness and brilliance of Gallic speech, and use upon you not spurs but reins — as we read also of the most eloquent men of Greece, who dried the Asian swelling with Attic salt, and pruned back the luxuriant vines with sickles, that the wine-presses of eloquence might overflow not with the foliage of words, but with the squeezings, as it were, of the grapes of meaning. Receive her as a parent, love her as a nurse, venerate her as holy. Nor imitate the example of others, who leave their own and seek the women of strangers, whose disgrace is in the open, seeking suspect companionships under the names of piety. I myself have known some, now of riper age and most of freedman stock, to delight in young men and seek spiritual sons, and, modesty being gradually overcome, to burst out under the feigned names of mothers into a marital license. Others forsake their virgin sisters and are coupled with strange widows. There are women who hate their own and are fondled by affection for those not their own, whose impatience, the index of the mind, admits no excuse and tears apart the empty veils of unchastity like spiders' webs. You may see not a few, with girded loins, in a dark tunic, with a long beard, unable to depart from women, dwelling under the same roof, going to banquets together, having young maids in their service, and, except for the name of marriage, all that belongs to marriage. Nor is it the fault of the Christian name if a feigner of religion be in vice; nay rather, it is the confusion of the heathen, when they see that those things displease the churches which do not please all good men.

For very many years, then, she so passed her age that she saw herself an old woman before she remembered that she had been a young one, praising that Platonic saying, who had said that philosophy is a meditation on death. Hence our Apostle too: I die daily by your salvation; and the Lord, according to the ancient copies: Unless a man take up his cross daily and follow me, he cannot be my disciple; and long before, through the prophet, the Holy Spirit: For your sake we are put to death all the day long; we are accounted as sheep for the slaughter; and after many ages that sentence: Remember always the day of death, and you shall never sin; and the precept of the most eloquent satirist: Live mindful of death; the hour flies; this that I speak is already gone. So then — as we had begun to say — she led her age and lived so as always to believe herself about to die. So she was clothed in garments that she might remember the sepulchre, offering a reasonable, living sacrifice, pleasing to God.

So the same sentence was pronounced upon both, and the executioner dragged the condemned away. The whole people poured out to the spectacle, and just as though the city were thought to be moving house, the crowd burst through the crammed gates and pressed thick together. And indeed the most wretched young man's head was struck off by the sword at the very first stroke, and his headless corpse rolled in its own blood. But when it came to the woman, and she had bent her knees to the ground and the flashing sword was raised over her trembling neck, and the executioner had hurled his practised right arm forward with all his strength — at the first touch of the body the deadly point halted, and, lightly grazing the skin, it drew only the blood of a slight scratch. The slayer was terrified at his own feeble hand and, marvelling at his beaten right arm as the sword seemed to wilt, he swung it round for a second blow. Once more the blade slid limply onto the woman and, as if the steel feared to touch the accused, it lay numb and harmless about her neck. And so the lictor, raging and gasping, twisted his cloak back over her neck, and, while he was summoning all his strength, he shook to the ground the brooch that bit at the edges of the mantle; unaware of it, he poised the sword for the wound — when the woman said: "There, the gold has fallen from your shoulder. Pick up what cost so much labour to earn, so that it is not lost."

But if you have nothing — as I know you will answer — why, being so well prepared for war, do you not serve as a soldier? Unless perhaps you think to do so in your own country, when the Lord did no signs in his own. And why this? Take the reason on his authority: "No prophet has honour in his own country." "I do not seek honour," you will say; "my own conscience is enough for me." Neither did the Lord seek it — he who fled away lest he be made king by the crowds. But where there is no honour, there is contempt; where contempt, there frequent injury; and where injury, there indignation; where indignation, there is no rest; where there is no rest, the mind is often drawn away from its purpose; and where, through this unrest, something is taken away from one's pursuit, it is made less by what is taken away; and where there is something less, it cannot be called perfect. From this reckoning the sum comes out: that a monk cannot be perfect in his own country. But not to wish to be perfect is to be at fault.

O how often, when I was set in the desert, in that vast solitude which, scorched by the sun's heat, offers a dreadful dwelling-place to monks, did I imagine myself amid the delights of Rome! I sat alone, for I was filled with bitterness. My limbs were shapeless and bristling in sackcloth; my squalid skin had taken on the foulness of an Ethiopian's flesh. Daily there were tears, daily there was groaning, and if ever sleep, threatening, overcame me as I struggled against it, I bruised my bare bones, scarcely clinging together, on the naked ground. Of food and drink I say nothing, since even the sick use only cold water, and to have taken anything cooked is held to be luxury. And yet I — I who out of fear of hell had condemned myself to such a prison, the companion only of scorpions and wild beasts — often imagined myself amid the dances of girls. My face was pale with fasting, and my mind was hot with desires in a cold body, and before the man himself, already dead in his flesh, the fires of lust alone seethed. So, destitute of all help, I lay at the feet of Jesus, I bathed them with tears, I wiped them with my hair, and I subdued the rebelling flesh with the fasting of whole weeks. I am not ashamed of my wretchedness; rather, I lament that I am not what I was. I remember that I often joined the day to the night with my cries, and did not cease beating my breast until calm returned at the Lord's rebuke. I came to dread even my own little cell as though it were privy to my thoughts, and, angry and stern with myself, I would go alone into the deserts. Wherever I saw the hollows of valleys, the rough places of mountains, the sheer drops of crags, there was the place for my prayer, there the prison-house of my most wretched flesh; and — as the Lord himself is my witness — after many tears, after fixing my eyes on heaven, I sometimes seemed to myself to be among the hosts of angels, and joyful and glad I would sing: \"After you we run, in the fragrance of your ointments.\"

Greet Paula and Eustochium—whether the world will it or not, they are mine in Christ—greet the mother Albina and the sisters, the two Marcellas, Marcellina too, and holy Felicity, and say to them: "We shall stand before the judgment seat of Christ; there it will be made plain in what spirit each one has lived." Remember me, you pattern of chastity and signal example of virginity, and calm the waves of the sea with your prayers.

Read the divine Scriptures often — indeed, let the sacred reading never be laid down from your hands. Learn what you may teach; hold fast the faithful word which is according to doctrine, that you may be able both to exhort in sound teaching and to convince the gainsayers. Continue in the things which you have learned and which have been entrusted to you, knowing from whom you have learned them, always ready to give an answer to everyone who asks you a reason of the hope that is in you. Let not your works confound your speech, lest, when you speak in the church, anyone silently reply: "Why, then, do you not do these things yourself?" He is a dainty master who, with full belly, disputes about fastings; even a thief can accuse avarice; let the mind and the mouth of Christ's priest agree. Be subject to your bishop, and look up to him as to the parent of your soul: to love is the part of sons, to fear the part of servants. "And if I am a father," he says, "where is my honour? And if I am a master, where is my fear?" In the same man you have more than one name to regard: monk, bishop, uncle. But let bishops too know that they are priests, not lords: let them honour clerics as clerics, that they too may be reverenced by clerics as bishops. There is a witty saying of the orator Domitius: "Shall I," he says, "hold you as a chief, when you do not hold me as a senator?" What Aaron and his sons were, that let us understand the bishop and the presbyters to be: one Lord, one temple, let there be also one ministry.
