Let them always recall what the apostle Peter enjoins upon priests: Feed the flock of the Lord which is among you, taking care of it not by constraint, but willingly, according to God; not for the sake of base gain, but freely; not as lording it over the clergy, but being made an example to the flock from the heart, so that, when the chief of the shepherds shall appear, you may receive the unfading crown of glory. It is a most wretched custom in certain churches for the presbyters to keep silent, and not to speak when the bishops are present, as though the bishops either envied them or did not deign to hear them. "And if anything," says the apostle Paul, "be revealed to another that sits by, let the first hold his peace. For you may all prophesy one by one, that all may learn and all may be comforted. And the spirits of the prophets are subject to the prophets: for God is not the God of dissension, but of peace." A wise son is the glory of his father; let the bishop rejoice in his own judgment, when he has chosen such priests for Christ.

That harlot in the Gospel was saved by being baptized in her own tears and by the hair, which had deceived many before, with which she wiped the feet of the Lord. She had no curling caps nor creaking little shoes nor eyes blackened with antimony — the fouler, the fairer. What place have rouge and white lead on the face of a Christian woman? Of these the one counterfeits the redness of the cheeks and lips, the other the whiteness of the face and neck: fires for young men, fuel for lusts, signs of an unchaste mind. How can she weep for her sins who lays her skin bare with tears and draws furrows in her face? That adornment is not the Lord's; that veiling is Antichrist's. With what confidence does she lift up to heaven a face that her Maker would not recognize? In vain is youth alleged and the age of girlhood asserted: a widow who has ceased to please her husband and is, according to the Apostle, truly a widow, has need of nothing but perseverance. She remembers her former pleasure, she knows what she has lost, in what she delighted: the burning arrows of the devil must be quenched with the cold of fastings and vigils. Either we must speak as we are dressed, or be dressed as we speak. Why do we promise one thing and display another? The tongue rings out chastity, and the whole body proclaims unchastity.

We know indeed that our Nepotian is with Christ and mingled among the choirs of the saints, and that what among us he searched out from afar on earth and sought by reasoning, there, seeing it close at hand, he says: As we have heard, so also we have seen in the city of the Lord of hosts, in the city of our God. But the longing for his absence we cannot bear, grieving not for his lot but for our own. The happier he is, the more are we in grief, that we lack so great a good. The sisters too wept for Lazarus, whom they knew would rise again; and, to express the true feelings of a man, the Saviour himself wept for him whom he was about to raise. His Apostle too, who had said, I desire to be dissolved and to be with Christ, and elsewhere, To me to live is Christ, and to die is gain, gives thanks that Epaphras was restored to him from the nearness of death, lest he should have sorrow upon sorrow — not from the fear of unbelief, but from the longing of love. How much more do you — both uncle and bishop, that is, a father in the flesh and in the spirit — long for your own heart, and sigh for it as if torn away from you! But I beseech you to set a measure to your grief, mindful of that maxim: Nothing in excess; and, your wound bound up a little, hear the praises of him whose virtue ever gladdened you, and grieve not that you have lost such a one, but rejoice that you have had such a one; and, as those who paint the regions of the earth on a small tablet, so in this little volume may you discern the marks of his virtues sketched, not fully drawn, and receive from us not strength but goodwill.

Hence suddenly, and against the expectation of all, she sailed to Jerusalem, where, received by the concourse of many, she for a little while used our hospitality; and recalling that companionship, I seem to myself still to see what I saw. Good Jesus, with what fervour, with what zeal she was intent upon the divine volumes, and, as if desiring to satisfy a kind of hunger, she ran through the prophets, the gospels, and the psalms, proposing questions and storing up their solutions in the little cabinet of her breast! Nor indeed was she satisfied with the desire of hearing, but, adding knowledge, she added grief, and, as if you were to add oil to a flame, she took the fuel of a greater ardour. One day, when we held the Numbers in the hands of Moses, and she modestly asked me what was meant by so great a heap of names, why the several tribes were variously joined in some places and in others, how Balaam the soothsayer so prophesied the future mysteries of Christ that hardly any of the prophets foretold of him so openly, I answered as I could, and seemed to satisfy her inquiry. Turning over the book, then, she came to that place where the catalogue is described of all the stations through which the people, going out of Egypt, came as far as the streams of the Jordan. And when she asked the causes and reasons of each, in some I hesitated, in others I ran with unstumbling foot, in most I simply confessed my ignorance. But then she began to press me the more, and, as if it were not lawful for me not to know what I did not know, to expostulate and to say that she was unworthy of such great mysteries. Why say more? The shame of refusing wrung from me a promise of a proper work of this kind of little discussion for her, which up to the present time, as I now understand, by the will of the Lord deferred, is rendered to her memory, so that, clothed in the priestly garments of the former volume to herself, she may rejoice that through the wilderness of this world she has at last come to the land of promise.

After she begins to be a little grown and to increase, after the example of her Bridegroom, in wisdom, in age, and in grace with God and men, let her go with her parents to the temple of the true Father, but let her not go out of the temple with them. Let them seek her on the road of the world, among the crowds and the throng of kinsfolk, and let them find her nowhere else but in the inner shrine of the Scriptures, inquiring of the prophets and apostles about the spiritual nuptials. Let her imitate Mary, whom Gabriel found alone in her chamber, and who therefore perhaps was terrified with fear, because she beheld a man whom she was not accustomed to see. Let her emulate her of whom it is said: All the glory of the king's daughter is from within; and let her too speak, wounded by the chosen dart of love: The king has brought me into his chamber. Let her never go out, lest those who go about the city find her, lest they strike and wound her, and, taking away the veil of her chastity, leave her naked in her blood; nay rather, when anyone knocks at her door, let her say: I am a wall, and my breasts are a tower. I have washed my feet; I cannot defile them.

As a boy I read in the schools — and we have beheld bronzes breathing in the public squares — that someone, scarcely clinging to his bones, burned with unlawful loves, and was deprived of life before the disease. What will you do, a girl of sound body, dainty, plump, ruddy, seething amid meats, amid wines and baths, next to married women, next to young men? Even if, when asked, you do not yield, yet you may think it a testimony to your beauty if you are asked. A lustful mind pursues the honourable more ardently, and suspects what is not allowed to be sweeter. The very cheap and dark dress is a sign of a silent mind, if it has no wrinkle, if it is dragged along the ground that you may seem taller, if the tunic is deliberately unstitched that something within may appear, and it covers what is foul and uncovers what is comely. The walker's little black and gleaming shoe too, by its creaking, calls young men to her. The breasts are compressed with bands, and the chest is bound more tightly with a crisping girdle. The hair flows down either onto the forehead or onto the ears. Sometimes the cloak falls, to bare the white shoulders, and, as though she had not wished to be seen, she hastily hides what she willingly drew back. And when in public she covers her face as if out of modesty, with a harlot's art she shows that alone which, being shown, can please the more.

But you, if you wish to be a monk and not to seem one, have care not of your household estate, which by renouncing you began to be this, but of your soul. Let the squalor of your garments be a sign of a white mind, let a cheap tunic prove your contempt of the world — provided only that the mind does not swell, that the dress and the speech do not disagree. Do not seek the warmth of the baths, you who desire to extinguish the heat of the body by the cold of fastings. Let these too be moderate, lest by their excess they weaken the stomach and, demanding a greater refreshment, break out into indigestion, which is the parent of lusts. Modest and temperate food is useful both to the flesh and to the soul. See your mother in such a way that you are not compelled through her to see others, whose faces may cling to your heart, And the silent wound lives beneath the breast. Know that the little maids who are in her service are a snare to you, because, the cheaper their condition, the easier the fall. John the Baptist too had a holy mother and was a pontiff's son, and yet he was not overcome either by his mother's affection or by his father's wealth, so as to live in his parents' house with peril to his chastity. He lived in the desert, and with eyes longing for Christ deigned to look upon nothing else. A rough garment, a leathern belt, food of locusts and wild honey, all things prepared for virtue and continence. The sons of the prophets — whom we read in the Old Testament as monks — built themselves little huts by the streams of the Jordan, and, the crowds of the cities left behind, lived on barley-meal and wild herbs. As long as you are in your own country, have your cell for a paradise; pluck the various fruits of the Scriptures, use these delights, enjoy their embrace. If your eye, your foot, your hand offend you, cast them off. Spare no one, that you may spare your soul alone. Whoever shall look upon a woman to lust after her has already committed adultery with her in his heart. Who shall glory that he has a chaste heart? The stars are not clean in the sight of the Lord: how much less men, whose life is a temptation! Woe to us, who, as often as we lust, so often we fornicate. My sword, he says, is drunk in heaven: how much more on the earth, which brings forth thorns and thistles. The vessel of election, in whose mouth Christ sounded, wears down his body and subjects it to servitude, and yet perceives the natural ardour of the flesh to fight against his own resolve, so that he is compelled to do what he does not wish, and, as if suffering violence, he cries out and says: Wretched man that I am, who shall deliver me from the body of this death? And do you reckon that you can pass without a fall and a wound, unless with all custody you keep your heart and say with the Saviour: My mother and my brethren are these, who do the will of my Father? That cruelty is piety; nay, what is so pious as for a holy son to guard a holy mother? She too wishes that you should live, not that she should see you for a time, that she may see you always with Christ. Anna begot Samuel not for herself, but for the tabernacle. The sons of Jonadab, who drank no wine or strong drink, who dwelt in tents and had for their seats wherever night had compelled them, are written in the psalm to have first endured captivity, because, when the army of the Chaldeans was laying Judaea waste, they were compelled to enter the cities.

Finally, when ecclesiastical necessity had drawn me too to Rome with the holy bishops Paulinus and Epiphanius — of whom the one ruled the church of Antioch in Syria, the other that of Salamis in Cyprus — and I was modestly shunning the eyes of noble women, she so acted, according to the Apostle, in season and out of season, that her diligence overcame my reserve. And because I was then reckoned of some name in the study of the Scriptures, she never met me but that she asked something of the Scriptures, nor did she at once acquiesce, but raised questions on the other side, not that she might contend, but that by asking she might learn the solutions of those things which she understood could be objected. What of virtue, of talent, of holiness, of purity I found in her, I fear to say, lest I exceed the credit of belief and strike a greater grief into you, recalling how great a good you have lost. This only will I say, that whatever in me had been gathered by long study and turned, as it were, into nature by daily meditation, this she tasted, this she learned and possessed, so that after my perfecting, if any contention arose over some testimony of the Scriptures, recourse was had to her as judge. And because she was very prudent and knew that which the philosophers call to prepon — that is, the becoming, what you should do — when asked she so answered that she said even her own things were not her own, but either mine or some other's, so that in the very thing she taught she confessed herself a pupil — for she knew it was said by the Apostle: But I do not permit a woman to teach — lest she should seem to do an injury to the male sex, and sometimes to priests inquiring about obscure and ambiguous matters.

I ask: what is this composure? She does not fear the death hanging over her, she rejoices when struck, the executioner turns pale; her eyes, which do not see the sword, see only the brooch, and, as if it were too little that she had no dread of her own destruction, she did a kindness to the man who raged against her. And now a third stroke: the mystery of the Trinity had been thwarted. Now the guard, terrified and unable to believe in his own steel, fitted the point to her throat, so that, since he could not cut, the sword might at least be buried in the body by the pressure of his hand. O thing unheard of in all the ages! — the sword bends back to its hilt and, as though looking up at its master in defeat, confessed that it could not strike.

But, dislodged from this footing, you will appeal to the clergy: Should I dare to say anything about these men, who certainly do remain in their own cities? Far be it from me to speak anything sinister of those who, succeeding to the apostolic rank, make the body of Christ with their sacred mouth, through whom we too are Christians, who, holding the keys of the kingdom of heaven, in a manner judge before the day of judgement, who keep the Lord's bride in sober chastity. But, as I laid down before, the case of the monk is one thing, the case of the clergy another. The clergy feed the sheep; I am fed. They live from the altar; for me, as for a fruitless tree, the axe is laid to the roots if I do not bring a gift to the altar. Nor can I plead poverty, when in the Gospel I see the old woman casting in the two coins that were all she had left. It is not lawful for me to sit before the presbyter; he, if I sin, is permitted to hand me over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, that the spirit may be saved.

And indeed in the old law whoever did not obey the priests was either set outside the camp and stoned by the people, or, with his neck laid under the sword, atoned for his contempt with his blood. But now the disobedient man is cut down by the spiritual sword, or, cast out of the church, is torn to pieces by the raging mouth of the demons. And if the loving flatteries of the brethren urge you too toward that same order, I shall rejoice at your rise, I shall fear for your fall. "He who desires the office of a bishop desires a good work." We know this; but join what follows: "But such a one must be blameless, the husband of one wife, sober, chaste, prudent, of good conduct, hospitable, apt to teach, no wine-bibber, no striker, but modest." And after the rest concerning him has been set forth, he applied no less care to the third rank, saying: "Deacons likewise must be chaste, not double-tongued, not given to much wine, not greedy of filthy gain, holding the mystery of the faith in a pure conscience. And let these too first be proved, and so let them minister, having no crime." Woe to that man who, not having a wedding garment, enters in to the supper! Nothing remains but that he hear at once: "Friend, how did you come in here?" — and, when he is struck dumb, that it be said to the servants: "Take him by his feet and hands and cast him into the outer darkness; there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth." Woe to him who, binding in a napkin the talent he received, while the others make their gains, has kept only what he received! At once he will be struck by the cry of the indignant master: "Wicked servant, why did you not give my money to the bank, that I, coming, might have exacted it with interest?" — that is: you should have set down at the altar what you could not carry. For while you, a sluggish trader, hold the single coin, you have taken the place of another who could have doubled the money. Wherefore, just as he who ministers well acquires a good standing for himself, so he who comes unworthily to the Lord's cup will be guilty of the Lord's body and blood.

But if those who, with their bodies wasted away, are assailed only by their thoughts suffer such things, what does a girl suffer who enjoys delights? Surely that word of the apostle: \"Living, she is dead.\" If, then, there can be any counsel in me, if one with experience may be trusted, this is the first thing I advise, this I solemnly charge: that the bride of Christ flee wine as poison. These are the first weapons of the demons against youth. Avarice does not shake us so, nor pride puff us up, nor ambition delight us. Other vices we are easily without: this enemy is shut up within. Wherever we go, we carry the foe with us. Wine and youth are a twofold kindling of pleasure. Why do we add oil to the flame? Why do we supply fuel of fire to a burning little body?

Paul says to Timothy: \"Drink no longer water, but use a little wine for your stomach's sake and your frequent infirmities.\" See for what causes the drinking of wine is allowed: scarcely does the pain of the stomach and frequent infirmity merit it. And lest we perhaps flatter ourselves on account of our ailments, he commanded that a little be taken, by the counsel rather of a physician than of an apostle — though the apostle too is a spiritual physician — and lest Timothy, overcome by weakness, should not be able to make his rounds of preaching the Gospel. Otherwise he remembered that he himself had said: \"wine, in which is excess,\" and \"It is good for a man not to drink wine and not to eat flesh.\" Noah drank wine and became drunk in the world still raw and young; and at that time he first planted a vineyard: perhaps he did not know that wine makes one drunk. And that you may understand the mystery of Scripture in all things — for the word of God is a pearl, and may be pierced on every side — after the drunkenness followed the uncovering of the thighs; lust was joined to excess. First the belly, and at once the rest: \"for the people ate and drank, and rose up to play.\" Lot, the friend of God, saved on the mountain and found, of so many thousands of peoples, the only just man, is made drunk by his daughters; and although they thought the race of men had failed and did this rather from desire of offspring than of lust, yet they knew the just man would not do this unless drunk; and so he did not know what he had done; and — although the will is not in the crime, the error is in the fault — from this are born the Moabites and Ammonites, enemies of Israel, who even to the fourteenth generation and for ever do not enter the church of God.

When you speak in church, let it be not the shout of the people but their groaning that is roused; let the tears of your hearers be your praise. Let the discourse of the presbyter be seasoned by the reading of the Scriptures. I would not have you a declaimer and a brawler and a babbler, but skilled in the mystery and most learned in the sacraments of your God. To roll out words and, by the swiftness of speaking, to win admiration from an unskilled crowd is the mark of ignorant men. A brazen brow often expounds what it does not know, and, when it has persuaded others, claims knowledge for itself as well. My teacher once, Gregory of Nazianzus, when I asked him to explain what was meant in Luke by the "second-first" Sabbath — that is, the secundoprimum — gracefully jested: "I will teach you," he said, "about this matter in church, where, with all the people applauding me, you will be compelled against your will to know what you do not know; or else, if you alone keep silent, you alone will be condemned by all for folly." Nothing is so easy as to deceive a cheap little crowd and an unlearned assembly by a glib tongue, for whatever it does not understand it admires the more. Marcus Tullius — of whom that most beautiful tribute was made: "Demosthenes took from you the being the first orator; you took from him the being the only one" — mark what he says in his oration for Quintus Gallius about the favour of the crowd and about unskilled speakers: "But at these games — for I speak of what I have myself lately experienced — a certain poet holds sway, a man very lettered, whose are those banquets of poets and philosophers, when he makes Euripides and Menander dispute with each other, and in another place Socrates and Epicurus, whose ages we know were separated not by years but by centuries. And how great is the applause and the shouting that he stirs! For he has many fellow-pupils in the theatre who likewise never learned their letters."

So much for what pertains to dress and adornment. As for the rest, the widow "who lives in pleasures" — it is not my word, but the Apostle's — "though living, is dead." What does this mean, that she says: "though living, is dead"? She seems indeed to be living to those who do not know, and not to be dead to sin; but to Christ, whom secret things do not deceive, she is dead. For the soul that sins shall itself die. Some men's sins are manifest, going before to judgment; but some they also follow after. In like manner also the good deeds are manifest, and those that are otherwise cannot be hid. What he says is of this kind: some sin so freely and openly that, after you have seen them, you at once understand them to be sinners; but others, who cunningly conceal their vices, we recognize from their subsequent conduct. Likewise also the good are in some openly apparent, in others we learn of it by long acquaintance. Why, then, is it needful for us to boast of a chastity which, without its companions and appendages — continence and frugality — cannot make itself credible? The Apostle wears down his own body and subjects it to the command of the soul, lest he himself should not keep what he enjoins on others: and shall fervent youth, with the body fed, be secure about its chastity?

It is a precept of the rhetoricians that the forefathers of him who is to be praised, and their deeds, should be recalled from far back, and that the discourse should thus come to the man himself by degrees, so that, of course, he may be made more illustrious by ancestral and paternal virtues, and may seem either not to have degenerated from good men, or himself to have adorned mediocre ones. But I will not look, in praising the soul, for the goods of the flesh, which he himself always despised, nor will I boast of his birth — that is, of goods belonging to others — since both Abraham and Isaac, holy men, begot sinners, Ishmael and Esau, and, on the other hand, Jephthah, numbered in the catalogue of the just by the Apostle's voice, was born of a harlot. The soul, he says, that sins, shall itself die; therefore the soul that has not sinned shall itself live. Neither the virtues nor the vices of parents are imputed to their children; we are reckoned from the time when we are born again in Christ. Paul, the persecutor of the Church, in the morning a ravening wolf of Benjamin, in the evening gave food to Ananias, bowing his head as a sheep. Therefore let our Nepotian too, like a wailing little infant and an untaught boy, be suddenly born to us from the Jordan.

But let us pursue what we began. While we were seeking a dwelling worthy of so great a woman, since she so desired solitude that she would not be without the lodging of Mary, behold, suddenly, as the messengers ran to and fro, the whole East trembled: that from the farthest Maeotis, between the icy Tanais and the savage peoples of the Massagetae, where the barriers of Alexander hold back the wild nations by the cliffs of the Caucasus, swarms of Huns had burst forth, which, flitting hither and thither on their swift horses, filled all things alike with slaughter and terror. The Roman army was then away, and was held in Italy by the civil wars. Herodotus relates that this nation, under Darius king of the Medes, held the East captive for twenty years, and exacted an annual tribute from the Egyptians and the Ethiopians. May Jesus turn such beasts away henceforth from the Roman world! Unlooked-for, they were everywhere present, and, outstripping report by their speed, they spared neither religion, nor dignity, nor age, nor wailing infancy. Those who had but lately begun to live were forced to die, and, not knowing their own evil, laughed amid the hands and weapons of the enemy. The rumour was consistent among all that they were making for Jerusalem, and that out of excessive greed for gold they were rushing to this city. At Antioch the walls, neglected through the carelessness of peace, were being repaired; Tyre, wishing to break off the island from the mainland, sought its ancient site. Then we too were compelled to fit out ships, to be on the shore, to guard against the coming of the enemy, and, while the winds raged, to fear the barbarians more than shipwreck — providing not so much for our own safety as for the chastity of the virgins. There was at that time a certain dissension among us, and domestic wars surpassed the battle of the barbarians. As for us, our seats, now fixed, and the long-rooted longing for the holy places held us in the East; but she, because she was all in her baggage and a pilgrim in all the world, returned to her native land, that she might live poor there where she had been rich, dwelling in another's house, who had before had many guests, and — that I may not draw out my discourse too long — that in the sight of the city of Rome she might distribute to the poor what she had sold with that very city as witness.

Let her not eat in public — that is, at the banquet of her parents — nor let her see foods which she might desire. And although some think it of greater virtue to despise the pleasure that is present, yet I judge it the safer continence not to know what you might seek. As a boy I once read in the schools: You can hardly find fault with what you allow to become a habit. Let her learn even then not to drink wine, in which is luxury. Before the years of robust age, heavy abstinence is perilous for the tender. Up to that time, if necessity demands, let her even go to the baths, and use a little wine for her stomach, and be sustained by the eating of meat, lest the feet fail before they begin to run. And I say these things by way of indulgence, not of command, fearing weakness, not teaching luxury. Otherwise, what Jewish superstition does in part in the renouncing of certain animals and foods, what the Brahmans of the Indians and the gymnosophists of the Egyptians observe in the single food of barley-meal and rice and fruits, why should not a virgin of Christ do wholly? If glass is worth so much, why should not the pearl be of greater price? Let her who is born of the promise so live as those lived who were begotten of the promise. With equal grace let her have equal labour. Let her be deaf to musical instruments; let her not know why the flute, the lyre, and the cithara were made.

You will answer: "Whence do you know me? And how do you cast your eyes upon me from so far?" Your brother's tears told me this, and his unbearable sobs at every moment. And would that he had lied, and had said this fearing it rather than charging it! But believe me, sister: no one who lies weeps. He grieves that a young man is preferred to him — not indeed long-haired, not of silken garments, but a fop and dainty in squalor — who himself seals the money-bag, holds the weaving-room, distributes the wool-tasks, rules the household, buys whatever is needed from the market, steward and master and forestalling the little duties of the servants, whom all the servants gnaw at, and whatever the mistress has not given, they cry out that he has filched. The race of servants is querulous, and however much you give them, it is always too little for them. For they do not consider out of how much, but how much is given, and they console their grief only by detractions, since that is what they can do. One calls him a parasite, another an impostor, this one a legacy-hunter, another by whatever new name. They boast that he himself sits by the little bed, applies the midwives to her when sick, carries the chamber-pot, warms the linen, folds the bands. Men more easily believe evil, and whatever is invented at home becomes rumour in public. Nor wonder if maids and servants invent these things about you, when the mother too complains of this very thing, and the brother.

Let others see what they think — for each is led by his own opinion — to me a town is a prison and solitude a paradise. Why do we desire the throng of cities, we who are reckoned by our singleness? Moses, that he might be set over the people of the Jews, is trained forty years in the desert; a shepherd of sheep, he became a shepherd of men; the apostles passed from the fishing of the lake of Gennesaret to the fishing of men. Then they had a father, a net, a little boat: following the Lord, they at once left all things, daily carrying their cross and not even having a staff in their hand. This I say, that, even if the desire of the clergy tickles you, you may learn what you can teach, and offer a reasonable sacrifice to Christ, lest you be a soldier before a recruit, lest you be a master before a disciple. It is not the part of my humility nor of my measure to judge of others, and to say anything sinister of the ministers of the churches. Let them have their order and their grade; if you should hold it, how you must live in it, the book published to Nepotian can teach you. Now we are examining the cradle and manners of the monk — and of that monk who, instructed in the liberal studies, in his youth laid the yoke of Christ on his neck.

In our place we heard that you at once clung to her companionship, and never departed from her even a nail's breadth, as it is said, using the same house, the same chamber, one bed, and that it became known to all the most distinguished in the city that you had found a mother and she a daughter. A suburban field was for you instead of a monastery, and the country chosen for its solitude. And you lived so for a long time, that by the imitation of you and the conduct of many we rejoiced that Rome had been made a Jerusalem. The monasteries of virgins were frequent, the multitude of monks innumerable, so that, on account of the throng of those serving God, what before had been a disgrace was afterward a glory. Meanwhile we consoled the absence of one another with mutual addresses, and what we could not in the flesh we rendered in the spirit. Always our letters met, surpassed, anticipated one another with services and greetings. She lost not much who was joined to me by continual letters.

Here, here let the example of the three young men come to me, who amid the cold globes of flame sent up hymns instead of weeping, and around whose loose trousers and holy hair the fire played without harm. Here let the story of blessed Daniel be recalled, beside whom the mouths of the lions, with fawning tails, feared their own prey. Now let noble Susanna, famous for her faith, enter the minds of all — she who, condemned by an unjust verdict, was saved when the Holy Spirit filled a young boy. See, the Lord's mercy is not unlike in both cases: the one was set free through the judge, that she might not come to the sword; this one, condemned by the judge, was acquitted through the sword.

Not all bishops are bishops. You look to Peter, but consider Judas too. You look up to Stephen, but look also at Nicolas, whom the Lord hates in his Apocalypse — who devised things so foul and unspeakable that the heresy of the Ophites was born from that root. Let each man prove himself, and so approach. Ecclesiastical dignity does not make a Christian. Cornelius the centurion, while still a heathen, is flooded with the gift of the Holy Spirit; the boy Daniel judges the elders; Amos, stripping mulberries from the brambles, is suddenly a prophet; David the shepherd is chosen for king; Jesus loves most the least of his disciples. Take a lower place, brother, so that, when a lesser man comes, you may be bidden to go up higher. On whom does the Lord rest, except on the humble and the quiet and him who trembles at his words? To whom more is entrusted, of him more is required. "The mighty shall suffer torments mightily." Nor should anyone congratulate himself only on the chastity of a clean body, since for every idle word that men have spoken they are to render an account on the day of judgement — since even an insult against a brother is a charge of murder. It is not easy to stand in Paul's place, to hold the rank of those who already reign with Christ, lest perhaps an angel come who tears the veil of your temple, who moves your candlestick from its place. Before building a tower, reckon up the cost of the work to come. Salt that has lost its savour is good for nothing but to be thrown out and trampled by swine. If a monk falls, the priest will pray for him; for the fall of a priest, who will pray?

Elijah, when he was fleeing from Jezebel and lay wearied under the oak, is roused by an angel coming to him, and it is said to him: \"Arise and eat.\" And he looked, and behold, at his head was a loaf of spelt and a jar of water. Could not God in truth have sent him spiced wine, and dishes of oil, and meats altered by some mixture? Elisha invites the sons of the prophets to a meal, and, feeding them with wild herbs, hears the harmonious cry of the diners: \"Death is in the pot, O man of God.\" He was not angry with the cooks — for he had no custom of a more sumptuous table — but, casting flour upon it, he sweetened the bitterness by the same power of the Spirit by which Moses had changed the waters of Marah. And when he had led those who came to seize him, blinded in eyes and mind alike, unwitting, into Samaria, hear with what banquets he commands them to be refreshed: \"Set before them bread and water; and let them eat and drink and be sent back to their master.\" A more opulent table could have been brought to Daniel too from the king's dishes, but Habakkuk carries him, I think, a reaper's rustic meal. And therefore he was also called \"a man of desires,\" because he did not eat the bread of desire nor drink the wine of concupiscence.

Avoid dark garments as much as white; finery and squalor are alike to be shunned, since the one savours of luxury, the other of vainglory. Not to go about without a linen cloak, but to have no money for linen garments, is praiseworthy; otherwise it is ridiculous and full of disgrace to boast, with a full purse, that you have no handkerchief or napkin. There are some who give little to the poor that they may receive more, and under the pretext of almsgiving seek riches; this is rather to be called hunting than almsgiving. Thus are wild beasts, thus birds, thus fishes caught: a little bait is set upon the hook, that the purses of matrons may be drawn out upon it. The bishop, to whom the church is entrusted, knows whom to set over the distribution and care of the poor. It is better not to have what I might give than shamelessly to beg. But it is also a kind of arrogance to wish to seem more merciful than the bishop of Christ. We cannot all do all things. One in the church is an eye, another a tongue, another a hand, another a foot, another an ear, a belly, and the rest. Read Paul to the Corinthians: diverse members make up one body. Let not the unlettered and merely simple brother therefore think himself holy if he knows nothing, nor let the skilled and eloquent in speech reckon his eloquence holiness. Of the two imperfect things, it is far better to have a holy rusticity than a sinful eloquence.

Nor in saying this do I condemn the foods which God created to be used with thanksgiving, but I assert that to young men and girls they are incentives to pleasures. Not the fires of Etna, not the land of Vulcan, not Vesuvius and Olympus seethe with such heat as the youthful marrow, filled with wine, inflamed with feasting. Avarice is trampled down by most, and is laid aside along with the purse; a slanderous tongue is corrected by enjoined silence; the care of the body and the fashion of dress is changed in the space of a single hour; all the other sins are external, and what is on the outside is easily cast off: lust alone, implanted by God for the procreation of children, if it has gone beyond its bounds, overflows into vice, and by a certain law of nature strains to burst forth into union. It is therefore a great virtue and one of anxious diligence to overcome what you are born in the flesh, not to live carnally, to fight with yourself daily and to watch the enclosed enemy with a hundred eyes, like Argus, as the fables tell. This is what the Apostle said in other words: Every sin that a man does is outside the body; but he who fornicates sins against his own body. The physicians, and those who have written on the nature of human bodies, and especially Galen in the books entitled On Healthful Things, say that the bodies of boys and young men, and of men and women in the perfect age, glow with an implanted heat, and that to these ages those foods are harmful which increase heat, and that it conduces to health to take cool things in food and drink — just as, on the contrary, hot foods and old wines profit the old, who suffer from phlegm and cold. Hence the Saviour too says: Take heed to yourselves, lest perhaps your hearts be weighed down with surfeiting and drunkenness and the cares of this life. And the Apostle: Wine, in which is luxury. Nor is it any wonder that the potter felt this about the little vessel which he himself fashioned, when even the comic poet, whose end is to know and describe human manners, said: Without Ceres and Bacchus, Venus grows cold.

Another, perhaps, would write that for his salvation you left the East and the desert, and lured me, your dearest companion, with the hope of returning, that first, if it could be done, you might preserve your widowed sister with her little one, and then, if she should reject the plan, at least preserve your sweetest nephew. For this is he of whom I once prophesied to you: "Though a little nephew hang upon your neck." Another, I say, would report that in the service of the palace, beneath the cloak and the gleaming linen, his body was worn by a hair-shirt; that, standing before the powers of the world, he wore a face pale with fastings; that, still under the garments of another, he served another, and had his belt for this, that he might come to the aid of widows, orphans, the oppressed, the wretched: but these delays of an imperfect service of God do not please me, and the centurion Cornelius, whom I read to have been just, I hear at once baptized.

We grieve only for this, that we have lost from the holy places the most precious necklace. Rome received back what she had lost, and the saucy and slanderous tongue of the heathen was confuted by the testimony of their own eyes. Let others praise her mercy, her humility, her faith: I will praise rather the ardour of her mind. She held by heart the book in which, as a young man, I once exhorted Heliodorus to the desert, and, beholding the walls of Rome, she lamented that she was shut in. Forgetful of her sex, unmindful of her frailty, and desirous only of solitude, she was there where she dwelt in mind. She could not be held by the counsels of her friends: so eager was she to burst out of the city as out of fetters. She called the management of money and the cautious distribution of it a kind of unbelief. She wished not to give alms to others, but, having poured out her own equally, herself to receive alms for Christ. So she hastened, so impatient was she of delays, that you would have believed she was about to set out. And so, while she is ever preparing, death could not find her unprepared.

Let her render to you daily a fixed task of the Scriptures. Let her learn by heart a number of verses of the Greeks. Let Latin learning follow at once; if it has not from the beginning composed the tender mouth, the tongue is corrupted into a foreign sound, and the native speech is defiled by outlandish faults. Let her have you as her teacher, let her untaught infancy admire you. Let her see nothing in you or in her father which, if she did it, she would sin. Remember that you are the parents of a virgin, and that you can teach her better by examples than by word. Flowers quickly perish; a pestilent breath quickly corrupts the violets and lilies and saffron. Let her never go out into public without you; let her not go to the basilicas of the martyrs and the churches without her mother. Let no young man, no curled fellow smile upon her. Let our little maiden so celebrate the days of vigils and the solemn night-watches that she does not depart even a nail's breadth from her mother. I would not have her love any one of her maids more than the rest, into whose ears she might often whisper. Whatever she says to one, let all know it. Let her companion please her not as one trim and beautiful, who modulates a sweet song with clear throat, but grave, pale, plainly clad, somewhat sad. Let there be set over her a virgin of approved faith and manners and chastity, advanced in years, who may teach her and accustom her by example to rise at night for prayer and psalms, in the morning to sing hymns, at the third, sixth, and ninth hour to stand in the line of battle like a warrior of Christ, and, the little lamp kindled, to render the evening sacrifice. So let the day pass, so let the night find her at work. Let reading succeed prayer, and prayer reading. The time will seem short which is occupied with such varieties of works.

Do, then, what I advise, what I entreat: that first you be reconciled to your mother, and then, if that cannot be done, at least to your brother. Or, if you abhor these names so dear as hostile, separate from him whom you are said to have preferred to your own. But if you cannot do even this — for you would return to your own if you could forsake him — at least use your companion more honourably. Let your houses be separated, and your table divided, lest slanderous men, since you dwell under one little roof, charge you also with having a bed in common. You can both have, for your needs, such solace as you wished, and in some part be free of public infamy — although the stain must be guarded against which, according to Jeremiah, can be washed out with no nitre, no fuller's herb. When you wish him to see you — and he will visit — call in witnesses: friends, freedmen, servants. A good conscience will flee the eyes of no one. Let him enter undismayed, let him go out secure. Silent eyes and silent speech and the bearing of the whole body sometimes speak either trepidation or security. Open your ears, I beg, and hear the outcry of the whole city. Already you have lost your own names, and have taken surnames from each other in turn: you are called his, and he is yours. This the mother hears, and the brother, and they are ready and they pray you to divide yourselves for them, and to make the private infamy of your union a common praise. Be with your mother, let him be with the brother. You will more boldly love your brother's companion: more honourably will the mother love her son's friend than her daughter's. But if you will not, if with wrinkled brow you despise my admonitions, this letter will proclaim to you with free voice: Why do you besiege another's servant? Why do you make a minister of Christ your servant? Look at the people, behold the faces of each. He reads in the church and all gaze upon you — except that with almost conjugal license you glory in your infamy, nor can you now be content with secret disgrace; you call wantonness liberty. The face of a harlot has come to be yours; you know not how to blush.

And first it must be treated whether you ought to live in a monastery alone or with others. To me it seems best that you should have the companionship of holy men, and not teach yourself and enter without a guide on a way you have never entered, and at once have to turn aside to the one side or the other and lie open to error, and walk either more or less than is needful — so that, running, you tire yourself, or, delaying, you fall asleep. In solitude pride quickly creeps up, and, if a man has fasted a little while and has not seen another, he thinks himself to be of some importance, and, forgetful of himself, of whence and whither he has come, within in body, in tongue he wanders abroad. He judges, against the Apostle's will, the servants of another; what gluttony demands, he stretches out his hands for; he sleeps as much as he wishes; he reveres no one, thinks all beneath himself, and is more often in the cities than in his cell, and among the brethren feigns modesty, who is jostled in the crowds of the streets. What then? Do we reprehend the solitary life? By no means, since we have often praised it. But we wish soldiers of this kind to go forth from the training-school of the monasteries: men whom the rudiments do not hold back, who have given a sample of their conduct over a long time, who have been the least of all, that they might become the first of all, whom neither hunger nor satiety ever overcame, who rejoice in poverty, whose dress, speech, countenance, gait is a teaching of the virtues, who do not know how, according to certain foolish men, to fashion portents of demons assailing them, that among the unskilled and the men of the crowd they may make a marvel of themselves and thereupon pursue gains.

In this tranquillity and service of the Lord, a heretical storm, arising in these provinces, disturbed everything, and was roused to such a fury that it spared neither itself nor any of the good. And as if it were too little to have stirred up all things here, it brought a ship full of blasphemies into the harbour of Rome, and straightway the dish found its cover, and muddy footsteps mingled with mire the purest fountain of the Roman faith. Nor is it any wonder if in the streets and in the market-place of wares a painted soothsayer beats the buttocks of fools and, with twisted cudgel, knocks out the teeth of those who bite, when the venomous and filthy doctrine found at Rome those whom it might draw in. Then the infamous translation of the books On First Principles; then a disciple Olbius, truly of his name, had he not stumbled against such a master; then the fiery contradiction of our men, and the troubled school of the Pharisees. Then the holy Marcella, who had long shut her eyes, lest she should be thought to do anything through rivalry, after she perceived that the faith praised by the apostolic mouth was being violated in very many — so that the heretic drew even some priests and monks, and especially men of the world, into assent to himself, and mocked the simplicity of the bishop, who judged others by his own disposition — publicly resisted, choosing rather to please God than men.

At last, then, the people armed themselves to deliver the woman. Every age, every sex put the executioner to flight, and as they gathered into a circle, almost no one could believe what he had seen. The neighbouring city is thrown into alarm at such news, and the whole troop of lictors masses together. From among them the one whose charge it was to oversee the condemned burst out into their midst and, fouling his filthy grey hair with a covering of dust, said: "It is my head, citizens, that you seek; you give me as a substitute for her! If you are merciful, if you are clement, if you wish to save the condemned woman, then surely I, who am innocent, ought not to perish." At this the people's heart was shaken with weeping, and a mournful numbness crept over them all; and, by a strange change of will, what before they had defended out of devotion now seemed a kind of devotion — to let her be put to death.

But since my discourse has sailed clear of the rocky places, and the fragile skiff has gone forward into the deep among the hollowed reefs and the foaming waves, the sails must be spread to the winds, and, the crags of the questions safely crossed, after the manner of joyful sailors the epilogue's chant must be sung. O desert blooming with the flowers of Christ! O solitude in which are born those stones from which, in the Apocalypse, the city of the great King is built! O wilderness rejoicing in the company of God! What are you doing in the world, brother, you who are greater than the world? How long do the shadows of roofs press upon you? How long does the smoky prison of these cities shut you in? Believe me, I see I know not what — something more of light. It is good to cast off the burden of the flesh and fly up to the pure brightness of the upper air. Do you fear poverty? But Christ calls the poor blessed. Are you frightened by toil? But no athlete is crowned without sweat. Do you think about food? But faith feels no hunger. Are you afraid to trust your limbs, wasted with fasting, to the bare ground? But the Lord lies down with you. Does the unkempt growth of a filthy head appal you? But your head is Christ. Does the endless vastness of the desert terrify you? But in your mind you may stroll through paradise. As often as you climb up there in thought, so often you will not be in the desert. Is the skin drawn rough for want of baths? But he who has once been washed in Christ need not wash again. And, to put it briefly, hear the apostle answering to all this: "The sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the coming glory which shall be revealed in us." You are pampered, dearest, if you wish both to rejoice here with the world and afterward to reign with Christ.

Innumerable are the passages scattered through the divine Scriptures that condemn gluttony and commend simple foods; but since it is not now my purpose to dispute about fasting, and to follow out the whole subject belongs to its own title and volume, let these few of many suffice. Otherwise, after the example of these you can gather for yourself how the first man too, more obedient to his belly than to God, was cast down into this valley of tears; how Satan tempted the Lord himself with hunger in the desert; and how the apostle cries out: \"Food for the belly, and the belly for food, but God shall destroy both this and that,\" and, of the luxurious: \"Whose god is their belly.\" For each man worships what he loves. From which it must be anxiously provided that hunger may bring back those whom fullness drove out of paradise.

Many build walls and lay down columns for the church: the marbles gleam, the panelled ceilings glitter with gold, the altar is set with gems — and yet there is no choosing of Christ's ministers. Nor let anyone object to me the wealthy temple in Judaea, the table, the lamps, the censers, the dishes, the cups, the little mortars, and the rest skilfully wrought of gold. These things were approved by the Lord then, when the priests sacrificed victims and the blood of beasts was the redemption of sins — though all these things had gone before as a figure. But they were written for our sakes, upon whom the ends of the ages have come; now, however, since a poor Lord has consecrated the poverty of his house, let us think upon the cross, and we shall reckon riches mire. Why do we wonder that Christ calls riches "unrighteous mammon"? Why do we look up to and love what Peter testifies he does not possess? Otherwise, if we follow only the letter, and the plain narrative delights us in gold and riches, let us observe the rest along with the gold: let Christ's bishops marry virgin wives; however good of mind a man be, if he have a scar and is deformed, let him be deprived of the priesthood; let leprosy of the body be preferred to the vices of the soul; let us grow and multiply and replenish the earth; let us neither sacrifice the lamb nor celebrate the mystical Passover, since these are forbidden by law to be done without the temple; let us pitch the tabernacle in the seventh month and sound the solemn fast with the trumpet. But if all these things we should understand spiritually, comparing spiritual with spiritual, and knowing with Paul that the law is spiritual, and singing the words of David, "Open my eyes, and I shall consider the wondrous things of your law," so as to understand even as our Lord himself understood and interpreted the Sabbath, then let us either reject gold along with the rest of the superstitions of the Jews, or, if gold pleases us, let the Jews please us too, whom along with their gold we must either approve or condemn.

First, therefore, if the firmness of your stomach allows it, take water as your drink until you pass the years of girlhood, since by nature it is most cold; or, if weakness forbids this, hear with Timothy: Use a little wine for your stomach and your frequent infirmities. Then, in the foods themselves, avoid whatever is hot — I speak not only of flesh, concerning which the vessel of election gives his sentence: It is good not to drink wine and not to eat flesh — but even among the pulses themselves whatever is flatulent and heavy is to be shunned; and know that nothing so conduces to the good of young Christians as the eating of herbs, whence he also says in another place: He who is weak, let him eat herbs — and the heat of the body must be tempered with cooler fare. But if the three children and Daniel fed on pulses, they were children, and had not yet come to the frying-pan in which the king of Babylon fried the elders, the judges. We do not seek the care of the body, which in them — apart from the privilege of the grace of God — had shone forth from food of this kind, but the vigour of the soul, which is made stronger by the weakness of the flesh. Hence it is that not a few of those who aim at a chaste life collapse in the middle of the journey, while they think abstinence consists in flesh alone, and load their stomachs with pulses, which, taken moderately and sparingly, are harmless. And to say what I think: nothing so inflames the body and titillates the genital members as undigested food and disordered belching. I would rather, my daughter, that you risked your modesty for a little while than your case. Whatever is a seed-bed of pleasures, I count as poison. Let sparing food and a belly always hungry be preferred to three-day fasts, and it is far better to take a little daily than to take enough rarely. That rain is best which descends gently upon the earth; a sudden and excessive downpour overturns the fields headlong.

Nevertheless, let us approve, as it were, certain cradles of his nascent faith, so that he who was a devoted soldier under another's standards may be granted the laurel after he has begun to serve his own King. His belt laid aside and his dress changed, whatever there was of his military savings he distributed to the poor. For he had read: He who wishes to be perfect, let him sell all that he has and give to the poor and follow me; and again: You cannot serve two masters, God and mammon. Apart from a cheap tunic and a covering to match, which excluded the cold by merely covering the body, he reserved nothing more for himself. His very dress, following the custom of the province, was remarkable neither for elegance nor for squalor. And though he burned daily either to go to the monasteries of Egypt, or to visit the choirs of Mesopotamia, or at least to occupy the solitudes of the islands of Dalmatia, which are separated from Altinum only by a strait, he did not dare to forsake his uncle the bishop, seeing in him all the examples of the virtues, and having at home the source from which he might learn. In one and the same man he both imitated the monk and venerated the bishop. Not, as is wont to happen in most cases, did constant nearness produce familiarity, and familiarity contempt for him; but he so revered him as a parent, and so admired him as though he beheld him new each day. Why say more? He becomes a cleric, and through the usual degrees is ordained presbyter. Good Jesus, what groans, what wailings, what refusal of food, what shunning of all eyes! Then for the first and only time he was angry with his uncle. He complained that he could not bear it, and pleaded that his youthful age was unsuited to the priesthood. But the more he resisted, the more he stirred up the zeal of all toward himself, and merited by refusing what he did not wish to be, and was the worthier for crying out that he was unworthy. We saw a Timothy of our own time, and gray hairs in wisdom, and a man chosen presbyter by Moses, whom Moses himself knew to be a presbyter. Therefore, understanding the clergy not as an honour but a burden, he made it his first care to overcome envy by humility, and then to give no tale of shameful rumour against himself, so that those who carped at his age might be astonished at his continence. To come to the aid of the poor, to visit the sick, to invite to hospitality, to soothe with kindness, to rejoice with those who rejoice, to weep with those who weep; he was the staff of the blind, the food of the hungry, the hope of the wretched, the solace of the mourning. Thus he was eminent in each single virtue, as though he had none of the rest. Among the presbyters and his equals, first in work, last in rank. Whatever good he had done, he ascribed to his uncle; if anything by chance had turned out otherwise than he thought, he said that his uncle did not know of it and that he himself had erred. In public he knew him as bishop, at home as father. He tempered the gravity of his manners with cheerfulness of countenance. You would understand his joy by a smile, not by loud laughter. He honoured the widows and virgins of Christ as mothers, and exhorted them as sisters, with all chastity. Now, after he had betaken himself home, and, leaving the cleric outside, had given himself to the hardness of the monks, frequent in prayers, watchful in supplication, he offered his tears to God, not to men; he moderated his fastings, charioteer-like, according to the weariness and strength of his body. He attended his uncle's table, and so tasted whatever was set before him that he both shunned superstition and preserved continence. His conversation, and every meal, was to propose something from the Scriptures, to listen gladly, to answer modestly, to take up what was right, not sharply to refute what was wrong, to instruct rather than to vanquish one disputing against him, and, with an ingenuous modesty that adorned his age, to confess simply whose each saying was; and in this way, by declining the glory of learning, he was held most learned. "That," he would say, "is Tertullian's, this Cyprian's, this Lactantius's, that Hilary's. So spoke Minucius Felix, so Victorinus, in this manner Arnobius." Me too, because he loved me for his uncle's fellowship, he sometimes brought forward into the open. By constant reading too and long meditation he had made his breast a library of Christ.

Amid the praises of the woman, suddenly my Pammachius rises before me. Paulina sleeps, that he himself may watch; she goes before her husband, that she may leave him behind a servant to Christ. He is the heir of his wife, and others are the possessors of the inheritance. A man and a woman vied which should pitch a tent in the harbour of Abraham, and this was the contest between the two, which should surpass in humanity. Each conquered, and each was conquered. Both confess themselves vanquished and victors, while what one desired, both accomplished. They join their wealth, they unite their wills, so that what rivalry would have scattered, concord might increase. No sooner said than done: a hospice is bought, and to the hospice the throng runs together. For there is no labour in Jacob, nor grief in Israel. They bring across the seas those whom the land may receive into its bosom. Rome sends hastening on those whom, about to sail, the soft shore may cherish. What Publius once did in the island of Malta toward one apostle — and, that I may give no place to contradiction, in one ship — this these do both frequently and toward many. Nor is the need of the poor alone sustained, but a bounty inclined toward all provides something even for those who have. The whole world alike has heard of the guest-house situated in the harbour of Rome. In one summer Britain learned what Egypt and Parthia had recognized in the spring.

Let her learn also to make wool, to hold the distaff, to set the basket in her lap, to turn the spindle, to draw the threads with her thumb. Let her despise the webs of silkworms, the fleeces of the Seres, and gold drawing out into threads. Let her prepare such garments as drive off the cold, not such as, when the bodies are clothed, leave them naked. Let her food be a little herb and fine flour, and rarely small fishes. And, that I may not draw out the precepts of the appetite at length, on which I have spoken more fully in another place, let her so eat that she is always hungry, that immediately after food she can read, pray, sing psalms. Long and immoderate fasts displease me in the tender, and especially the youngest, ages, by which weeks are joined together, and oil in food and fruits are avoided. By experiment I have learned that the little ass, when it is tired on the road, seeks the byways. Let the worshippers of Isis and Cybele do this, who, with a gluttonous abstinence, devour Phasian birds and smoking turtle-doves, lest, forsooth, they pollute the gifts of Ceres. Let this be the precept in perpetual fasting, that unbroken strength may be supplied for a long journey, lest, running in the first stage, we collapse in the middle. For the rest, as I wrote before, in Lent the sails of continence are to be spread, and all the charioteer's reins are to be loosened for the hastening horses — although the condition of worldlings is one thing, that of virgins and monks another. The worldly man in Lent boils down the gluttony of his belly, and, living on his own juice after the manner of snails, prepares his paunch for future feasts and fattening; the virgin and the monk so let loose their horses in Lent that they remember they must always be running. A finished labour is greater, an unending one more moderate; for there we take breath, here we walk on perpetually.

Again you cry out that I am malignant, again suspicious, again a rumour-monger. Am I suspicious, am I malevolent — I who, as I said at the beginning of the letter, wrote for this reason, because I did not suspect — or you, negligent, dissolute, a despiser, who, being twenty-five years old, have so shut up in your arms, as in a net, a young man not yet well-bearded? An excellent tutor indeed, to admonish you, to terrify you with the harshness of his brow, and, although in no age is lust safe, yet at least with gray head to defend you from open disgrace! It will come, it will come, the time — the day glides on while you do not know it — and this pretty fellow of yours, because women quickly grow old, especially those who are near men, will find either a richer or a younger one. Then you will repent your obstinacy, when you have lost both your property and your reputation, when what had been ill joined will be well divided — unless perhaps you are secure, and, the love of so long a time growing strong, do not fear separation.

We have lately seen, and lamented, the wealth of a Croesus caught out by one man's death, and the alms of a city, gathered as though for the uses of the poor, left behind to his stock and posterity. Then the iron, which lay hidden in the deep, floated upon the water, and amid the palm-trees of Marah the bitterness was shown. Nor is it any wonder: such a companion and master too he had, who made the hunger of the needy his own riches, and held to his own misery what was left to the wretched. Whose cry at last reached heaven and overcame the most patient ears of God, so that an angel sent said to that most wicked Nabal of Carmel: Fool, this night they shall take away your soul from you; but what you have prepared, whose shall it be?

The Saviour praises in the Gospel the steward of iniquity, because he had acted prudently — against his master indeed, yet for himself. The heretics, seeing the greatest fires kindled from a small spark, and that the flame long laid beneath had now reached the rooftops and could not be hidden — what had deceived many — ask for and obtain ecclesiastical letters, that, communicating with the Church, they might seem to depart. Not much time in between, there succeeds to the pontificate that distinguished man Anastasius, whom Rome did not long deserve to have, lest the head of the world should be beheaded under such a bishop; nay rather, he was for this reason snatched away and translated, lest he should try by his prayers to bend a sentence once passed, the Lord saying to Jeremiah: Pray not for this people, neither make supplication for them for good; for if they fast, I will not hear their prayers, and if they offer holocausts and victims, I will not receive them; for by sword, famine, and pestilence I will consume them. You may say: "To what does this tend?" To the praise of Marcella. This was the beginning of the damnation of the heretics, when she brings forward witnesses who had first been instructed by them and afterward knit together by the heretic's error; when she shows the multitude of the deceived; when she presses the impious volumes On First Principles, which, corrected by the hand of a scorpion, are pointed out; when the heretics, summoned by frequent letters to defend themselves, dared not come, and so great was the force of conscience that they preferred to be condemned in their absence rather than convicted present. Of this so glorious victory the origin is Marcella, and you the head and cause of these goods — you who know that I narrate true things, who know that I say scarcely a few of many, lest the odious repetition should make the reader loathe it, and I should seem, among the malevolent, under the occasion of praising another, to vent my own spleen. I will pass to the rest.

So a new sword, a new slayer is brought up. The victim stands, protected only by the favour of Christ. Struck once, she is shaken; assailed a second time, she trembles; wounded a third time, she falls — and, O majesty of divine power to be exalted! — she who before had been struck a fourth time and yet was unhurt now seemed to die a little, only so that no innocent man should perish in her place.

It will come, that day will come, on which this corruptible and mortal shall put on incorruption and immortality. Blessed is the servant whom the Lord shall find watching. Then at the voice of the trumpet the earth with its peoples will quake; you will rejoice. When the Lord comes to judge, the world will bellow its grief; tribe will beat its breast against tribe; the once most powerful kings will tremble with naked flank; Jupiter, then truly afire, will be brought forward with his offspring; foolish Plato too will be led in with his disciples; Aristotle's arguments will not avail him. Then you, a countryman and poor, will exult, will laugh and say: "Behold my crucified God; behold the Judge who, wrapped in rags, wailed in the manger. This is that son of the workman and the hireling woman; this is he who, carried in his mother's bosom, God fled before man into Egypt; this is he clothed in scarlet, this crowned with thorns, this the magician possessed of a demon and the Samaritan. Look at the hands, Jew, which you nailed; look at the side, Roman, which you pierced. See the body, whether it is the same that you said the disciples carried off secretly in the night." That it may fall to you, brother, to say these things, to be present at these things, what is the toil that is now hard?

But if you should wish to answer that you were born of noble stock, always among delights, always on feathers, and that you cannot abstain from wine and richer foods nor live more strictly by these rules, I will answer: Live then by your own law, since you cannot live by God's. Not that God, the creator and lord of the universe, takes delight in the rumbling of our entrails, in the emptiness of the belly, and in the burning of the lungs, but because chastity cannot otherwise be safe. Job, dear to God and by his own testimony blameless and upright, hear what he suspects about the devil: \"His strength is in the loins, and his power in the navel.\" Decently, by names exchanged, the genitals of man and woman are so called. Hence it is promised that one shall sit upon his throne from David's loins; and seventy-five souls entered Egypt that came forth from Jacob's thigh; and after the breadth of his thigh withered when God wrestled with him, he ceased from the work of begetting children; and he who is to keep the Passover is bidden to do so with loins girded and mortified; and to Job God says: \"Gird up your loins like a man\"; and John is girded with a leather belt; and the apostles are bidden to have the lamps of the Gospel in their hands with loins girded. But of Jerusalem, found smeared with blood in the field of error, it is said in Ezekiel: \"Your navel was not cut.\" All the devil's strength against men, then, is in the loins; all his might against women is in the navel.

You must avoid the banquets of worldly men, and especially of those who are swollen with honours. It is shameful that, before the doors of a priest of the crucified and poor Lord — who fed even on borrowed food — the lictors of consuls and soldiers should keep watch, and that the judge of the province should dine better at your house than in the palace. But if you allege that you do these things in order to plead for the wretched and the oppressed: the worldly judge defers more to a self-controlled cleric than to a rich one, and reveres your holiness more than your wealth; or, if he be such a man as will not hear clerics save among the dishes, I shall gladly do without a benefit of this kind, and shall plead with Christ as my judge, who can better come to my aid; for it is better to trust in the Lord than to trust in man, better to hope in the Lord than to hope in princes. Never smell of wine, lest you hear that saying of the philosopher: "This is not to offer a kiss, but to offer a toast." Drunken priests both the Apostle condemns and the old law forbids. They that serve the altar shall not drink wine and strong drink. "Strong drink" in the Hebrew tongue is the name for any drink that can intoxicate, whether it is made with ferment, or fruit-juices are boiled down into a sweet and outlandish drink, or the fruit of palms is pressed into liquor, or a thicker water is strained from cooked grain. Whatever intoxicates and overturns the steadiness of the mind, flee it as you would wine. Nor do I say this so as to condemn a creature of God — since the Lord too is called a wine-drinker, and to Timothy with a sick stomach a little draught of wine was allowed — but we require, in drinking, a measure proportioned to age, to health, and to the constitution of the body. But if without wine I burn — and I burn with youth and am inflamed with the heat of the blood and am of a juicy and vigorous body — I shall gladly do without the cup in which there is the suspicion of poison. It is finely said among the Greeks, though I do not know whether it sounds as well among us: "A fat belly does not beget a fine perception."

When you eat, think that you must at once pray, at once read. Have a fixed number of verses from the Holy Scriptures; render this task to your Lord, and do not yield your limbs to rest before you have filled the basket of your breast with this weft. After the Holy Scriptures, read the treatises of learned men — those only whose faith is known. You have no need to seek gold in mire: with many pearls buy the one pearl. Stand with Jeremiah in the many ways, that you may come to that way which leads to the Father. Transfer the love of necklaces and gems and silken garments to the knowledge of the Scriptures. Enter the land of promise flowing with milk and honey; eat fine flour and oil; be clothed with Joseph in many-coloured garments; let your ears be pierced with Jerusalem by the word of God, that the precious grains of the new harvests may hang from them. You have the holy Exuperius, of approved age and faith, who may frequently instruct you with his admonitions.

How often did he beg, in letters from across the sea, that I would write something to him! How often did he set before me the nocturnal petitioner of the Gospel, and the widow who importuned the harsh judge! And when I refused by silence rather than by letters, and put the modesty of one keeping silent to the blush of the one asking, he set up against me his uncle as a pleader, who might both ask more freely on another's behalf and obtain more easily out of reverence for his priesthood. I did, then, what he wished, and in a little book consecrated our friendship to eternal memory; on receiving which he boasted that he had surpassed the wealth of Croesus and the riches of Darius. He held it with his eyes, in his bosom, in his hands, in his mouth; and while he often unrolled it in his bed, the sweet page fell upon the breast of the sleeper. But if any of the strangers or friends came, he rejoiced over himself at my testimony, and whatever was lacking in the little work he made up by measured pauses and variety of delivery, so that in his reciting it he himself seemed daily either to please or to displease. Whence this fervour, save from the love of God? Whence the untiring meditation on the law of Christ, save from longing for him who gave the law? Let others add coin to coin and, choking their purse, hunt the wealth of matrons by their attentions; let them be richer monks than they had been worldlings, possessing under a poor Christ the wealth they had not had under a wealthy devil, and let the Church sigh over them as rich whom the world held beggars before: our Nepotian, trampling on gold, pursues sheets of writing; but, as he is a despiser of himself in the flesh and walks the more adorned for his poverty, so he searches out all the adornment of the Church.

What is written, To those who fear the Lord all things work together for good, we saw proved at the death of so great a woman. By a kind of presage of things to come, she had written to many monks, that they should come and release her, labouring under a heavy burden, and that she should make to herself friends of the unrighteous mammon, who might receive her into the everlasting tabernacles. They came, they were made her friends: she fell asleep — which she wished — and, her baggage at last laid down, flew lighter to heaven. How great a marvel Fabiola, living, was to Rome, she showed in death. She had not yet breathed out her spirit, had not yet rendered her soul, owed to Christ, And already flying rumour, the herald of so great a grief, was gathering the peoples of the whole city to her funeral. Psalms resounded, and the gilded roofs of the temples were shaken by the alleluia echoing on high. Here a choir of young men, there of old, who in song bear the praises and the deeds of the woman. Not so did Furius triumph over the Gauls, not so Papirius over the Samnites, not so Scipio over Numantia, not so Pompey over the nations of Pontus. They conquered bodies; she subdued spiritual wickednesses. I hear that neither the streets, nor the porticoes, nor the roofs overhanging from above, could hold the troops of those who went before and the surging multitude that looked on at her funeral in companies. Then Rome beheld her own peoples in one: all favoured themselves in the glory of the penitent. Nor is it any wonder if men exulted over the salvation of her over whose conversion the angels rejoiced in heaven.

If ever you go out to the suburbs, do not leave your daughter at home; let her not know how, nor be able, to live without you; when she is alone, let her tremble. Let her have no conversations with worldlings, no companionship with evil virgins, let her not be present at the weddings of the servants, nor be mingled with the games of a noisy household. I know that some have given a precept that a virgin of Christ should not bathe with eunuchs, nor with married women, because the one do not lay aside the minds of men, the other display foulness with their swelling wombs. To me bathing displeases altogether in a grown virgin, who ought to blush at her own self and not be able to see herself naked. For if by vigils and fastings she wears down her body and reduces it to servitude, if she desires to extinguish the flame of lust and the incentives of her fervent age by the cold of continence, if by sought-out squalor she hastens to disfigure her natural beauty, why, on the contrary, should she rouse with the warmth of the baths the fires that have been lulled?

You too, mother, who because of your age do not fear curses, do not wish to be avenged in such a way that you sin. Let your daughter rather learn from you to be separated than you from her to be disjoined. You have a son and a daughter and a son-in-law — nay, a companion of your daughter; why do you seek the solace of strangers and rouse fires already lulled? It is more honourable for you at least to bear with your daughter's fault than to seek occasion for your own. Let your son the monk be with you, the protection of piety and widowhood. What place has a stranger with you, especially in that house which could not hold a son and a daughter? You are now of such an age that you could have grandchildren by your daughter. Invite both to yourself. Let her who went out alone return with a man — I said a man, not a husband; let no one slander me: I meant to signify the sex, not marriage — or, if she blushes and draws back and thinks the house in which she was born narrow, do you go to her little lodging. Although it be cramped, it can more easily hold a mother and a brother than a stranger, with whom certainly she could not remain in one chamber. Let there be in one house two women, two men. But if that third man too, your nurse-of-old-age, will not depart, and stirs up seditions and tumults, let there be a pair, let there be a team of three: your brother and son will furnish them both a sister and a mother.
