Let others call him stepfather and son-in-law; let him call her foster-mother and sister.

I wish, therefore, both for the causes I set forth above, that you should not dwell with your mother, and especially lest, by refusing the dainty foods she offers, you sadden her, or, if you accept them, add oil to the fire, and, amid the throng of girls, see by day what you may think of by night. Let the book never depart from your hand and your eyes; let the psalter be learned word for word; let prayer be without intermission, the sense watchful and lying open to no vain thoughts. Let the body and the mind alike be stretched toward the Lord. Conquer anger by patience; love the knowledge of the Scriptures, and you will not love the vices of the flesh. Nor let your mind be at leisure for various perturbations, which, if they settle in the breast, will lord it over you and lead you down to the greatest offence. Do also some work, that the devil may always find you occupied. If the apostles, having the power to live by the gospel, laboured with their hands, lest they should burden anyone, and gave refreshment to others, of whom they ought to reap carnal things for spiritual, why do you not prepare what will go to your own uses? Either weave a basket of rushes or plait a hamper of pliant osiers; let the ground be dug, let the little beds be divided by an even boundary; in which, when the seeds of herbs have been cast or the plants set in order, let irrigating waters be led, that you may stand by as a spectator of most beautiful verses: Behold, from the brow of the sloping path he draws the water, and it, falling, stirs a hoarse murmur over the smooth stones, and tempers the parched fields with its bubblings. Let unfruitful trees be grafted, whether with buds or with shoots, and after a little while you may pluck the sweet fruits of your labour. Construct hives for bees, to which the Proverbs send you, and learn the order of the monasteries and the royal discipline in little bodies. Let nets too be woven for catching fish; let books be written, that the hand may both work for food and the soul be filled with reading. Every idle man is in desires. The monasteries of the Egyptians keep this custom, that they receive no one without work and labour, not so much for the necessities of sustenance as for the salvation of the soul, lest it should wander in pernicious thoughts and, after the manner of fornicating Jerusalem, spread its feet to everyone who passes by.

The whirlwind, passing over from the western parts to the East, threatened very many with great shipwrecks. Then was fulfilled: Do you think that, when the Son of man comes, he shall find faith on the earth? The charity of many being grown cold, the few who loved the truth of the faith were joined to our side, whose head was publicly sought, against whom all resources were prepared, so that Barnabas too was led into that dissimulation — nay, that open parricide, which he committed not by his strength but by his will. But behold, the whole storm, the Lord blowing, was destroyed, and the prophetic oracle fulfilled: You shall take away their spirit, and they shall fail and return to their dust. In that day all their thoughts shall perish; and that of the Gospel: Fool, this night your soul is taken from you; but what you have prepared, whose shall it be?

The clergy, whose office it was, wrapped the blood-stained corpse in linen, and, building up the hollowed ground with stones, prepared a tomb as the custom is. The sun in its hastened course sought its setting, and night came on to hide the Lord's mercy. Suddenly the woman's breast throbs, and as her eyes searched for the light her body quickened back to life: now she breathes, now she sees, now she is raised up and speaks, now she can break out into that cry: "The Lord is my helper; I will not fear what man may do to me."

Do you wish to know that it is as we say? Take examples. Samson, stronger than a lion, harder than rock, who, alone and unarmed, pursued a thousand armed men, grows soft in the embraces of Delilah. David, chosen according to the heart of the Lord, who had often sung with holy lips of the Christ to come, after he was caught by the nakedness of Bathsheba as he walked upon the roof of his house, joined murder to adultery. Where note this too, briefly, that there is no safe gaze, not even at home. Wherefore, repenting, he speaks to God: \"Against you only have I sinned, and done this evil before you.\" For the king feared no other man. Solomon, through whom Wisdom herself sang, who discoursed from the cedar of Lebanon to the hyssop that grows out of the wall, departed from the Lord because he was a lover of women. And lest anyone trust even in nearness of blood, Amnon the brother burned with unlawful fire for his sister Tamar.

Impose on yourself only as much fasting as you can bear. Let your fasts be pure, chaste, simple, moderate, not superstitious. What profit is it not to eat oil, and to seek out certain troubles and difficulties of foods? Dried figs, pepper, nuts, the fruit of palms, fine flour, honey, pistachios — the whole cultivation of gardens is harassed, that we may not eat the common bread. I hear, moreover, of some who, against the nature of things and of men, drink no water and eat no bread, but sip dainty little broths and crushed herbs and the juice of beets, not from a cup but from a shell. For shame! Do we not blush at follies of this kind, nor weary of the superstition? Besides, we even seek a reputation for abstinence amid delicacies. The strongest fast is water and bread; but because this has no glory, and we all live on bread and water, it is reckoned, as it were, no public and common fast.

Make to yourself friends of the unrighteous mammon, who may receive you into the everlasting tabernacles. Bestow your riches on those who buy not Phasian birds but common bread, who drive out hunger, who do not increase luxury. Understand the needy and the poor. Give to everyone who asks you, but most of all to those of the household of faith: clothe the naked, feed the hungry, visit the sick; as often as you stretch out your hand, think of Christ, and take care lest, while your Lord begs, you increase the riches of strangers.

In comparison indeed with what was said above, the things we are about to say are slight, but even in small things the same spirit is shown. For just as we admire the Creator not only in heaven and earth, in the sun and ocean, in elephants, camels, horses, oxen, leopards, bears, lions, but also in the tiniest animals — the ant, the gnat, flies, little worms, and that kind of creature whose bodies we know better than their names — and venerate the same skill in all, so the mind devoted to Christ is equally intent on greater things and on lesser, knowing that an account must be rendered even for an idle word. He was anxious, therefore, whether the altar gleamed, whether the walls were free of soot, whether the floors were wiped clean, whether there was a doorkeeper frequent at the gate, the curtains always at the doorways, whether the sanctuary was clean, the vessels shining; and his pious solicitude, disposed over all the ceremonies, neglected no duty, lesser or greater. Wherever in the church you sought him, you would find him. Antiquity admires the noble man Quintus Fabius, who is also a writer of Roman history, but who got his name more from painting than from letters; and Scripture testifies that our Bezalel was full of wisdom and the spirit of God, and Hiram too, the son of a Tyrian woman, in that the one fashioned the furniture of the tabernacle, the other of the temple. For just as glad crops and rich fields sometimes luxuriate in stalks and ears, so distinguished talents and a mind full of virtues overflow into the elegance of various arts. Hence among the Greeks that philosopher is praised who boasted that everything he used, even to his cloak and ring, was made by his own hand. This same thing we can say of him too, who would overshade the basilicas of the church and the chapels of the martyrs with various flowers and the foliage of trees and the tendrils of vines, so that whatever pleased in the church, both in arrangement and in appearance, bore witness to the labour and zeal of the presbyter.

This, Fabiola, is the aged gift of my talent that I have given you, these offerings of my duties. We have praised virgins, widows, and married women whose garments have ever been white, who follow the Lamb wherever he goes. Happy the proclamation that is stained by no defilement of the whole life! Far off be malice, let envy depart. If the householder is good, why is our eye evil? She who had fallen among robbers was carried back on the shoulders of Christ. There are many mansions with the Father. Where sin abounded, grace did much more abound. To whom more is forgiven, he loves the more.

In place of gems or silk, let her love the divine books, in which let her be pleased not by the variegated painting of gold and Babylonian skin, but by a corrected and learned punctuation according to the faith. Let her learn first the Psalter, let her divert herself with these songs, and in the Proverbs of Solomon let her be trained for life. In Ecclesiastes let her grow accustomed to trample upon the things of the world; in Job let her pursue the examples of virtue and patience. Let her pass to the Gospels, never thereafter to set them down from her hands; let her drink in the Acts of the Apostles and the Epistles with all the will of her heart. And when she has enriched the storehouse of her breast with these riches, let her commit to memory the Prophets and the Heptateuch and the books of Kings and Chronicles and the volumes of Ezra and Esther, that last of all she may learn without danger the Song of Songs, lest, if she read it at the outset, under the carnal words, not understanding the epithalamium of the spiritual nuptials, she be wounded. Let her beware of all apocrypha, and, if ever she should wish to read them, not for the truth of their doctrines but out of reverence for their signs, let her know that they are not of those by whose titles they are inscribed, that many faulty things are mixed in with them, and that it is a matter of great prudence to seek gold in mire. Let her always hold in hand the works of Cyprian; let her run with unstumbling foot through the letters of Athanasius and the books of Hilary. Let her delight in the treatises and the talents of those in whose books the piety of the faith does not waver; let her read the rest so as to judge rather than to follow.

These things I dictated in rapid speech for a brief little night's work, wishing to satisfy the longing of him who asked, and exercising myself as if upon a subject for the schools — for that very day, in the morning, he was knocking at my door who was about to set out — and at the same time, to show my detractors that I too can say whatever comes to my mouth. Hence too I have touched briefly on a few things from the Scriptures, and have not woven my discourse, as I am wont to do in other books, with their flowers. The composition is extemporary, and so poured forth by the light of a little lamp, with such facility, that the hands of the secretaries could not keep pace with my tongue, and the volubility of my speech overwhelmed their signs and shorthand. This I have said for this reason, that whoever does not pardon my talent may pardon at least the time.

While I was a young man, and the deserts of solitude walled me in, I could not bear the incentives of the vices and the ardour of nature; which, though I broke with frequent fastings, yet my mind seethed with thoughts. To subdue it, I gave myself for training to a certain brother who had believed from among the Hebrews, so that, after the subtleties of Quintilian and the rivers of Cicero and the gravity of Fronto and the smoothness of Pliny, I should learn an alphabet and meditate on hissing and panting words. What labour I spent there, what difficulty I endured, how often I despaired and how often I ceased and again began in my contention to learn, my own conscience, who suffered it, is witness, as is that of those who led their life with me. And I give thanks to the Lord that from the bitter seed of letters I gather sweet fruits.

While these things are doing in Jebus, a terrible rumour is brought from the West, that Rome was besieged, and the safety of the citizens redeemed with gold, and that, despoiled, they were surrounded again, so that after their substance they should lose their lives also. My voice sticks, and sobs interrupt the words as I dictate. The city is taken which took the whole world — nay, it perishes by famine before the sword, and scarcely a few were found to be taken. The rage of the starving broke out to unspeakable foods, and they tore one another's limbs, while the mother did not spare the wailing infant and received again into her womb him whom a little before she had brought forth. By night Moab was taken, by night its wall fell. O God, the nations have come into your inheritance, they have polluted your holy temple, they have made Jerusalem a place for the keeping of fruit, they have made the corpses of your servants meat for the birds of heaven, the flesh of your saints for the beasts of the earth. They have poured out their blood like water round about Jerusalem, and there was none to bury them. Who could unfold in speech the destruction of that night, the deaths, or could equal the grief with tears? An ancient city falls, that ruled for many years; everywhere along the streets are scattered lifeless bodies, and throughout the houses, and on every side the image of death.

Meanwhile a certain old woman, who was supported by the resources of the Church, gave back to heaven the spirit that was owed, and, as if by design in the running order of events, her body was laid in the tomb as a substitute. While the light was still uncertain, the devil came in the person of a lictor, looking for the corpse of the slain woman, and asked to be shown the grave; he supposes her to be living, and marvels that she could have died. The fresh turf is shown by the clergy, and the earth lately heaped up is flung back at him with these words as he demands it: "Of course — dig up the bones already buried, make fresh war upon the tomb, and if that is too little, tear her limbs to pieces to be mangled by birds and beasts; one struck seven times must suffer something more than death."

It grieves me to say how many virgins fall daily, how many the Church, our mother, loses from her bosom, above how many stars the proud enemy sets his throne, how many rocks the serpent hollows out and dwells in their holes. You may see very many who become widows before they were brides, covering an unhappy conscience with a lying garb alone, who, unless the swelling of the womb and the wailing of infants betray them, walk with neck erect and dancing feet. Others provide themselves with barrenness beforehand, and commit murder upon a human being not yet sown. Some, when they perceive that they have conceived from their sin, contrive poisons to procure abortion, and frequently die themselves as well, and are led to the dead guilty of three crimes: self-murderesses, adulteresses against Christ, and parricides of a son not yet born. These are they who are wont to say: \"All things are pure to the pure. My conscience is enough for me. God desires a clean heart. Why should I abstain from foods which God created for use?\" And if ever they wish to seem witty and merry and have gorged themselves with wine, joining sacrilege to their drunkenness they say: \"Far be it from me to abstain from the blood of Christ.\" And whomever they see sad and pale, they call wretched and a nun and a Manichee; and rightly so, for to such a way of thinking, fasting is heresy. These are they who walk conspicuously through the public square and with furtive nods of the eyes draw after them a flock of young men, who always hear through the prophet: \"You have the face of a harlot; you are shameless.\" Let there be only a thin line of purple in the dress, and the head loosely bound so that the hair falls down, a cheaper slipper, and the mantle fluttering about the shoulders, tight sleeves clinging to the arms, and a broken gait with sagging knees: this is the whole of virginity with them. Let such women have their own admirers and perish more profitably under the name of virgin: gladly do we fail to please such as these.

Take care that you do not go fowling for the little rumours of men, that you do not exchange an offence against God for the praise of peoples. "If I yet pleased men," says the Apostle, "I should not be the servant of Christ"; he ceased to please men and became a servant of Christ. Through good report and evil, on the right hand and on the left, the soldier of Christ marches; he is neither lifted up by praise nor broken by blame, he is not puffed up by riches, nor cast down by poverty, and he despises both glad things and sad. By day the sun shall not burn him, neither the moon by night. I would not have you pray on the corners of the streets, lest the breath of popular favour break the straight course of your prayers; I would not have you broaden your fringes and, for ostentation, wear pious phylacteries and, with a repugnant conscience, surround yourself with Pharisaic ambition. It is better to carry these things in the heart than on the body, to have God as your supporter, not the gaze of men. Do you wish to know what ornaments the Lord seeks? Have prudence, justice, temperance, fortitude. Be enclosed within these regions of heaven; let this team of four, like a charioteer, bear you, swift, to the goal of Christ. Nothing is more precious than this necklace, nothing more variegated than this variety of gems. On every side you are adorned, girding and protecting; and they are to you both an ornament and a defence: the gems are turned into shields.

Flee the company of young men. Let the roof of your house not look upon the long-haired, the trim, the wanton. Let the singer be driven off as harmful; banish from your dwelling the lute-girls and harp-girls and that whole choir of the devil, like the death-bringing songs of the Sirens. Do not go out again and again into public, and be carried about with the liberty of widows, an army of eunuchs going before you. It is a most wretched custom when the frail sex and the weak age abuses its own discretion and thinks that whatever pleases it is permitted. All things indeed are lawful, but not all things are expedient. Let no curl-headed steward, nor handsome foster-brother, nor fair and ruddy attendant cleave to your side: sometimes the mind of mistresses is judged by the dress of their servants. Seek the society of holy virgins and widows, and, if the necessity of conversing with men presses upon you, do not avoid witnesses, and let there be such confidence in your conversation that, when another enters, you neither take fright nor blush. The face is the mirror of the mind, and the silent eyes confess the secrets of the heart. We have lately seen a scandal flit through the whole East: the age, the dress, the bearing, the gait, the indiscriminate company, the choice banquets, the royal apparel told of the nuptials of Nero and Sardanapalus. Let the wound of others be our caution; When the pestilent man is scourged, the fool will be the wiser. Holy love has no impatience; a false rumour is quickly suppressed, and a later life judges of an earlier. It cannot indeed be that anyone should pass through the courses of this life without the bite of men, and it is the consolation of the worse to carp at the good, while they think the fault of sinners is lessened by the multitude of those who sin; but nevertheless the fire of the stubble quickly subsides, and the overflowing flame, its nourishment failing, gradually dies away. If last year the report lied, or, if indeed it spoke the truth, the vice has ceased, the rumour too will cease. I say this not because I fear anything sinister of you, but because, with the affection of piety, I am fearful even for what is safe. O if you could see your sister, and if it fell to you to hear in person that eloquence of her sacred mouth, you would discern great spirits in a little body, you would hear the whole furniture of the Old and New Testament glowing forth from her heart! She holds fasting for sport, prayer for delight. She holds the timbrel after the example of Miriam, and, when Pharaoh was drowned, leads the choir of virgins, singing: Let us sing to the Lord, for he has been gloriously magnified; the horse and the rider he has thrown into the sea. Such are the psaltery-girls she teaches for Christ, such the lute-girls she trains for the Saviour. So the day, so the night is spent, and, with oil prepared for the lamps, the coming of the Bridegroom is awaited. Imitate therefore your kinswoman also: let Rome have what Bethlehem, narrower than the city of Rome, possesses.

Well done, in virtue. Of one whose beginnings are such, what will the end be? O wretched human condition, and vain is all our living without Christ. Why do you withdraw, why do you turn aside, O speech? For as though we could put off his death and make his life longer, so we fear to come to the end. All flesh is grass, and all its glory as the flower of grass. Where now is that comely face, where the dignity of the whole body, with which, as with a beautiful garment, the beauty of the soul was clothed? It withered, alas, as the lily under the blowing south wind, and the purple of the violet gradually passed into pallor. And when he burned with fevers and the heat drained the fountains of his veins, with weary breath he consoled his sorrowing uncle. His face was glad, and while all around were weeping, he alone smiled. To cast off his cloak, to stretch out his hands, to see what others did not see, and, as if rising to meet them, to greet those who came: you would understand that he was not dying but migrating, and changing his friends, not leaving them. The tears roll down my face, and with hardened mind I cannot disguise the grief I suffer. Who would believe that at such a time he remembered our intimacy, and that, with his soul struggling, he knew the sweetness of our studies? Taking his uncle's hand: "This tunic," he said, "which I used in the ministry of Christ, send to him who is most beloved by me, in age my father, in fellowship my brother, and whatever of affection was owed by you to your nephew, transfer it to him whom you loved equally with me." And with such words he failed, holding his uncle by the hand, touching me in remembrance.

You will answer: "How shall I, a woman of the world, in so great a throng of men at Rome, be able to keep all these things?" Do not, then, take up a burden which you cannot bear; but, after you have weaned her with Isaac and clothed her with Samuel, send her to her grandmother and her aunt. Render the most precious gem to the chamber of Mary, and lay it in the cradle of the wailing Jesus. Let her be nourished in a monastery, let her be among the choirs of virgins, let her not learn to swear, let her think lying sacrilege, let her be ignorant of the world, let her live angelically, let her be in the flesh without the flesh, let her think the whole race of men like herself; and, to be silent about the rest, let her at least free you from the difficulty of guarding and the peril of keeping watch. It is better for you to long for her when absent than to fear at every turn — with whom she speaks, what she says, to whom she nods, whom she gladly looks upon. Hand over the little one to Eustochium, whose very wailing is now a prayer for you, hand her over as a companion, as a future heir of her sanctity. Let her see her, let her love her, let her admire her from her earliest years, whose very speech and dress and gait is a teaching of the virtues. Let her be in the bosom of her grandmother, who may repeat in the granddaughter whatever she sent before in the daughter, who has learned by long use to nourish, to teach, to keep virgins, in whose crown the chastity of the hundredfold number is daily woven. Happy virgin, happy Paula daughter of Toxotius, who through the virtues of her grandmother and aunt is nobler in sanctity than in birth! O if it might fall to you to see your mother-in-law and your kinswoman, and to behold great spirits in little bodies! On account of the modesty implanted in you, I would not doubt that you would go before your daughter and exchange the first sentence of God for the second law of the Gospel. Would that you might count little the longing for other children, and offer yourself rather to God! But because there is a time of embracing and a time to be far from embraces, and the wife has not power over her own body, and let each one, in the calling in which he was called, in that abide with the Lord, and he who is under the yoke ought so to run that he does not leave his companion in the mire, render wholly in your offspring what for the present you have deferred in yourself. Anna, after she offered to the tabernacle the son she had vowed to God, never received him back, thinking it unseemly that a future prophet should grow up in the house of one who still desired to have other children. Finally, after she conceived and bore, she did not dare to approach the temple and appear empty before the Lord, unless she first rendered what she owed, and, such a sacrifice offered, returned home and begot for herself five children, because she had borne the firstborn to God. Do you marvel at the happiness of the holy woman? Imitate her faith. I myself, if you send me Paula, will, an old man, form her stammering words, far more glorious than the philosopher of the world — who instructed not a king of the Macedonians, doomed to perish by Babylonian poison, but a handmaid and bride of Christ, to be offered to the heavenly kingdoms.

I will tell another thing too, which I saw in Egypt. There was a Greek young man in a monastery who by no greatness of continence, by no greatness of work, could extinguish the flame of the flesh. The father of the monastery saved him, when in this peril, by this device. He commands a certain grave man to pursue the man with quarrels and abuse, and, after the injury had been inflicted, to come first to the complaints. The witnesses, when called, spoke for him who had done the insult. He wept against the lie; no one else believed the truth; the father alone cunningly set up his defence, lest the brother should be swallowed up by an excessive sadness. Why say more? Thus a year was passed, at the end of which the young man, being asked about his former thoughts, whether he still endured any trouble, said: "Good heavens, one is not allowed to live, and one wishes to fornicate?" If he had been alone, by what helper would he have overcome?

While meanwhile, amid such confusion of things, the bloody victor enters the house of Marcella too — Let it be lawful for me to speak what I have heard, nay, to relate what holy men saw, who were present and took part, who say that you too were joined with her in the peril — she is said to have received those who entered with undismayed face; and when gold and buried wealth were demanded of her, and she pleaded her cheap tunic in excuse, yet she did not gain credence for her voluntary poverty. Beaten with cudgels and scourges, they say she felt not the torments, but, prostrate, pleaded this with tears, this at their feet — that they should not separate you from her company, that her youth should not endure what an aged age could not fear. Christ softened the hard hearts, and amid the bloody swords piety found a place. And when the barbarians had led both her and you to the basilica of the blessed Paul, that it might show you either safety or a sepulchre, she is said to have broken out into such gladness that she gave thanks to God, that he had kept you whole for her, that captivity had not made her poor, but found her so, that she lacked daily food, that, filled with Christ, she felt not hunger, that she spoke both with voice and deed: Naked came I out of my mother's womb, and naked shall I return. As it seemed good to the Lord, so was it done. Blessed be the name of the Lord.

Confounded by such odium, the executioner withdrew, and the woman was secretly tended at home; and, lest the frequent coming and going of a doctor to the church should open a path to suspicion, she was sent off with her hair cut short, together with some virgins, to a more secluded little farm. There, little by little, with her dress changed to a man's garb, the wound closed into a scar. And — O truly, the height of justice is the height of malice! — after such great miracles, the laws still rage against her.

It shames me to say it — what an outrage! It is sad, but true: from what source has the plague of \"agapetae\" entered the churches? From what source comes the name of wives without marriage? Or rather, from what source this new kind of concubines? I will say more: from what source these one-man harlots? They are kept in the same house, in one bedroom, often in one bed, and they call us suspicious if we suppose anything. A brother deserts his virgin sister, a virgin scorns her unmarried brother, and, while they pretend to be in the same resolve, they seek the spiritual solace of strangers, that they may have carnal commerce at home. Men of this kind God rebukes in the Proverbs of Solomon, saying: \"Will a man bind fire in his bosom, and his garments not be burned? Or will he walk on the coals of fire, and his feet not be scorched?\"

Take care also that you have neither an itching tongue nor itching ears — that is, neither disparage others yourself, nor listen to others disparaging. "You sat," he says, "and spoke against your brother, and laid a stumbling-block against your mother's son; these things you did, and I was silent. You thought iniquity, that I would be like you; I will reprove you, and set you before your own face." It is to be understood: "Your words, and all that you have spoken of others, that by your own sentence you may be judged, being yourself caught in those very things which you reproved in others." Nor indeed is that a just excuse: "When others report a thing to me, I cannot help doing an injury." No one willingly reports to an unwilling hearer. An arrow is never driven into a stone; sometimes, rebounding, it strikes the one who aimed it. Let the slanderer learn, when he sees that you do not gladly listen, not to slander readily. "With slanderers," says Solomon, "do not mingle, for their destruction shall come suddenly, and the ruin of both, who knows it?" — that is, of him who slanders as well as of him who lends his ear to the slanderer.

You have wealth; it is easy for you to supply to the needy the means of sustenance. Let virtue spend what was being prepared for luxury; let no woman who is about to despise marriage fear poverty. Redeem virgins, whom you may lead into the Saviour's chamber; receive widows, whom, like certain violets, you may mingle among the lilies of virgins and the roses of martyrs; in place of the crown of thorns, in which Christ bore the sins of the world, weave such garlands. Let that most noble man, your father, rejoice and assist; let him learn from his daughter what he had learned from his wife. Already his head is white, his knees tremble, his teeth fall out, and he furrows his unseemly brow with wrinkles; death is near at the doors, the pyre is being marked out close by: willing or unwilling, we are old men. Let him prepare for himself the provision needful for a long journey. Let him carry with him what he must leave behind unwillingly; nay rather, let him send on before him to heaven what, if he does not part with it, the earth will take.

I know that you would not have wished thus to prove the love of your fellow-citizens toward you, and that you would rather have sought the affection of your country in prosperity. But a duty of this kind is more pleasant in good fortune, more welcome in ill. The whole city mourned him, all Italy mourned him. The earth received his body, his soul was rendered to Christ. You sought a nephew, the Church a priest. Your successor has gone before you. What you were, he, after you, deserved to be by the judgment of all. And so from one house a double dignity of the episcopate came forth: while in the one there is congratulation that he held it, in the other grief that he was snatched away, that he might not hold it. It is the maxim of Plato that all the life of the wise man is a meditation upon death. The philosophers praise this and bear it to the skies, but far more strongly the Apostle: I die daily, he says, by your glory. It is one thing to attempt, another to do; one thing to live as one about to die, another to die as one about to live. The former is to die from glory; the latter dies ever toward glory. We too, therefore, ought to premeditate in our minds that one day we shall be what — willing or unwilling — cannot be far off. For if we exceeded nine hundred years of life, as the human race lived before the flood, and the times of Methuselah were granted us, yet the past length would be nothing, since it would have ceased to be. For between him who lived ten years and him who lived a thousand, after the same end of life has come and the unrefusable necessity of death, all that has passed is just as much — except that the older man sets out the more laden with the burden of his sins. For wretched mortals, the best day of life flies first; diseases come on, and sad old age, and toil, and the harshness of unrelenting death snatches them away. The poet Naevius says: A mortal must of necessity suffer many ills. Hence antiquity feigned that Niobe, who wept much, was turned into stone, and others into various beasts, and Hecuba into a dog; and Hesiod, lamenting the births of men, rejoices at their funerals; and Ennius prudently says: The common people, he says, in this surpass the king's estate: the people may weep, the king honourably may not. As with a king, so with a bishop — nay, less with a king than with a bishop. For the king rules over the unwilling, the bishop over the willing; the one subjects by terror, the other lords it by service; the one guards bodies unto death, the other preserves souls unto life. Upon you the eyes of all are turned; your house and conduct, set as it were on a watchtower, are the mistress of public discipline. Whatever you do, all think they must do for themselves. Take care that you commit nothing which either those who wish to find fault may seem worthily to have torn apart, or those who wish to imitate you may be compelled to transgress. Conquer as far as you can — nay, more than you can — the softness of your mind, and check the abundantly flowing tears, lest a great affection for a nephew be reckoned, among unbelieving minds, as despair toward God. He is to be longed for by you as one absent, not as one dead, so that you may seem to await him, not to have lost him.

The philosophers of the world are wont to drive out an old love with a new love, as a nail with a nail. This too the seven princes of the Persians did to Ahasuerus, that they might restrain his longing for Queen Vashti by the love of other girls. They remedy a vice with a vice and a sin with a sin; let us overcome vices with the love of the virtues. Decline, he says, from evil and do good; seek peace and pursue it. Unless we hate evil, we cannot love good. Nay rather, good must be done, that we may decline from evil; peace must be sought, that we may flee wars. Nor is it enough to seek it, unless, when found and fleeing, we pursue it with all zeal — that peace which surpasses all understanding, in which is the dwelling of God, as the prophet says: And his place was made in peace; and the pursuit of peace is beautifully named, according to that saying of the Apostle: Pursuing hospitality — so that we may invite guests not with a light and hasty word and, so to speak, with the tips of the lips, but hold them with all the ardour of the mind, as though they carried away with them something of our gain and profit.

After some months, sound, whole, with a vigorous little body, she fell asleep in the Lord, and left you the heir of her little poverty — nay, through you the poor — closing her eyes in your hands, rendering her spirit in your kisses, while amid your tears she smiled with the conscience of a good life and the rewards of things to come. These things to you, venerable Marcella, and these things to you, Principia, my daughter, I have dictated in one short night's work, not with the elegance of eloquence but with the will of a mind most grateful toward you, desiring to please both God and my readers.

See where the sequence of events has drawn me on! For now we have come to the name of our own Evagrius. If I should suppose that I am able to speak of the labour he undertook for Christ, I would have no wisdom; if I should wish to keep wholly silent, I could not, for my voice breaks out into joy. For who is able to celebrate with worthy praise that he rescued Auxentius, brooding over Milan, all but buried by this man's vigilance before he was dead; that the bishop of Rome, already almost caught in the snares of faction, both conquered his adversaries and yet did no harm to the men he had overcome?
But of this I myself, shut out by the narrow limits of space, say nothing, and I leave it to be recorded by others after me.

I content myself only with the end of the present matter: by his diligence he approached the emperor, wearied him with prayers, softened him by the justice of the cause, and won him over by his earnest care, so that he might restore to liberty the woman who had been restored to life.

Therefore, having driven out and banished those women who do not wish to be virgins but to seem so, now all my discourse is directed to you, who, as you have begun to be the first noble virgin of the city of Rome, so much the more must labour, lest you lose both the present goods and those to come. And indeed you have learned the troubles of marriage and the uncertainties of wedlock from a domestic example, since your sister Blesilla, older in age but younger in resolve, after taking a husband, was widowed in the seventh month. O unhappy human condition, ignorant of the future! She lost both the crown of virginity and the pleasure of marriage. And although she holds the second grade of chastity, yet what crosses do you suppose she bears at every moment, seeing daily in her sister what she herself has lost, and, since with greater difficulty she is without the pleasure she has tasted, having a lesser reward of continence? Yet let her too be secure, let her rejoice: the hundredfold and the sixtyfold fruit both spring from the one seed of chastity.

It is your duty to visit the sick, to know the households, the matrons and their children, and not to be ignorant of the secrets of men of rank. Let it therefore be your duty to keep not only your eyes chaste, but your tongue as well. Never discuss the beauty of women, nor let one household learn through you what is going on in another. Hippocrates binds his disciples by an oath before he teaches them, and compels them to swear in his own words; he extorts silence by a solemn pledge; he prescribes their speech, their gait, their dress, and their manners: how much more ought we, to whom the medicine of souls has been entrusted, to love the households of all Christians as our own. Let them know us rather as comforters in their sorrows than as banqueters in their prosperity. The cleric is easily despised who, often invited to dinner, does not refuse.

Young widows are wont — some of whom have already turned back after Satan, when they have wantoned against Christ — being in heat, to say: "My little patrimony perishes daily, the inheritance of my forefathers is squandered, a servant has spoken insolently, a maid has neglected my command. Who will go out into public? Who will answer for the tributes of the fields? Who will educate my little ones? Who will rear my home-born slaves?" And — oh, the wickedness! — they set this up as the reason for marriage, the very thing that alone ought to have hindered the marriage. A mother brings in over her sons not a stepfather but an enemy, not a parent but a tyrant. Inflamed with lust, she forgets her own womb, and amid her little ones, who know not her miseries, she who was lately a new bride is decked out, mourning. Why do you allege your patrimony, why the insolence of the servants? Confess the baseness. No woman takes a husband for this, that she may not sleep with her husband. Or, if indeed lust does not goad you, what so great madness is it to prostitute chastity after the manner of harlots, that riches may be increased, and that, for a cheap and perishable thing, chastity, which is both precious and eternal, should be defiled? If you have children, why do you seek marriage? If you have none, why do you not fear the barrenness you have proved, and prefer an uncertain thing to certain modesty? The marriage-tablets are now drawn up for you, so that after a little while you may be compelled to make a will. The husband's infirmity will be feigned, and what he will wish you, who are to die, to do, he, who is to live, will himself do. Or, if it should happen that you have children by a second husband, there is domestic strife, a war within the household. It will not be permitted you to love your children, nor to look with even eyes upon those whom you have borne. You will hold out food secretly; he will envy the dead, and unless you hate your sons, you will still seem to love their father. But if, having offspring by a former wife, he has brought you into his house, even if you are most gentle, all the comedies and the mime-writers and the common topics of the rhetoricians will declaim against the most cruel stepmother. If the stepson falls ill and his head aches, you will be defamed as a poisoner. If you do not give him food, you will be called cruel; if you give it, a worker of evil. I ask you, what so great good have second marriages that they can outweigh these evils?

But what am I doing, healing a grief which I think is already assuaged both by time and by reason, instead of rather setting before you the recent miseries of kings and the calamities of our own time, so that he who has been deprived of this light is not so much to be mourned as to be congratulated, that he has escaped from such great evils? Constantius, the patron of the Arian heresy, while preparing against an enemy and being borne in haste to battle, dying in the little village of Mopsus, left the empire, to his great grief, to his foe. Julian, the destroyer of his own soul and the butcher of a Christian army, felt Christ in Media, whom he had first denied in Gaul; and while he wished to extend the bounds of the Romans, he lost those already extended. Jovian, having only tasted the goods of royalty, perished, suffocated by the fumes of coals, showing all what human power is. Valentinian, his native soil laid waste and his country left unavenged, was extinguished by a vomiting of blood. His brother Valens, conquered in the Gothic war in Thrace, had there the same place for his death and his sepulchre. Gratian, betrayed by his own army and not received by the cities he came to, was a mockery to his enemy, and the walls of your city, Lyons, bear witness to the traces of the bloody hand. The young Valentinian, almost a boy, after flight, after exile, after recovering the empire with much blood, was slain not far from the city, the conscious witness of his brother's death, and his lifeless corpse was dishonoured by hanging. What shall I say of Procopius, Maximus, Eugenius, who certainly, while they held power, were a terror to nations? All stood captive before the faces of their conquerors, and — what is most wretched for those once most powerful — were pierced first by the ignominy of slavery before the enemy's sword.

No art is learned without a master. Even dumb animals and the herds of wild beasts follow their leaders. Among bees there are chiefs; the cranes follow one in a lettered order. There is one emperor, one judge of a province. Rome, as it was founded, could not have two brothers at once as kings, and is dedicated by parricide. In the womb of Rebecca, Esau and Jacob waged wars. There are single bishops of the churches, single archpresbyters, single archdeacons, and the whole ecclesiastical order rests upon its own rulers. In a ship there is one helmsman, in a house one master; in however great an army the signal of one is awaited. And, that I may not make the reader loathe me by repeating more, through all these things my discourse tends to this: to teach you that you are not to be let go at your own discretion, but ought to live in a monastery under the discipline of one father and in the company of many, that from one you may learn humility, from another patience, that this one may teach you silence, that one gentleness; that you may not do what you wish, may eat what you are bidden, may have as much as you have received, may be clothed in what you have received, may pay the tasks of your work, may be subject to one to whom you do not wish, may come weary to your bed and sleep while walking, may be compelled to rise before sleep is finished, may say a psalm in your turn — in which not the sweetness of the voice but the affection of the mind is sought, as the Apostle writes: I will sing with the spirit, I will sing also with the mind; and: Singing in your hearts; for he had read that it was commanded: Sing psalms wisely — may serve the brethren, may wash the feet of guests, may keep silence when you have suffered an injury, may fear the superior of the monastery as a lord, love him as a parent, may believe that whatever he has commanded is salutary for you, and may not judge of the sentence of your elder, whose duty it is to obey and to fulfil what is commanded, as Moses says: Hear, O Israel, and be silent. Occupied with so great affairs, you will be at leisure for no thoughts; and, while you pass from one thing to another and work succeeds work, you will retain in mind that alone which you are compelled to do.

I do not want you to keep the company of married women, I do not want you to approach the houses of the noble, I do not want you often to see what, in despising, you wished not to be. If little women are wont to applaud themselves over husbands who are judges and set in some dignity, if the ambition of those who pay court runs together to the emperor's wife, why do you do an injury to your own husband? Why, bride of God, do you hasten to a man's wife? Learn in this respect a holy pride; know that you are better than they. And I do not want you only to avoid the company of those who are puffed up by their husbands' honours, whom troops of eunuchs hedge about, and in whose clothes metals are woven, drawn out into thread; but flee also those whom necessity has made widows — not that they ought to have wished for their husbands' death, but that they ought to seize gladly the chance for chastity that is given. But now they only change their dress; the old ambition is not changed. A line of half-men goes before their litters, and their skin, stuffed full, is stretched out with ruddy cheeks, so that you would think they had not lost their husbands but were seeking them. Their house is full of flatterers, full of guests. The clergy themselves — who ought to have been their masters and their fear — kiss the heads of their patronesses and, with hand stretched out, so that you would think they wished to bless them if you did not know better, take a fee for their visit. They meanwhile, who see the priests in need of their protection, are lifted up into pride, and, because, having known the dominion of husbands, they prefer the liberty of widowhood, are called chaste and nuns, and after a doubtful dinner dream of the apostles.

Let us never accept while asking, and rarely while asked. For somehow even the very man who entreats you to take, when you have taken, judges you the cheaper, and, strange to say, admires you the more if you have scorned his request. A preacher of continence, let him not arrange marriages. He who reads the Apostle, "It remains that they that have wives be as though they had none," why does he compel a virgin to marry? He who is a priest of one marriage, why does he exhort a widow to be twice-married? How can men be the agents and stewards of others' houses and estates, who are bidden to despise their own means? To snatch something from a friend is theft; to defraud the Church is sacrilege. To have received what is to be distributed to the poor, and, while many are starving, to be cautious or timid, or — what is most manifest wickedness — to subtract anything from it, surpasses the cruelty of all robbers. I am tortured with hunger, and do you judge how much is enough for my belly? Either distribute at once what you have received, or, if you are a timid steward, dismiss the giver, that he may himself distribute his own. I would not have your little bag full on my occasion. No one can keep my own better than I can. He is the best steward who reserves nothing for himself.

Do we wish to know what widows ought to be? Let us read the Gospel according to Luke: And there was, he says, Anna a prophetess, daughter of Phanuel, of the tribe of Asher. Anna is interpreted "grace"; Phanuel in our tongue sounds "the face of God"; Asher is rendered either "into blessedness" or "into riches." Because, then, from her youth until eighty-four years she had borne the burden of widowhood and did not depart from the temple of God, persevering day and night in fastings and prayers, therefore she merited spiritual grace, and is called the daughter of the face of God, and is reckoned among her forefathers in blessedness and riches. Let us recall the widow of Sarepta, who preferred Elijah's hunger to her own safety and her sons', and, herself about to die that very night with her son, left her guest surviving, choosing rather to lose life than almsgiving, and in a handful of meal prepared for herself a seed-bed of the Lord's harvest. The meal is sown, and a cruse of oil springs up. In Judaea there was a scarcity of grain — for the grain of wheat had there died — and among the Gentiles streams of oil flowed for the widow. We read of Judith — if anyone, however, is willing to receive the volume — a widow worn out with fastings and squalid in mourning dress, who mourned not her dead husband but, in the squalor of her body, sought the coming of her Bridegroom. I see her hand armed with a sword, her right hand bloody; I recognize the head of Holofernes, carried back from the midst of the enemy. A woman conquers men, and chastity beheads lust; and, her dress suddenly changed, she returns to her victorious squalor, cleaner than all the adornments of the world.

Someone may say: "Such is the condition of kings, and lightnings strike the highest mountains." Let me come to private dignities, and I will not speak of those who do not last two years; and, to pass over the rest, it is enough for us to write of the various ends of three recent consulars. Abundantius, in need, is in exile at Pityus; the head of Rufinus was carried on a pike to Constantinople, and his severed right hand, to the disgrace of his insatiable avarice, begged alms from door to door; Timasius, cast down suddenly from the highest step of dignity, thinks himself to have escaped because he lives, inglorious, at Assa. I tell not the calamities of the wretched but the frail state of the human condition — my mind shudders to follow the ruins of our times. It is twenty years and more that between Constantinople and the Julian Alps Roman blood is daily shed. Scythia, Thrace, Macedonia, Thessaly, Dardania, Dacia, Epirus, Dalmatia, and all the Pannonias the Goth, the Sarmatian, the Quadian, the Alan, the Huns, the Vandals, the Marcomanni lay waste, drag off, and plunder. How many matrons, how many virgins of God, and free and noble bodies, have been a sport to these beasts! Bishops taken captive, presbyters slain and clerics of various offices, churches overthrown, horses stabled at the altars of Christ, the relics of martyrs dug up: everywhere mourning, everywhere groaning, and the image of death on every side. The Roman world is falling, and yet our neck, held erect, is not bent. What spirit do you think the Corinthians now have, the Athenians, the Lacedaemonians, the Arcadians, and all Greece, over whom the barbarians rule? And indeed I have named but a few cities, in which there were once no small kingdoms. The East seemed exempt from these evils, and was only dismayed by the reports: behold, last year, from the farthest cliffs of the Caucasus, there were let loose upon us not the wolves of Arabia, but of the north, who in a short time overran so many provinces. How many monasteries were taken, how many waters of rivers were changed by human blood! Antioch was besieged, and the rest of the cities past which flow the Halys, the Cydnus, the Orontes, and the Euphrates. Flocks of captives were dragged off; Arabia, Phoenicia, Palestine, Egypt were captives in their fear. "Not if I had a hundred tongues and a hundred mouths, a voice of iron, could I run through all the names of the punishments." For I have not proposed to write a history, but briefly to weep our own miseries. Otherwise, to set forth these things worthily, even Thucydides and Sallust are mute.

I myself have seen some who, after they renounced the world — in their garments only and in the profession of the voice, not in their possessions — changed nothing of their former conduct. Their household estate was rather increased than diminished; the same services of servants, the same apparatus of the banquet; in glass and an earthen dish gold is eaten, and amid the crowds and swarms of their ministers they claim for themselves the name of solitaries. But those who are poor and of slender little substance, and seem to themselves clever, proceed into public like the floats of processions, that they may exercise a canine eloquence. Others, with shoulders raised on high and croaking I know not what within themselves, with eyes fixed dully on the ground, weigh out swelling words, so that, if you added a herald, you would think the prefecture was advancing. There are those who, from the dampness of their cells and immoderate fastings, the weariness of solitude and excessive reading, while day and night they din in their own ears, are turned to madness and need the remedies of Hippocrates more than our admonitions. Very many cannot do without their former arts and trades, and, their names of traders changed, ply the same commerce, seeking not food and clothing, which the Apostle commands, but greater profits than men of the world. And formerly indeed the rage of sellers was restrained by the aediles, whom the Greeks call agoranomoi, nor was the sin unpunished; but now, under the title of religion, unjust gains are exercised, and the honour of the Christian name makes fraud rather than suffers it. And — which it is shameful to say, but necessary, that at least thus we may blush at our disgrace — publicly stretching out our hands in rags, we hide gold, and, against the opinion of all, we die rich, with full purses, we who lived as though poor. For you, when you are in a monastery, it will not be permitted to do these things; and, the custom gradually growing strong, you will begin to wish what at first you were compelled to do, and your labour will delight you, and, forgetful of the past, you will always pursue the things that are before, by no means considering what evil others do, but what good you ought to do.

Let those be your companions whom you see made thin by fasting, who have pallor on their faces, whom both age and life have approved, who daily sing in their hearts: \"Where do you feed? Where do you lie down at noon?\" — who say from the heart: \"I desire to be dissolved and to be with Christ.\" Be subject to your parents; imitate your Bridegroom. Let going out in public be rare; let your martyrs be sought in your own chamber. There will never be a reason for going out lacking, if you always go out only when it is necessary. Let food be moderate, and let the belly never be filled. For very many there are who, sober from wine, are drunk from the abundance of their food. When you rise at night to prayer, let not indigestion cause you fear, but emptiness. Read more frequently, and learn as much as you can. Let sleep steal upon you holding the book, and let the holy page receive your falling face. Let your fasts be daily and your refreshment shun fullness. It profits nothing to carry an empty belly through two or three days if it is at once overwhelmed, if the fast is made up for by satiety. At once the filled mind grows sluggish, and the watered ground brings forth the thorns of lusts. If ever you feel the outer man sighing for the flower of youth, and, after taking food, the sweet train of lusts shakes you when you have settled yourself on your couch, snatch up the shield of faith, on which the fiery darts of the devil are quenched. \"All of them are adulterous; their hearts are like an oven.\" But you, accompanying the footsteps of Christ and intent on his words, say: \"Was not our heart burning within us on the way, when Jesus opened to us the Scriptures?\" — and that: \"Your word is fiery, and your servant loved it.\" It is hard for the human soul not to love, and it is necessary that our mind be drawn to some affection. The love of the flesh is overcome by the love of the spirit; desire is extinguished by desire. Whatever is lessened on the one side grows on the other. Rather, repeat continually: \"On my bed in the nights I sought him whom my soul loves.\" \"Mortify,\" says the apostle, \"your members which are upon the earth.\" Hence he himself said confidently: \"I live, yet now not I, but Christ lives in me.\" He who mortified his members and walked in an image does not fear to say: \"I have become like a wineskin in the frost; for whatever moisture was in me has been dried up,\" and: \"My knees are weakened by fasting,\" and: \"I have forgotten to eat my bread; from the voice of my groaning my bone has cleaved to my flesh.\"

You have compelled me, dearest Nepotian — now that my little book on virginity, which I wrote at Rome for the holy Eustochium, has been stoned — after ten years to open my mouth again at Bethlehem, and to expose myself to be pierced by all men's tongues. For either I ought to have written nothing, that I might not undergo the judgment of men — which you forbade me to do — or, in writing, I ought to know that the darts of all the evil-speakers will be hurled against us. I beseech them to be quiet and to cease their reviling; for we have written not as adversaries but as friends, nor have we inveighed against those who sin, but warned them not to sin. And we have been stern judges not against them only but against ourselves as well, and, wishing to take the mote from another's eye, we have first cast out our own beam. We have injured no one, no one has been so much as marked by description, no one has my speech assailed by name: the discussion of the vices is general. Whoever shall wish to be angry with me first confesses of himself that he is such a man.

Some, unskilfully, count Deborah too among the widows, and think the leader Barak the son of Deborah, though Scripture records otherwise. For us she shall be named for this: that she was a prophetess and is reckoned in the order of the judges. And because she could say, How sweet are your words to my throat, sweeter than honey and the honeycomb to my mouth, she received the name of "bee," fed on the flowers of the Scriptures, suffused with the fragrance of the Holy Spirit, and composing with prophetic mouth the sweet juices of ambrosia. Naomi, whose name sounds with us "comforted," whom we may interpret "the consoled," her husband and children having died abroad, brought back chastity to her native land, and, sustained by this provision, kept her Moabite daughter-in-law, that the prophecy of Isaiah might be fulfilled: Send forth a lamb, O Lord, the ruler of the earth, from the rock of the desert. I come to the widow in the Gospel, the poor little widow, richer than all the people of Israel, who, taking a grain of mustard seed and putting leaven into the three measures of meal, tempered by the grace of the Holy Spirit the confession of the Father and the Son, and cast two mites into the treasury — whatever she could have in her substance — and offered all her riches in both Testaments of her faith. These are the two seraphim glorifying the Trinity thrice, and laid up in the treasury of the church, whence too, with the tongs of both instruments, the burning coal is taken up that purges the lips of the sinner.

Happy Nepotian, who does not see these things; happy, who does not hear them. Wretched we, who either suffer them, or, suffering, behold our brethren in such great sufferings; and yet we wish to live, and we think those who lack these things rather to be wept for than blessed. We feel God offended long since, and we do not appease him. By our sins the barbarians are strong, by our vices the Roman army is overcome; and, as if this were not enough for disasters, civil wars have consumed almost more than the enemy's sword. Wretched the Israelites, in comparison with whom Nebuchadnezzar is called the servant of God; unhappy we, who so displease God that through the fury of the barbarians his anger rages against us. Hezekiah did penance, and a hundred and eighty-five thousand of the Assyrians were destroyed by one angel in one night; Jehoshaphat sang praises in concert to the Lord, and the Lord conquered for him as he praised; Moses fought against Amalek not with the sword but with prayer. If we wish to be lifted up, let us be cast down. For shame, and the mind stupid even to unbelief! The Roman army, conqueror and lord of the world, is conquered by these men, dreads these men, is terrified at the sight of these men, who cannot walk, who, if they touch the ground, think themselves dead; and we do not understand the words of the prophets: A thousand shall flee, one pursuing; nor do we cut off the causes of the disease, that the disease may likewise be taken away, and at once behold the arrows yielding to the javelins, the tiaras to the helmets, the nags to the war-horses.

Nor indeed be led by the multitude of those who sin, nor be made anxious by the throng of those who perish, so that you silently think: "What? Shall all then perish who dwell in the cities? Behold, they enjoy their own possessions, they minister to the churches, they go to the baths, they do not scorn ointments, and yet they live in the flower of all things." To which I have answered before, and now will answer briefly: that in the present little work I am not disputing about clerics, but instructing a monk. The clerics are holy, and the life of all of them is praiseworthy. So, then, act and live in a monastery that you may deserve to be a cleric, that you may stain your youth with no defilement, that you may proceed to the altar of Christ as a virgin from the bridal-chamber, and may have a good testimony from those outside, and that women may know your name and not know your face. When you come to the perfect age, if only life be your companion, and either the people or the bishop of the city should choose you into the clergy, do the things that are the clerics', and among them follow the better ones, because in every condition and grade the worst are mixed with the best.

Be a cicada of the nights. \"Wash your bed every night; water your couch with tears.\" \"Watch, and be like the sparrow in solitude.\" \"Sing with the spirit, sing also with the mind\": \"Bless the Lord, O my soul, and forget not all his recompenses; who is gracious to all your iniquities, who heals all your infirmities and redeems your life from corruption.\" Which of us can say from the heart: \"For I have eaten ashes like bread and mingled my drink with weeping\"? Is it not to be wept and groaned over, when the serpent invites me again to forbidden foods, when, having cast me out of the paradise of virginity, he wishes to clothe me in the garments of skins which Elijah, returning to paradise, threw down to the ground? What have I to do with pleasure, which perishes in a moment? What with this sweet and deadly song of the sirens? I do not wish to lie under that sentence which was pronounced upon the condemned human race: \"In pain and anxiety you shall bring forth, O woman\" — this law is not mine — \"and your turning shall be to your husband.\" Let her turn to a husband who has not Christ for her husband; and finally, \"by death you shall die\" — such is the end of marriage. My resolve is without sex. Let marriage have its time and its title: for me, virginity is dedicated in Mary and in Christ.

Why should I recall ancient things and bring forth the virtues of women from books, when you can set before your eyes many in the city in which you live, whose example you ought to imitate? And, that I may not seem to run through them one by one in flattery, the holy Marcella suffices for you, who, answering to her stock, told us something from the Gospel. Anna had lived seven years with her husband after her virginity, this woman seven months; the one awaited the coming of Christ, this one holds him whom the other received; the one sang of him as he wailed in the cradle, this one proclaims him triumphant; the one spoke of him to all who awaited the redemption of Jerusalem, this one cries out with the redeemed nations: A brother does not redeem; a man shall redeem, and from another psalm: A man is born in her, and the Most High himself has founded her. I know that about two years ago I published books against Jovinian, in which I crushed, by the authority of the Scriptures, the questions raised on the other side, where the Apostle allows second marriages. And it is not necessary to write the same things over again, since you can borrow from there what has been written. This only, that I may not exceed the measure of a letter, I would have you admonished of: think that you are to die every day, and you will never think of a second marriage.

We have exceeded the measure of consoling, and, while we forbid the mourning of one man's death, we have lamented the dead of the whole world. Xerxes, that most powerful king, who overturned mountains and bridged seas, when from a lofty place he had beheld an infinite multitude of men and an innumerable army, is said to have wept, because after a hundred years none of those whom he then beheld would survive. O if we could climb to such a watchtower, from which we might behold the whole earth beneath our feet! Then I would show you the ruins of the whole world, nations dashed against nations and kingdoms against kingdoms; some tortured, some slain, some overwhelmed by the waves, some dragged into slavery; here a wedding, there a wailing; some being born, others dying; some flowing with riches, others begging; and not the army of Xerxes only, but the men of the whole world, who now live, soon to be gone in a brief space. Speech is overcome by the magnitude of the matter, and all that we say is too little.

Do not leap quickly to writing, and be led by a light madness. Learn for a long time what you may teach. Do not believe your praisers — nay, do not gladly lend your ear to mockers, who, when they have warmed you with flatteries and in a manner made you bereft of mind, if you suddenly look back, you may catch either the necks of storks bent behind you, or an ass's little ears agitated by the hand, or a dog's panting tongue stretched out. Disparage no one, nor think yourself holy if you tear others to pieces. We often accuse what we ourselves do, and, eloquent against ourselves, inveigh against our own vices, judging mute about the eloquent. Grunnius used to advance to speak with a tortoise's gait, and at certain intervals scarcely got out a few words, so that you would think him hiccuping, not speaking out. And yet, when, the table being set, he had laid out a heap of books, with eyebrow drawn up, nostrils contracted, and brow wrinkled, he snapped with two little fingers, by this sign provoking the disciples to listen. Then to pour out sheer trifles and to declaim against individuals; you would say Longinus the critic was there, and the censor of Roman eloquence noting whom he wished and excluding him from the senate of the learned. This man, well-moneyed, was the more pleasing at dinners. Nor is it any wonder, who was wont to bait many, and, a wedge formed of garrulous men clamouring around him, advanced into public, within a Nero, without a Cato, wholly ambiguous, so that out of contrary and diverse natures you would say one monster and a new beast had been compacted, according to that poetic verse: A lion in front, a dragon behind, the very middle a chimera.

Someone may say: \"And do you dare to disparage marriage, which has been blessed by the Lord?\" It is no disparagement of marriage when virginity is set before it. No one compares the bad with the good. Let married women too take pride, since they are second to virgins. \"Grow,\" he says, \"and multiply, and fill the earth.\" Let him grow and multiply who is to fill the earth: your company is in heaven. \"Grow and multiply.\" This edict is fulfilled after paradise, and nakedness, and the fig leaves that foretold the itch of marriage. Let him marry and be given in marriage who eats his bread in the sweat of his face, for whom the earth brings forth thorns and briars, whose grass is choked by brambles: my seed is fruitful with a hundredfold crop. \"Not all receive the word of God, but those to whom it is given.\" Let necessity make another a eunuch; let will make me one. \"There is a time for embracing and a time for keeping the hands from embrace; a time for casting stones and a time for gathering them.\" After sons of Abraham were begotten from the hardness of the nations, the holy stones began to roll over the earth. For they pass through the whirlwinds of this world and are rolled in the chariot of God with the swiftness of wheels. Let them sew tunics who have lost the seamless tunic from above, who delight in the wailing of infants weeping in the very dawn of the light that they are born. Eve was a virgin in paradise: after the garments of skins came the beginning of marriage. Your region is paradise. Keep what you were born, and say: \"Return, my soul, to your rest.\" And that you may know that virginity belongs to nature, marriage to what comes after the fall: virgin flesh is born of marriage, rendering in its fruit what it had lost in its root. \"A rod shall come forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower shall rise from the root.\" The rod is the mother of the Lord, single, pure, sincere, with no germ from without cleaving to it, and, in the likeness of God, fruitful in a single union. The flower of the rod is Christ, saying: \"I am the flower of the field and the lily of the valleys.\" He who in another place is proclaimed a stone cut from the mountain without hands, the prophet signifying that a virgin was to be born of a virgin. For hands are taken to mean the work of marriage, as there: \"His left hand is under my head, and his right hand shall embrace me.\"

To the meaning of this sense agrees also that the animals which were led into the ark by Noah two by two are unclean — an uneven number is clean — that Moses and Joshua the son of Nun are bidden to walk into the holy land with bare feet, and the disciples are appointed to the preaching of the Gospel without the burden of shoes and the bonds of skins; that the soldiers who divided the garments of Jesus by lot had no boots to take. For the Lord could not have what he had forbidden in his servants.

Let us return, then, to ourselves, and, as it were descending from heaven, let us for a little while look upon our own affairs. Do you perceive, I beg you, when you became an infant, when a boy, when a youth, when of robust age, when an old man? Daily we die, daily we are changed, and yet we believe ourselves to be eternal. This very thing that I dictate, that is written, that I read over, that I correct, is drawn from my life. As many as are the points of the scribe's pen, so many are the losses of my days. We write and write back, the letters cross the seas, and, as the keel cleaves its trusting furrows through every wave, the moments of our age are diminished. We have only this gain, that we are joined to one another by the love of Christ. Charity is patient, is kind; charity does not envy, does not act perversely, is not puffed up, bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things; charity never fails. This always lives in the breast; through this our Nepotian, absent, is present, and embraces with both hands those divided by such great spaces of earth. We have a pledge of mutual love. Let us be joined in spirit, bound in affection, and let us imitate in his son the fortitude of mind which the blessed pope Chromatius showed at the death of his brother. Let our little page sing of him, let all our letters sound of him. Whom we cannot hold in body, let us hold in remembrance, and of him with whom we cannot speak, let us never cease to speak.

Never, therefore, may you see such men, nor attach yourself to men of this kind, lest you incline your heart to words of malice and hear: Sitting, you disparaged your brother, and against your mother's son you laid a stumbling-block; and again: The sons of men, their teeth are arms and arrows; and elsewhere: His words are softer than oil, and yet they are darts; and more openly in Ecclesiastes: If a serpent bite in silence, so is he who secretly disparages his brother. But you say: "I myself do not disparage; what can I do when others speak?" These things we hold out to excuse our excuses in sins. Christ is not mocked by craft. By no means is it my sentence, but the Apostle's: Do not err; God is not mocked. He sees in the heart, we in the face. Solomon says in the Proverbs: The north wind scatters clouds, and a sad face the tongues of disparagers. For just as an arrow, if it be shot against a hard material, sometimes returns upon the shooter and wounds the wounder, and that is fulfilled: They were turned to me into a crooked bow; and elsewhere: He who casts a stone on high, it will fall back upon his head — so the disparager, when he sees the sad face of the hearer — nay, not even of the hearer, but of one stopping his ears, that he may not hear the judgment of blood — at once falls silent, his face grows pale, his lips cling together, his saliva dries up. Whence the same wise man says: Do not mingle with disparagers, for their destruction shall come suddenly; and the ruin of both, who knows it? — namely, both of him who speaks and of him who hears the speaker. Truth does not love corners nor seek whisperers. To Timothy it is said: Against a presbyter do not quickly receive an accusation. But him who sins reprove before all, that the rest also may have fear. It is not easy to believe of the perfect age, which both a past life defends and the title of dignity honours; but, since we are men and sometimes, against the maturity of our years, slip into the vices of boys, if you wish me to be corrected when I offend, rebuke me openly, only do not bite me secretly: The just man shall correct me in mercy and rebuke me, but let not the oil of the sinner fatten my head. For whom the Lord loves, he corrects, and scourges every son whom he receives. And through Isaiah God cries: My people, they who call you blessed seduce you and overturn the paths of your feet. For what does it profit me if you report my evils to others, if, without my knowing, you wound another with my sins — nay, with your detractions — and, while you eagerly tell all, so speak to each one as though you had told no other? This is not to amend me, but to satisfy your own vice. The Lord commands that those who sin against us ought to be reproved in secret, or with a witness called in, and, if they refuse to hear, to be referred to the Church, and those obstinate in evil to be held as heathens and publicans.

I praise marriage, I praise wedlock, but because it begets virgins for me: I gather roses from thorns, gold from the earth, the pearl from the shell. \"Will he who ploughs plough all day?\" Will he not also rejoice in the fruit of his labour? Marriage is the more honoured when what is born from it is the more loved. Why do you envy your daughter, mother? She was nourished by your milk, reared from your flesh, grew up in your bosom; you guarded her with watchful affection — and are you indignant that she did not wish to be the wife of a soldier but of a king? She has done you a great benefit: you have begun to be the mother-in-law of God. \"Concerning virgins,\" says the apostle, \"I have no commandment of the Lord.\" Why? Because that he himself should be a virgin was not of any command but of his own will. For we must not listen to those who feign that he had a wife, since, discoursing on continence and urging perpetual chastity, he added: \"But I wish all to be as I myself am,\" and below: \"But I say to the unmarried and to widows: it is good for them if they remain so, as I also do,\" and in another place: \"Have we not the power to lead about a wife as the other apostles do?\" Why has he no commandment of the Lord concerning virginity? Because there is a greater reward in what is not compelled but offered; because, if virginity had been commanded, marriage would have seemed taken away, and it would have been most harsh to compel against nature and to wrest the life of angels from men, and in a manner to condemn what was created.

These things I speak more expressly, that I may free my young man from the itch both of the tongue and of the ears, that, reborn in Christ, I may present him without wrinkle and spot, like a chaste virgin, and holy both in mind and body, lest he glory in the name alone and, the lamp quenched, without the oil of good works, be shut out from the Bridegroom. You have there the holy and most learned bishop Proculus, who with living and present voice may surpass my sheets and direct your way with daily discourses, and not suffer you, by turning aside to the one side or the other, to leave the royal road, by which Israel, hastening to the land of promise, promises that it will pass. And would that the voice of the Church, lamenting together, were heard: Lord, give us peace, for you have rendered all things to us. Would that what we renounce of the world were a matter of will, not of necessity, and that poverty had the glory of being sought, not the torment of being imposed. But, according to the miseries of this time and the swords raging everywhere, he is rich enough who does not lack bread, too powerful who is not compelled to serve. The holy Exuperius, bishop of Toulouse, an imitator of the widow of Sarepta, hungering feeds others, and with patient mouth is tortured by another's fasting and famine, and has spent all his substance on the bowels of Christ.
