Nothing is richer than he who carries the body of the Lord in a wicker basket, the blood in glass, who has cast avarice out of the temple, who, without a scourge and the rebuke of those selling doves — that is, the gifts of the Holy Spirit — overturned the tables of mammon and scattered the money of the money-changers, that the house of God might be called a house of prayer and not a den of robbers. Follow from nearby his footsteps, and those of the others who are like his virtues, whom the priesthood makes both humbler and poorer; or, if you desire perfect things, go out with Abraham from your country and from your kindred, and go where you know not. If you have substance, sell it and give to the poor; if you have it not, you are freed from a great burden; naked, follow the naked Christ. Hard, great, difficult — but the rewards are great.

There was a different happiness under the old law. \"Blessed is he who has seed in Sion and a household in Jerusalem,\" and \"cursed is the barren woman who did not bear,\" and: \"Your sons shall be like young olive plants around your table,\" and the promise of riches, and: \"There shall be none weak among your tribes.\" Now it is said: \"Do not consider yourself a dry tree; you have a place for sons and daughters in the heavens, an everlasting one.\" Now the poor are blessed, and Lazarus is set before the rich man in his purple; now he who is weak is the stronger. The world was empty, and — to say nothing of the types — the only blessing was that of children. Therefore Abraham, already old, is joined to Keturah, and Jacob is bought with mandragoras, and fair Rachel laments her closed womb, in figure of the Church. But little by little, as the harvest grew, the reaper was sent in. Elijah a virgin, Elisha a virgin, and many of the sons of the prophets virgins. To Jeremiah it is said: \"And do you take no wife.\" Sanctified in the womb, with captivity drawing near, he is forbidden to take a wife. The apostle says the same thing in other words: \"I think, then, that this is good because of the present necessity, that it is good for a man so to be.\" What is this necessity that takes away the joys of marriage? \"The time is shortened; it remains that those who have wives be as though they had none.\" Nebuchadnezzar is at hand. The lion has come up from his lair. Of what use to me are marriages that will be slaves to a most proud king? Of what use the little ones, whom the prophet bewails, saying: \"The tongue of the suckling clave to the roof of its mouth in thirst. The little ones asked for bread, and there was none to break it for them\"? As we have said, then, this good of continence was found only in men, and Eve was continually bringing forth in pains. But after a virgin conceived in the womb and bore us a child, whose government is upon his shoulder, the mighty God, the father of the world to come, the curse was loosed. Death through Eve, life through Mary. And therefore the gift of virginity flowed more richly upon women, because it began from a woman. As soon as the Son of God set foot upon the earth, he established for himself a new household, that he who was adored by the angels in heaven might have angels on earth. Then continent Judith cut off the head of Holofernes; then Haman — which is interpreted \"iniquity\" — was burned in his own fire; then James and John, leaving their father, their net, and their boat, followed the Saviour, abandoning together the affection of blood, the bonds of the world, and the care of a household. Then for the first time was heard: \"Whoever wishes to come after me, let him deny himself and take up his cross and follow me.\" For no soldier goes to battle with his wife. The disciple who wished to go to bury his father is not permitted. \"The foxes have holes and the birds of heaven nests; but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head\" — lest perhaps you be saddened if you live in narrow quarters. \"He who is without a wife is anxious about the things of the Lord, how he may please God; but he who has a wife is anxious about the things of this world, how he may please his wife.\" The woman and the virgin are divided: she who is not married thinks of the things of the Lord, that she may be holy in body and spirit; for she who is married thinks of the things of the world, how she may please her husband.

How many troubles marriage has, and by how many anxieties it is bound, I think I have briefly set forth in that book which we published against Helvidius, on the perpetual virginity of blessed Mary. To repeat the same things now would be very long, and, if anyone pleases, he can draw from that little spring. But, lest I seem to have wholly omitted it, I will now say this: that since the apostle bids us pray without ceasing, and one who in marriage pays the debt cannot pray, either we always pray and are virgins, or we cease to pray that we may serve marriage. \"And if a virgin marries,\" he says, \"she does not sin; yet such shall have tribulation of the flesh.\" And at the beginning of the little book I declared beforehand that I would say either nothing at all or little about the straits of marriage, and now I give the same notice. But if it pleases you to know by how many troubles a virgin is free and by how many a wife is bound, read Tertullian's work to a philosopher friend, and the other little books on virginity, and the excellent volume of blessed Cyprian, and the writings of Pope Damasus composed on this matter in verse and prose, and the works which our own Ambrose lately wrote to his sister. In these he has poured himself out with such eloquence that he has sought out, arranged, and expressed whatever pertains to the praise of virgins.

We go forward by a different track: we do not extol virginity, but preserve it. Nor is it enough to know what is good, unless what is chosen is more carefully guarded — for the one is a matter of judgment, the other of labour; and the one is shared with many, the other with few. \"He who perseveres,\" he says, \"to the end shall be saved,\" and: \"Many are called, but few chosen.\" Therefore I charge you before God and Christ Jesus and his chosen angels not lightly to bring out into public the vessels of the temple, which only the priests were allowed to see, lest any profane person look upon the sanctuary of God. Uzzah, touching the ark which was not lawful, was struck down by sudden death. For not even a golden and silver vessel was so dear to God as the temple of a virgin's body. The shadow went before; now is the truth. You indeed speak with simplicity and do not despise even those you do not know, but the eyes of the unchaste see otherwise. They do not know how to consider the beauty of souls, but only of bodies. Hezekiah shows the treasure of God to the Assyrians, but the Assyrians saw what they desired. And so, when Judaea was shaken by frequent wars, the vessels of the Lord were the first to be taken and carried off; and among the banquets and the troops of concubines — since it is the crown of vices to pollute what is honourable — Belshazzar drinks from the cups.

\"Do not incline your ear to evil words.\" Often men who speak something unbecoming test the will of the mind. If you, virgin, listen willingly to what is said, if you dissolve into laughter at every jest, they praise whatever you say, deny whatever you deny. They call you witty and holy and one in whom there is no guile, saying: \"Behold a true handmaid of Christ, behold all simplicity — not like that horrid, ugly, rustic, terrible woman who perhaps for that very reason could not find a husband.\" We are led by a natural evil: we willingly favour our flatterers, and although we answer that we are unworthy, and a warm blush floods our face, yet within the soul rejoices at its own praise. The bride of Christ is the ark of the covenant, gilded within and without, the guardian of the law of the Lord. As in that there was nothing but the tables of the covenant, so in you let there be no thought from without. Upon this mercy-seat, as upon the cherubim, the Lord wishes to sit. He sends his disciples to loose you from worldly cares upon an ass's colt, that, leaving the straw and bricks of Egypt, you may follow Moses into the wilderness and enter the land of promise. Let there be no one to forbid — not mother, not sister, kinswoman, brother: the Lord has need of you. And if they should wish to hinder, let them fear the scourges of Pharaoh, who, unwilling to let the people of God go to worship him, suffered the things that are written. Jesus, entering the temple, cast out all that was not of the temple. For God is jealous, and does not wish his Father's house to become a den of thieves. Otherwise, where coins are counted, where there are cages of doves and simplicity is slain, where in a virgin's breast the care of worldly affairs seethes, at once the veil of the temple is rent; the Bridegroom rises in anger and says: \"Your house shall be left to you desolate.\" Read the Gospel and see how Mary, sitting at the feet of the Lord, is set before the zeal of Martha — and certainly Martha was with diligent hospitality preparing a meal for the Lord and the disciples: \"Martha, Martha,\" he says, \"you are anxious and troubled about many things; but few things are necessary, or one. Mary has chosen the good part, which shall not be taken from her.\" Be you too a Mary; prefer doctrine to food. Let your sisters run about and seek how to have Christ as a guest; do you, once the burden of the world has been cast off, sit at the Lord's feet and say: \"I have found him whom my soul sought; I will hold him and not let him go,\" and let him answer: \"One is my dove, my perfect one; she is the only one of her mother, the chosen of her that bore her\" — namely, the heavenly Jerusalem.

Let the secrecy of your chamber always guard you; let the Bridegroom always play with you within. You pray: you speak to the Bridegroom; you read: he speaks to you. And when sleep overcomes you, he will come behind the wall and put his hand through the opening and touch your belly, and, trembling, you will rise and say: \"I am wounded with love,\" and again you will hear from him: \"A garden enclosed is my sister, my bride; a garden enclosed, a fountain sealed.\" Take care not to go out of the house, not to wish to see the daughters of a foreign land, though you have patriarchs for brothers and rejoice in Israel for a parent: Dinah, going out, is corrupted. I do not want you to seek the Bridegroom through the streets, I do not want you to go round the corners of the city. You may say: \"I will rise and go about the city, in the market-place and in the streets, and seek him whom my soul loves,\" and you may ask: \"Have you seen him whom my soul loves?\" — no one will deign to answer you. The Bridegroom cannot be found in the streets — \"Strait and narrow is the way that leads to life\" — and indeed it follows: \"I sought him and did not find him; I called him and he did not answer me.\" And would that it were enough not to have found him. You will be wounded, you will be stripped, and groaning you will tell: \"The watchmen who go about the city found me; they struck me, they wounded me, they took my veil from me.\" But if she who had said, \"I sleep, and my heart wakes,\" and, \"My kinsman is a little bundle of myrrh to me; he shall lodge between my breasts,\" suffers this in going out, what shall become of us who are still of youth, who remain outside while the bride enters with the Bridegroom? Jesus is jealous; he does not want your face to be seen by others. Though you should excuse yourself and plead: \"I covered my face with a drawn veil; I sought you, I said to you: Tell me, you whom my soul loves, where you feed, where you lie down at noon, lest I become as one veiled over the flocks of your companions\" — he will be indignant, he will swell with anger, and will say: \"If you do not know yourself, O fairest among women, go out in the footsteps of the flocks and feed your kids in the tents of the shepherds.\" Though you be fair, he says, and your beauty be loved by the Bridegroom above all women, yet unless you know yourself and guard your heart with all watchfulness, unless you flee the eyes of young men, you will go out from my chamber and feed the kids that are to stand on the left.

Therefore, my Eustochium, daughter, lady, fellow-servant, sister — for one name is of age, another of merit; the one is of religion, the other of love — hear Isaiah speaking: \"My people, enter into your chambers, shut your door, hide yourself a little, a very little, until the wrath of the Lord pass by.\" Let the foolish virgins wander outside; be you within with the Bridegroom, for, if you shut the door and according to the Gospel precept pray to your Father in secret, he will come and knock and say: \"Behold, I stand before the door and knock. If anyone open to me, I will enter and sup with him, and he with me.\" And you will at once answer anxiously: \"It is the voice of my kinsman knocking: Open to me, my sister, my neighbour, my dove, my perfect one.\" Nor is there reason for you to say: \"I have stripped off my tunic; how shall I put it on? I have washed my feet; how shall I soil them?\" Rise at once and open, lest while you delay he pass by and you afterward complain, saying: \"I opened to my kinsman; my kinsman had passed by.\" For what need is there that the doors of your heart be shut to the Bridegroom? Let them be opened to Christ, shut to the devil, according to that: \"If the spirit of one who has power ascends upon you, do not give place to him.\" Daniel in his upper room — for he could not stay in a lowly place — had his windows open toward Jerusalem: do you too have your windows open, but those by which the light may enter, by which you may see the city of God. Do not open those windows of which it is said: \"Death has entered through your windows.\"

This too you must avoid more cautiously: that you be not seized by the ardour of vainglory. \"How,\" says Jesus, \"can you believe, you who receive glory from men?\" See what an evil it is, which he who has it cannot believe. But let us say: \"For you are my glorying,\" and: \"He who glories, let him glory in the Lord,\" and: \"If I still pleased men, I should not be a servant of Christ,\" and: \"Far be it from me to glory, save in the cross of my Lord Jesus Christ, through whom the world is crucified to me and I to the world,\" and that: \"In you we shall be praised all the day,\" and: \"In the Lord shall my soul be praised.\" When you give alms, let God alone see. When you fast, let your face be joyful. Let your dress be neither too clean nor squalid, and not remarkable for any difference, lest the passing crowd halt to look at you and you be pointed at with the finger. A brother is dead, a sister's body must be carried to burial: take care, lest, while you do this too often, you yourself die. Do not wish to seem too religious nor more humble than is necessary, lest by fleeing glory you seek it. For very many, while shunning witnesses of their poverty, mercy, and fasting, desire to please in this very thing, that they despise to please; and, in a wondrous manner, praise, while it is shunned, is sought after. Of the other passions in which the mind of man rejoices, sickens, hopes, and fears, I find more men free; from this fault very few are who have been without it, and he is the best who, as in a fair body, is sprinkled only with the rare blemish of a mole.

And indeed I do not warn you not to glory in riches, not to boast of nobility of birth, not to set yourself before others: I know your humility, I know that you say from the heart: \"Lord, my heart is not lifted up, nor are my eyes raised high.\" I know that pride, by which the devil fell, has no place at all either with you or with your mother. Therefore I have refrained from writing about it. For it is most foolish to teach what he whom you teach already knows. But let not this very thing breed boastfulness in you, that you have despised the boastfulness of the world; let no silent thought creep in, that, because you have ceased to please in gilded clothes, you try to please in squalor; and that, when you come into an assembly of brothers or sisters, you sit on a lowly stool, plead that you are unworthy, deliberately make your voice faint as though spent with fasting, and, imitating the gait of one fainting, lean on another's shoulders. For there are some who disfigure their faces that they may appear to men to be fasting; who, as soon as they see anyone, groan, lower their brows, and with covered face scarcely free one eye to see; their dress is dark, their girdle of sackcloth, and their hands and feet are dirty; only the belly, since it cannot be seen, seethes with food. To these is daily sung that psalm: \"God has scattered the bones of those who please themselves.\" Others, in a man's garb, with changed dress, blush to be the women they were born, cut off their hair, and shamelessly raise eunuch faces. There are those who clothe themselves in haircloth and in cunningly made cowls and, that they may return to infancy, imitate owls and screech-owls.

But that I may not seem to dispute only about women, flee men also whom you see in chains, who have womanish hair contrary to the apostle, the beards of goats, a black cloak, and bare feet hardened to the cold. All these are tokens of the devil. Such a man Rome once bewailed in Antimus, such of late in Sophronius. These men, after they have entered the houses of the noble and deceived little women laden with sins, ever learning and never coming to the knowledge of the truth, feign sadness, and, as though by long fasting, prolong their stolen meals of the night; I am ashamed to say the rest, lest I seem to inveigh rather than to admonish.

There are others — I speak of men of my own order — who seek the presbyterate and the diaconate for this reason, that they may see women more freely. All their care is for their clothes, that they smell well, that the foot does not slap in a loose shoe. Their hair is curled with the mark of the curling-iron, their fingers gleam with rings, and, lest the road, being damper, splash them, they scarcely press the tips of their toes. When you see such men, count them bridegrooms rather than clergy. Some have set all their study and life upon this, to know the names, the houses, and the manners of married women. Of these I will briefly and concisely describe one who is the chief master of this art, that, the master being known, you may the more easily recognize the disciples. He rises in haste with the sun; the order of his greetings is arranged; he seeks out the short cuts of the streets, and almost into the very bedchambers of the sleeping the importunate old man pushes his way. If he sees a cushion, an elegant napkin, or any piece of household furniture, he praises it, marvels at it, handles it, and, lamenting that he is in need of these things, does not so much obtain as extort them, because each woman fears to offend the city's courier. To him chastity is an enemy, fasting an enemy; he tests a luncheon by its savours, and the fattened bird commonly called the \"chick-clucker.\" His tongue is barbarous and impudent and always armed for abuse. Wherever you turn, he is the first in your face. Whatever new thing has sounded abroad, he is either the author or the exaggerator of the report. His horses are changed at every hour, so sleek, so spirited, that you would think him a brother of the Thracian king.

The cunning enemy fights with various ambushes. \"The serpent was wiser than all the beasts which the Lord God had made upon the earth.\" Hence the apostle too says: \"We are not ignorant of his devices.\" Neither affected squalor nor exquisite neatness befits Christians. If you are ignorant of anything, if you doubt anything from the Scriptures, ask one whom his life commends, whom his age excuses, whose reputation does not reject, who can say: \"For I have betrothed you to one husband, to present you a chaste virgin to Christ.\" Or if there is no one who can explain, it is better to be secure in not knowing something than to learn it with danger. Remember that you walk in the midst of snares, and that many veteran virgins have lost from their hands the unquestioned crown of chastity on the very threshold of death. If you have any maidservants as companions of your resolve, do not be lifted up against them, do not be puffed up as a mistress. You have begun to have one Bridegroom, you sing psalms to Christ together, you receive the body together — why should the table be different? Let others too be challenged. Let the honour of virgins be an invitation to the rest. But if you perceive any one weaker in faith, take her up, console her, coax her, and make her chastity your gain. If any one pretends, fleeing servitude, read to her openly the apostle: \"It is better to marry than to burn.\" But those virgins and widows who, idle and curious, go around the houses of married women, who, with the blush of their brow worn away, have outdone the parasites of the mimes — cast them off like certain plagues. \"Evil conversations corrupt good manners.\" Their only care is for the belly and what is next to the belly. Such women are wont to exhort and say: \"My little pet, use your goods and live while you live,\" and: \"Are you keeping it for your children?\" Wine-bibbing and lascivious, they insinuate every evil, and soften even hearts of iron to delights; and when they have lived wantonly against Christ, they wish to marry, having condemnation because they have made void their first faith.

Do not wish to seem too eloquent, nor to play with metre in lyric songs. Do not, with delicate taste, follow the enfeebled lisping of married women, who now with clenched teeth, now with loosened lips, govern a stammering tongue into half-formed words, thinking everything rustic that is natural. So pleasing to them is adultery even of the tongue. \"For what fellowship has light with darkness, what agreement has Christ with Belial?\" What has Horace to do with the psalter? What Virgil with the Gospels? What Cicero with the apostle? Is not a brother scandalized if he sees you reclining in an idol's temple? And although all things are pure to the pure, and nothing is to be rejected that is received with thanksgiving, yet we ought not to drink at once the cup of Christ and the cup of demons. Let me tell you the story of my own misfortune.

When, many years ago, for the sake of the kingdom of heaven I had cut myself off from home, parents, sister, kindred, and — what is harder than these — from the custom of more delicate food, and was going to Jerusalem to do my service, I could not do without the library which I had put together for myself at Rome with the utmost zeal and labour. And so, wretched man, I would fast that I might read Cicero. After the frequent vigils of the nights, after the tears which the remembrance of past sins wrung from the depths of my heart, I would take Plautus in hand. If ever, returning to myself, I began to read the prophet, the uncultured speech made me shudder, and because I did not see the light with my blind eyes, I thought the fault was not in my eyes but in the sun. While the old serpent thus mocked me, about the middle of Lent a fever, poured into my marrow, invaded my exhausted body and, without any respite — what would be incredible even to tell — so fed upon my unhappy limbs that I scarcely clung to my bones. Meanwhile my funeral was being prepared, and the vital warmth of the soul, while my whole body was now growing cold, throbbed only in my breast, which was still warm; when suddenly, snatched up in the spirit, I was dragged before the tribunal of the Judge, where there was such light and such brightness from the splendour of those standing around that, cast down upon the ground, I did not dare to look up. Being asked my condition, I answered that I was a Christian. And he who presided said: \"You lie; you are a Ciceronian, not a Christian; for where your treasure is, there is your heart also.\" At once I was struck dumb, and amid the blows — for he had ordered me to be beaten — I was tortured more by the fire of conscience, pondering with myself that verse: \"And in hell who will confess to you?\" Yet I began to cry out and to say, wailing: \"Have mercy on me, Lord, have mercy on me.\" This cry resounded amid the scourges. At last those who stood by, falling at the knees of the one presiding, prayed that he would grant pardon to my youth, that he would give place of repentance to my error, exacting torment thereafter if I should ever again read the books of pagan literature. I, who under such constraint would have been willing to promise even greater things, began to swear and, calling upon his name, to say: \"Lord, if I ever again possess worldly books, if I read them, I have denied you.\"

Dismissed on these terms of the oath, I returned to the upper world, and, to the wonder of all, opened my eyes, so drenched with such a flood of tears that even the unbelieving were brought to faith by my grief. Nor indeed had it been a slumber or empty dreams, by which we are often deluded. The tribunal before which I lay is witness, the judgment which I feared is witness — may it never be my lot to undergo such an inquiry! — that I had bruised shoulders, that I felt the blows after my sleep, and that thereafter I read the things of God with as much zeal as I had not read mortal things before.

You must also avoid the evil of avarice — not that you may not covet what belongs to others (for that the public laws too punish), but that you may not keep your own things, which are another's. \"If you have not been faithful in what is another's,\" he says, \"who will give you what is your own?\" The weights of gold and silver are another's to us; our possession is spiritual, of which it is said elsewhere: \"The redemption of a man is his own riches.\" \"No one can serve two masters; for either he will hate the one and love the other, or he will bear with the one and despise the other. You cannot serve God and mammon\" — that is, riches. For in the pagan tongue of the Syrians riches are called mammon. The thought of food is the thorns of faith, the root of avarice, the care of the heathen. But you will say: \"I am a delicate girl, and I cannot labour with my own hands. If I come to old age, if I begin to be ill, who will pity me?\" Hear Jesus speaking to the apostles: \"Do not think in your hearts what you shall eat, nor for your body what you shall put on. Is not the soul more than food, and the body more than clothing? Look at the birds of heaven, for they neither sow nor reap nor gather into barns, and your heavenly Father feeds them.\" If clothing is lacking, the lilies will be set before you; if you are hungry, you will hear the poor and the hungry called blessed; if any pain afflicts you, read: \"For this I am well pleased in my infirmities,\" and: \"There was given to me a goad of my flesh, an angel of Satan, to buffet me, lest I be exalted.\" Rejoice in all the judgments of God; \"for the daughters of Judah rejoiced in all your judgments, O Lord.\" Let that word always sound in your mouth: \"Naked I came forth from my mother's womb, and naked shall I return,\" and: \"We brought nothing into this world, and we can carry nothing away.\"

But now you may see very many cramming their wardrobes with clothes, changing their tunics daily, and yet unable to overcome the moths. She who is more religious wears out one garment and trails her rags from full chests. Parchment is dyed purple, gold is melted into letters, the books are clothed with gems, and before the doors Christ dies naked and in want. When she stretches out her hand, the trumpets sound; when she calls to a love-feast, a crier is hired. I saw lately — I keep silent the names, lest you think it a satire — a most noble of Roman women, in the basilica of blessed Peter, with half-men going before her, distributing single coins to the poor with her own hand, that she might be thought more religious. Meanwhile — as it is very easy to know by experience — a certain old woman, covered with years and rags, ran on ahead to receive a second coin; and when she came to her in due order, a fist is offered instead of a penny, and for so great a crime blood is shed.

\"The root of all evils is avarice,\" and therefore it is called by the apostle \"the service of idols.\" \"Seek first the kingdom of God, and all these things shall be added to you.\" \"The Lord will not slay the soul of the just with hunger.\" \"I have been young and now am old, and I have not seen the just man forsaken, nor his seed seeking bread.\" Elijah is fed by ministering ravens; the widow of Zarephath, herself about to die that night with her sons, feeds the prophet in her hunger, and, in a wondrous manner, with her jar filled, he who had come to be fed feeds her. \"Silver and gold,\" says Peter the apostle, \"I do not have; but what I have, this I give you. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, rise and walk.\" But now many, though they say nothing in word, speak by their deed: \"Faith and mercy I do not have; but what I have, gold and silver, I do not give you.\" \"Having food and clothing, with these we are content.\" Hear what Jacob asks in his prayer: \"If the Lord God will be with me and keep me in this way by which I journey, and give me bread to eat and a garment to put on.\" He prayed only for what is necessary, and after twenty years returns to the land of Canaan rich as a lord and richer as a father. Endless examples from the Scriptures abound, which teach that avarice too must be fled.

But since this is now said of it in passing, and is reserved, if Christ grant it, for its own volume, I will relate what happened not many years ago at Nitria. A certain one of the brethren, more sparing than avaricious, and not knowing that the Lord was sold for thirty pieces of silver, left at his death a hundred solidi which he had earned by weaving linen. A council was held among the monks — for in that same place about five thousand dwell in separate cells — as to what should be done. Some said the money should be distributed to the poor, others that it should be given to the Church, some that it should be sent back to his relatives. But Macarius and Pambo and Isidore and the others whom they call \"fathers,\" the Holy Spirit speaking in them, decreed that it should be buried with its owner, saying: \"Your money be with you unto perdition.\" Nor let anyone think this was done cruelly: so great a terror seized them all throughout Egypt that to have left even a single solidus was a crime.

And since we have made mention of monks, and I know that you gladly hear what is holy, lend me your ear a little. There are three kinds of monks in Egypt: the cenobium, which in the native tongue they call \"sauhes,\" and which we may call \"those living in common\"; the anchorites, who dwell alone through the deserts and are named from this, that they have withdrawn far from men; and the third kind is that which they call \"remnuoth,\" the worst and most neglected, and which in our province is either the only or the chief one. These live two or three together, and not many more, living by their own will and authority, and they bring into the common stock parts of what each has earned, so that they may have food in common. But they dwell for the most part in cities and fortified places, and, as if it were the skill that were holy, not the life, whatever they sell is of a higher price. Among these there are often quarrels, for, living by their own provision, they do not endure to be subject to anyone. In truth they are wont to contend in fasting and make a matter of secrecy into a victory. Among them everything is affected: loose sleeves, billowing boots, coarser dress, frequent sighs, the visiting of virgins, the disparaging of clergy; and if ever a feast-day comes, they gorge themselves to vomiting.

Having banished these as certain plagues, let us come to those who live more numerously in common, that is, those whom we have said are called the cenobium. The first bond among them is to obey their superiors and to do whatever they command. They are divided into decuries and centuries, so that the tenth man presides over nine men, and again the hundredth has ten such superiors under him. They remain apart, but with their cells joined. Until the ninth hour it is as a court vacation: no one goes to another except those whom we have called \"deans,\" so that, if anyone perhaps wavers in his thoughts, he may comfort him with his words. After the ninth hour they come together in common, the psalms resound, the Scriptures are recited according to custom, and, the prayers being finished and all sitting down, the one whom they call \"father\" begins to discourse. While he speaks, such silence reigns that no one dares to look at another, no one to clear his throat. The speaker's praise is in the weeping of the hearers. Silently the tears roll down their faces, and the grief does not even break out into sobs. But when he begins to announce the kingdom of Christ, the future blessedness, and the glory to come, you may see all, with a moderate sighing and eyes lifted to heaven, say within themselves: \"Who will give me wings like a dove's, and I will fly away and be at rest?\" After this the assembly is dissolved, and each decury goes with its father to the tables, at which they minister in turn through the several weeks. There is no noise at the food, no one talks while eating. They live on bread, vegetables, and greens, seasoned with salt and oil. Wine is taken only by the old men, for whom, and for the children, a luncheon is often provided, that the wearied age of the one may be sustained and the beginning age of the other not broken. Then they rise together, and, a hymn being said, return to their lodgings. There each man talks with his own until evening and says: \"Did you see this man and that, how much grace is in him, what silence, what a moderate gait?\" If they see one weak, they console him; if one fervent in the love of God, they exhort him to zeal. And because at night, apart from the public prayers, each man keeps watch in his own cell, they go around the cells of each and, with ear set close, diligently examine what they are doing. Whomever they catch more sluggish, they do not rebuke, but, concealing what they know, they visit him more often and, beginning first themselves, provoke him to pray rather than compel him. The day's work is fixed, which, when handed to the dean, is brought to the steward, who himself, every month, gives account with great trembling to the father of all. By him, too, the foods, when they are made, are tasted; and since it is not lawful for anyone to say, \"I have no tunic or cloak or mat woven of rushes,\" he so manages all things that no one asks for anything, no one lacks anything. But if anyone begins to fall sick, he is moved to a more spacious infirmary and is cherished by so great a service of the old men that he seeks neither the delights of cities nor a mother's affection. On the Lord's days they give themselves only to prayer and readings — which indeed they do at all times when their little tasks are finished. Daily something is learned from the Scriptures. The fasting of the whole year is equal, except for Lent, in which alone it is granted to live more strictly. At Pentecost the dinners are changed into luncheons, that both the ecclesiastical tradition may be satisfied and they may not burden the belly with doubled food. Such are the Essenes whom Philo, the imitator of Plato's style, and such as Josephus, the Greek Livy, describes in the second book of the history of the Jewish captivity.

But since, writing now of virgins, I have disputed almost superfluously of monks, I will come to the third kind, whom they call anchorites, and who, going out from the cenobiums, carry nothing more into the deserts than bread and salt. The author of this life was Paul, its illustrator Antony, and — to ascend to higher things — its prince was John the Baptist. Such a man the prophet Jeremiah too describes, saying: \"It is good for a man when he has borne the yoke from his youth. He shall sit alone and be silent, because he has lifted the yoke upon himself; he shall give his cheek to the one who strikes him, he shall be filled with reproaches, because the Lord will not cast off for ever.\" Their labour and their manner of life, in the flesh but not of the flesh, I will set forth at another time, if you wish. Now let me return to the matter, for, discoursing of avarice, I had turned to the monks. Setting their example before you, you will despise not gold and silver and the other riches only, but the very earth and heaven, and, joined to Christ, you will sing: \"The Lord is my portion.\"

After this, although the apostle bids us pray without ceasing, and to the saints even sleep itself is a prayer, yet we ought to have set hours for prayer, so that, if perhaps we have been detained by some work, the time itself may remind us of our duty: the third hour, the sixth, the ninth, and also daybreak and evening — there is no one who does not know these. Let no food be taken by you without prayer first sent up, nor let you withdraw from the table without thanks being rendered to the Creator. In the night we must rise two or three times and go over those parts of the Scriptures that we hold by memory. Let prayer arm us as we go out of our lodging; let prayer meet us as we return from the street before any sitting down; nor let the little body rest before the soul is fed. At every act, at every step, let the hand trace the cross. Disparage no one, nor lay a stumbling-block against the son of your mother. \"Who are you, to judge another's servant? To his own master he stands or falls; but he shall stand, for God is able to make him stand.\" Nor, if you have fasted two days, think yourself better than one who has not fasted. You fast and are angry; he eats and perhaps speaks gently; you digest your mental vexation and the hunger of your belly by quarrelling; he is more moderately fed and gives thanks to God. Hence Isaiah cries daily: \"Such a fast I have not chosen, says the Lord,\" and again: \"For in the days of your fasts your own wills are found, and you goad all who go under your power. If you fast for strifes and disputes and strike the humble with your fists, why do you fast for me?\" What can that fast be whose anger — I will not say night seizes, but a whole month leaves behind? Considering yourself, do not glory in another's ruin, but in your own work.

Nor set before yourself the example of those women who, making provision for the flesh, reckon up the incomes of their possessions and the daily expenses of the household. For the eleven apostles were not broken by the treachery of Judas, nor, when Phygellus and Alexander made shipwreck, did the rest halt from the course of faith. And do not say: \"This woman and that enjoys her own property; she is honoured by all; brothers and sisters come together to her: has she therefore ceased to be a virgin?\" First, it is doubtful whether such a one is a virgin. For God does not see as man sees. Man looks on the face, God looks on the heart. Next, even if she is a virgin in body, whether she is a virgin in spirit I do not know. But the apostle so defined a virgin: \"That she be holy both in body and spirit.\" Finally, let her keep her own glory to herself; let her overcome the verdict of Paul, enjoy her delights, and live. Let us follow better examples. Set before yourself blessed Mary, who was of such great purity that she deserved to be the mother of the Lord. When the angel Gabriel had come down to her in the likeness of a man, saying: \"Hail, full of grace, the Lord is with you,\" she was confounded and could not answer; for never had she been greeted by a man. At last she learns who the messenger is and speaks; and she who had dreaded a man converses fearlessly with the angel. You too can be the mother of the Lord. \"Take yourself a great roll, a new one, and write in it with a man's pen, of one swiftly taking away the spoils,\" and, when you have gone in to the prophetess and conceived in the womb and brought forth a son, say: \"From fear of you, Lord, we have conceived and travailed and brought forth; we have made the spirit of your salvation upon the earth.\" Then your son too will answer you and say: \"Behold my mother and my brethren.\" And, in a wondrous manner, he whom a little before you had described in the breadth of your breast, whom in the newness of your heart you had marked with flying pen, after he has taken spoils from the enemy, after he has stripped principalities and powers and fixed them to the cross, being conceived, grows up, and, made greater, begins to have you as a bride instead of a mother. Great is the labour, but great too is the reward — to be what the martyrs are, to be what the apostles are, to be what Christ is.

All these things, indeed, profit only then, when they are done in the Church, when we celebrate the Passover in one house, if we enter the ark with Noah, if Rahab, justified, holds us within while Jericho perishes. But for the rest, virgins such as are said to be among the various heresies and such as are with the most impure Manichee are to be reckoned harlots, not virgins. For if the devil is the author of their body, how can they honour the workmanship of their enemy? But because they know that the name of virgin is glorious, they cover wolves under sheep's clothing. Antichrist counterfeits Christ, and they clothe the foulness of their life with the false honour of the name. Rejoice, sister, rejoice, daughter, rejoice, my virgin: what others pretend, you have truly begun to be.

All these things which we have set forth will seem hard to one who does not love Christ. But he who has held all the pomp of the world as filth and counted all things under the sun as vain, that he may gain Christ; who has died with his Lord and risen again, and crucified the flesh with its vices and lusts — he will freely proclaim: \"Who shall separate us from the love of Christ? Tribulation? Or distress? Or persecution? Or famine? Or nakedness? Or peril? Or the sword?\" And again: \"For I am sure that neither death nor life, nor angel, nor principality, nor things present, nor things to come, nor might, nor height, nor depth, nor any other creature, shall be able to separate us from the love of God which is in Christ Jesus our Lord.\" The Son of God, for our salvation, was made the son of man; for ten months he waits in the womb to be born; he endures loathings; he is brought forth bloody; he is wrapped in swaddling-clothes; he is mocked with caresses; and he in whose fist the world is enclosed is contained in the narrowness of a manger. I say nothing of how, until his thirtieth year, content with the poverty of his parents, he was obscure: he was beaten and is silent; he is crucified and prays for those who crucify him. \"What, then, shall I render to the Lord for all that he has rendered to me? I will take the cup of salvation and call upon the name of the Lord.\" \"Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints.\" This is the only worthy recompense, when blood is repaid with blood, and we, redeemed by the blood of Christ, gladly fall for our Redeemer. Which of the saints was crowned without a contest? Just Abel is slain; Abraham is in peril of losing his wife; and — that I may not extend the volume to immense length — seek and you will find that each one suffered diverse things. Solomon alone was among delights, and perhaps for that reason he fell. \"For whom the Lord loves he corrects; and he scourges every son whom he receives.\" Is it not better to fight for a short time, to bear the rampart, the arms, the rations, to grow weary under the breastplate, and afterward to rejoice as victor, than, through the impatience of a single hour, to be a slave for ever?

To those who love, nothing is hard; no labour is difficult to one who desires. Consider how much Jacob endured for Rachel, his promised bride. \"And Jacob served,\" says the Scripture, \"for Rachel seven years. And they were in his sight as a few days, because he loved her.\" Hence he himself afterward recalls: \"By day I was scorched with heat, and with frost by night.\" Let us too love Christ, let us always seek his embraces, and everything difficult will seem easy. We shall count brief all things that are long, and, wounded by his dart, at every passing of the hours we say: \"Woe is me, for my pilgrimage is prolonged.\" \"For the sufferings of this world are not worthy to be compared with the glory to come, which shall be revealed in us; because tribulation works patience, and patience trial, and trial hope, and hope does not confound.\" When what you endure seems hard to you, read Paul's second letter to the Corinthians: \"In very many labours, in prisons more abundantly, in stripes beyond measure, in deaths often. From the Jews five times I received forty stripes save one; three times I was beaten with rods, once I was stoned, three times I suffered shipwreck; a night and a day I was in the deep of the sea; in journeys often, in perils of rivers, in perils of robbers, in perils from my own nation, in perils from the Gentiles, in perils in the city, in perils in the desert, in perils in the sea, in perils among false brethren, in labours, in hardships, in many watchings, in hunger and thirst, in very many fastings, in cold and nakedness.\" Which of us can claim for himself even the least portion of this catalogue of virtues? Surely he afterward said confidently: \"I have finished the course, I have kept the faith. There remains for me the crown of righteousness, which the Lord will render to me.\" If the food is too tasteless, we are saddened, and we think we are doing God a favour when we drink water more diluted: the cup is broken, the table overturned, blows resound, and water too lukewarm is avenged like blood. \"The kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and the violent seize it.\" Unless you do violence, you will not take the kingdom of heaven. Unless you knock importunately, you will not receive the bread of the sacrament. Does it not seem to you a matter for the violent, when the flesh longs to be what God is, and to ascend thither, whence the angels fell, to judge the angels?

Go forth, I beg, a little from the body, and paint before your eyes the reward of the present labour, which neither eye has seen nor ear heard nor has entered into the heart of man. What will that day be, when Mary, the mother of the Lord, will come to meet you, attended by choirs of virgins; when, after the Red Sea and Pharaoh drowned with his army, holding the timbrel she will lead the chant for those who answer: \"Let us sing to the Lord, for he is gloriously magnified. The horse and his rider he has cast into the sea\"? Then Thecla will fly joyful into your embraces. Then the Bridegroom himself will come to meet you and say: \"Rise, come, my neighbour, my beautiful one, my dove, for behold, the winter is past, the rain is gone.\" Then the angels will marvel and say: \"Who is this that looks forth like the dawn, beautiful as the moon, chosen as the sun?\" The daughters will see you and praise you, and the queens and concubines will proclaim you blessed. Then another choir of chastity will come to meet you: Sarah will come with the married, Anna the daughter of Phanuel with the widows. They will be, as in different flocks, the mothers of your flesh and of your spirit. The one will rejoice that she bore you; the other will exult that she taught you. Then truly the Lord will mount upon the ass and enter the heavenly Jerusalem. Then the little ones, of whom the Saviour speaks in Isaiah, \"Behold, I and the children whom the Lord has given me,\" lifting up the palms of victory, will sing with one voice: \"Hosanna in the highest; blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord; hosanna in the highest.\" Then the hundred and forty-four thousand will hold harps before the throne and the elders, and will sing a new song, and no one will be able to know that song except the appointed number: \"These are they who have not defiled themselves with women — for they have remained virgins; these are they who follow the Lamb wherever he goes.\" As often as the empty ambition of the world delights you, as often as you see anything glorious in the world, pass over in your mind to paradise; begin to be what you will be, and you will hear from your Bridegroom: \"Set me as a seal upon your heart, as a seal upon your arm,\" and, fortified in deed and mind alike, you will cry out: \"Many waters cannot quench love, and rivers shall not cover it.\"
To Marcella

That we may console the absence of our bodies by the converse of our spirits, let each of us do what he is best able to do. You send gifts, we send back letters of thanks—yet on this condition, that, since these are the gift of veiled virgins, we should show that there are certain mysteries even in these little presents. The sackcloth is a sign of prayer and of fasting; the stools, that the virgin should not move her feet abroad; the tapers, that with the light kindled the coming of the bridegroom may be awaited; the cups show the mortifying of the flesh and a spirit always made ready for martyrdom—for the cup of the Lord that makes us drunk is exceedingly good. And as for the fly-whisks you offer the matrons, to be waved against the little creatures, they signify that luxuries, which are soon to perish along with this perishing world, should be kept far from those women, and that they should drive out the oil of a more agreeable life. Let this be the type of virgins, this the figure of matrons. To us, however, your gifts are fitting, though in a contrary sense: to sit suits the idle, to lie in sackcloth befits the penitent, to have cups belongs to those who drink—though, both because of fears in the night and because of a mind whose conscience is always dreading evil, it is welcome to have kindled the tapers too.
